## The table of a compound statement

Connectives can be nested, with parentheses to show the order, as in $\lnot(P \land Q)$. By convention $\lnot$ applies to the shortest thing after it, so $\lnot P \lor Q$ means $(\lnot P) \lor Q$. Between $\land$ and $\lor$ I will always write the parentheses.

A formula with $n$ different letters has a table with $2^n$ rows, because each letter is independently T or F: 4 rows for two letters, 8 for three. To fill in the table, work from the inside out, one column at a time, each new column computed from columns already there.

Here is a case that matters. An inspector reports of the kitchen: "it is not the case that there is both smoke and heat". That is $\lnot(S \land H)$. What does it tell us about smoke and heat separately?

**Pause and try.** Which of these is the same as $\lnot(P \land Q)$: (a) $\lnot P \land \lnot Q$, or (b) $\lnot P \lor \lnot Q$? Before computing whole tables, test both in the single row where $P$ is true and $Q$ is false.

**Answer.** In that row $P \land Q$ is F, so $\lnot(P \land Q)$ is T. Formula (a) gives $\text{F} \land \text{T}$, which is F, so (a) is not the same. Formula (b) gives $\text{F} \lor \text{T}$, which is T. One row can rule a candidate out but cannot rule one in; the figure checks (b) in the other three rows.

[Figure 3, steps: The truth table of \lnot(P \land Q) built one column at a time, then compared with two candidates. The guess \lnot P \land \lnot Q is wrong in the two middle rows. The formula \lnot P \lor \lnot Q has the same column in every row.]

  - step: Start with the four rows and the innermost part, P and Q. It is true in the first row only.
  - step: Negate that column, flipping each entry. This is the column of not (P and Q).
  - step: The tempting guess, (not P) and (not Q), is true only in the last row. It disagrees in rows two and three.
  - step: The formula (not P) or (not Q) matches in all four rows.
The natural guess is to push the "not" inside the way a minus sign goes through a sum, and it fails. In words: "not both smoky and hot" does not say that the kitchen is neither. It says that at least one of the two is missing, and when a $\lnot$ moves inside the parentheses the $\land$ has to turn into $\lor$.

## Logical equivalence

We have now twice met two formulas with the same column: the two formulas for the menu's "or", and the pair in the figure. That relationship deserves a name.

**Definition.** Two compound statements built from the same letters are **logically equivalent**, written $A \equiv B$, if they have the same truth value in every row of the truth table, that is, for every assignment of truth values to the letters. A compound statement is a **tautology** if it is true in every row, and a **contradiction** if it is false in every row.

For example $P \lor \lnot P$ is a tautology and $P \land \lnot P$ is a contradiction; each has only two rows to check. Note that $\equiv$ is not a fourth connective. $A \equiv B$ is a claim *about* two formulas, and it is either established by comparing tables or refuted by a single row. Because a connective sees only truth values, a part of a formula may always be replaced by an equivalent part without changing the table of the whole. That is what makes the following laws usable as rules of algebra.

**Theorem.** For all statements $P$, $Q$, $R$:

- (Double negation) $\lnot\lnot P \equiv P$.
- (De Morgan's laws) $\lnot(P \land Q) \equiv \lnot P \lor \lnot Q$ and $\lnot(P \lor Q) \equiv \lnot P \land \lnot Q$.
- (Distributive laws) $P \land (Q \lor R) \equiv (P \land Q) \lor (P \land R)$ and $P \lor (Q \land R) \equiv (P \lor Q) \land (P \lor R)$.

**Proof.** Each claim is a finite check.

(1) There are two rows. If $P$ is T then $\lnot P$ is F and $\lnot\lnot P$ is T. If $P$ is F then $\lnot P$ is T and $\lnot\lnot P$ is F.

(2) The first law is the figure above: both columns read T only in the last three rows. For the second, $P \lor Q$ has column T, T, T, F, so $\lnot(P \lor Q)$ has column F, F, F, T. And $\lnot P \land \lnot Q$ is $\text{F} \land \text{F}$, $\text{F} \land \text{T}$, $\text{T} \land \text{F}$, $\text{T} \land \text{T}$ in the four rows, which is F, F, F, T.

(3) The first distributive law is the eight-row table in the next figure. The second needs no new table. Write $P \lor (Q \land R)$ as the negation of its own negation and push the inner $\lnot$ through with De Morgan's laws. That leaves a conjunction inside, to which the first distributive law applies with $\lnot P$, $\lnot Q$, $\lnot R$ in place of $P$, $Q$, $R$. De Morgan and double negation then remove the negations again:

$$
P \lor (Q \land R) \equiv \lnot\bigl(\lnot P \land \lnot(Q \land R)\bigr) \equiv \lnot\bigl(\lnot P \land (\lnot Q \lor \lnot R)\bigr) \equiv \lnot\bigl((\lnot P \land \lnot Q) \lor (\lnot P \land \lnot R)\bigr)
$$

$$
\equiv \lnot(\lnot P \land \lnot Q) \land \lnot(\lnot P \land \lnot R) \equiv (P \lor Q) \land (P \lor R).
$$

[Figure 4, animation: The eight-row truth table that proves the first distributive law, filled in row by row. The column for P \land (Q \lor R) and the column for (P \land Q) \lor (P \land R) agree in all eight rows.]

A table is a proof because it is exhaustive: the rows cover every case there is, and each entry follows from the definitions.

The first distributive law has the shape of $a(b + c) = ab + ac$, with $\land$ as multiplication and $\lor$ as addition. The second has no counterpart in arithmetic, where $a + bc$ is not $(a + b)(a + c)$.

The switch model shows the first law as a fact about wiring. Build one circuit for each side and try all eight switch positions.

[Figure 5, animation: Two circuits for the two sides of the distributive law, run through all eight positions of the switches P, Q, R. The two switches marked P move together. The lamps are lit in exactly the same positions.]

To an engineer the equivalence says the two circuits are interchangeable, and the left one is cheaper, with three switches where the right one needs four.

## Venn diagrams are truth tables too

There is a third way to see these laws, and it is the one most people meet first. Draw a box for all the situations under discussion, a circle enclosing those in which $P$ is true, and a second circle enclosing those in which $Q$ is true. Then $P \land Q$ is the overlap of the circles, $P \lor Q$ is everything inside at least one of them, and $\lnot P$ is everything outside the circle for $P$.

[Figure 6, steps: De Morgan's law on a Venn diagram. The two circles cut the box into four regions, one for each row of the truth table. The region for \lnot(P \land Q) is everything except the overlap, and so is "outside P" together with "outside Q".]

  - step: The circles cut the box into four regions, labeled with the truth values of P and Q.
  - step: P and Q is true in the overlap, the region T T.
  - step: Its negation is true everywhere else: the other three regions.
  - step: Start again. Not P is the two regions outside the circle for P.
  - step: Add the regions outside the circle for Q. Together they cover everything except the overlap.
The picture is a proof, provided you see why. The four regions are the four rows, and shading a region is writing T in that row. A Venn argument is a truth table drawn in the plane, so it can be trusted exactly when the drawing contains a region for every combination of truth values. Two overlapping circles give all 4 combinations, and three in the usual arrangement give all 8. Four circles cannot give all 16, because four circles divide the plane into at most 14 regions, so for four letters the circle picture breaks down while the table carries on.

## Worked examples

**Worked example.** **Compute a table and find a simpler equivalent: $(P \lor Q) \land \lnot P$.**

Work inside out. In the four rows (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), (F, F) the column of $P \lor Q$ is T, T, T, F and the column of $\lnot P$ is F, F, T, T. Their conjunction is true only where both are true, giving F, F, T, F.

A column with a single T, in the row where $P$ is false and $Q$ is true, is the column of $\lnot P \land Q$. So $(P \lor Q) \land \lnot P \equiv \lnot P \land Q$.

*Check by the laws.* Distribute $\lnot P$ over the disjunction: $\lnot P \land (P \lor Q) \equiv (\lnot P \land P) \lor (\lnot P \land Q)$. The first bracket is a contradiction, and "F or $X$" has the truth value of $X$, so what remains is $\lnot P \land Q$.

**Worked example.** **Negate a rule.** A safety rule reads: "the door is locked, and the alarm is set or a guard is on duty". When is the rule violated?

Write $L$, $A$, $G$ for the three parts. The rule is $L \land (A \lor G)$, and it is violated when its negation is true. Apply De Morgan to the outer $\land$, then to the inner $\lor$:

$$
\lnot\bigl(L \land (A \lor G)\bigr) \equiv \lnot L \lor \lnot(A \lor G) \equiv \lnot L \lor (\lnot A \land \lnot G).
$$

In words: the door is not locked, or else the alarm is off and no guard is on duty.

*Check one row.* Take $L$ true, $A$ false, $G$ false. The rule is $\text{T} \land (\text{F} \lor \text{F})$, which is F, and our formula gives $\text{F} \lor (\text{T} \land \text{T})$, which is T, as it should.

## Every truth table has a formula

We have three connectives. The number of possible tables is much larger: a table on two letters has 4 rows, each of which may be T or F, so there are $2^4 = 16$ different columns, and on three letters there are $2^8 = 256$. Are some of them out of reach of $\land$, $\lor$ and $\lnot$?

The exclusive or shows what to do. Its column is true in the rows (T, F) and (F, T). The formula $P \land \lnot Q$ is true in the row (T, F) and in no other row. The formula $\lnot P \land Q$ is true in the row (F, T) and in no other. Join them with "or" and the result is true in exactly those two rows. The same recipe works on any column whatever. Here it is on a column with three letters: a vote among three sensors, true when at least two of them fire.

[Figure 7, steps: Building a formula for a given truth table: true when at least two of P, Q, R are true. Each true row gets a conjunction that is true in that row only, and their disjunction reproduces the column.]

  - step: A table that was not produced by a formula: the wanted column is true when at least two of the three letters are true.
  - step: Pick out the rows where the wanted value is T. There are four.
  - step: For each such row write an AND of three pieces: the letter where the row has T, its negation where it has F.
  - step: Join the four ANDs with OR. The result is true in exactly the four chosen rows, so it has the wanted column.
**Theorem.** Let $n \ge 1$. Every truth table on the letters $P_1, \dots, P_n$, meaning every way of assigning T or F to each of the $2^n$ rows, is the truth table of some formula built from the letters using only $\land$, $\lor$ and $\lnot$.

**Proof.** For a row $r$, let $M_r$ be the conjunction of $n$ pieces, where the $k$-th piece is $P_k$ if $P_k$ is T in row $r$ and $\lnot P_k$ if $P_k$ is F in row $r$.

*Claim: $M_r$ is true in row $r$ and false in every other row.* In row $r$ every piece is true by the way it was chosen, so the conjunction is true. Any other row $s$ differs from $r$ in the value of at least one letter $P_k$, the $k$-th piece of $M_r$ is false in row $s$, and a conjunction with a false piece is false.

Now take any table. If it has at least one T, let $A$ be the disjunction of the formulas $M_r$ over all rows $r$ where the table has T. In such a row $r$, the piece $M_r$ is true, so $A$ is true. In a row $s$ where the table has F, every $M_r$ in the disjunction has $r \ne s$ and so is false in row $s$, which makes $A$ false. Hence $A$ has the given table. If the table has no T at all, the formula $P_1 \land \lnot P_1$ has it.

The formula produced by this proof is called the **disjunctive normal form** of the table. For the vote it is

$$
(P \land Q \land R) \lor (P \land Q \land \lnot R) \lor (P \land \lnot Q \land R) \lor (\lnot P \land Q \land R).
$$

The theorem promises a formula and makes no promise of a short one. The vote is also given by $(P \land Q) \lor (P \land R) \lor (Q \land R)$, which is less than half as long. A set of connectives that can express every truth table is called **functionally complete**, and the theorem says that $\{\land, \lor, \lnot\}$ is such a set.

**Pause and try.** Write the disjunctive normal form for the table on $P$, $Q$ whose column, in the usual order of rows, is T, F, T, T. Then find a shorter formula with the same column.

**Answer.** The true rows are (T, T), (F, T) and (F, F), so the normal form is $(P \land Q) \lor (\lnot P \land Q) \lor (\lnot P \land \lnot Q)$. For something shorter, look at the single false row instead: the column is false exactly when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false, so it is $\lnot(P \land \lnot Q)$, which by De Morgan and double negation is $\lnot P \lor Q$. This column belongs to "if $P$ then $Q$", the subject of the [next lesson](@logic/implication).

## One connective is enough

Three connectives suffice, and fewer will do. De Morgan's second law, negated on both sides, gives $P \lor Q \equiv \lnot(\lnot P \land \lnot Q)$, so every $\lor$ can be traded for $\land$ and $\lnot$, and the pair $\{\land, \lnot\}$ is already complete. We cannot drop $\lnot$ and keep going (a problem below asks you to prove it), but we can fuse the two survivors into one. Define a new connective, written $P \uparrow Q$ and called **NAND** for "not and", by

$$
P \uparrow Q \;=\; \lnot(P \land Q).
$$

Its column is F, T, T, T: false only when both parts are true.

**Theorem.** Every truth table is the truth table of a formula built from letters using $\uparrow$ alone.

**Proof.** By the previous theorem it is enough to express $\lnot$, $\land$ and $\lor$ with $\uparrow$, and then to replace each connective in a disjunctive normal form by its expression.

*Not.* $P \uparrow P = \lnot(P \land P)$, and $P \land P$ has the truth value of $P$. So $\lnot P \equiv P \uparrow P$.

*And.* By the line above, $(P \uparrow Q) \uparrow (P \uparrow Q) \equiv \lnot(P \uparrow Q) = \lnot\lnot(P \land Q) \equiv P \land Q$.

*Or.* $(P \uparrow P) \uparrow (Q \uparrow Q) \equiv \lnot P \uparrow \lnot Q = \lnot(\lnot P \land \lnot Q) \equiv \lnot\lnot P \lor \lnot\lnot Q \equiv P \lor Q$, by De Morgan and double negation.

[Figure 8, steps: The NAND gate and the three constructions from the proof. One gate with its pins joined gives NOT, two gates give AND, three give OR. Each table is computed from the wiring shown.]

  - step: A NAND gate: its output is F only when both inputs are T.
  - step: Connect one input to both pins. The output is the negation of the input.
  - step: Follow a NAND gate with a gate wired as NOT. The negations cancel, leaving P and Q.
  - step: Negate each input with its own gate, then NAND the results. By De Morgan the output is P or Q.
Chip designers care, because one kind of gate is the easiest thing to manufacture in bulk. The Apollo guidance computer was built entirely from a three-input relative of NAND called NOR, which a problem below investigates.

## Where truth tables stop

A sentence must have a truth value before it can enter a table. "This sentence is false" has none that is consistent, since if it is true then it is false, and if it is false then it is true. And words such as "because" or "probably" are not connectives of this kind at all.

Tables grow fast. Twenty letters need $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ rows, and 300 letters need more rows than there are atoms in the observable universe. For formulas of that size, equivalences are established by algebra with the laws above.

**Common mistake.** **Moving a "not" inside without flipping the connective.** Writing $\lnot(P \land Q)$ as $\lnot P \land \lnot Q$ treats $\lnot$ like a minus sign in front of a sum. Test it in the row where $P$ is true and $Q$ is false: the first is T and the second is F. "She is not both rich and famous" allows her to be rich; "she is not rich and not famous" does not.

**Common mistake.** **Reading "or" as "one but not both".** A student who is told "$n$ is even or $n$ is a multiple of 3" and then finds that $n = 6$ sometimes concludes the claim was false. It is true: $P \lor Q$ is true when both parts are. In the same way $3 \le 3$ is true.

## Stepping back

The hard part of this subject is at the very start: agreeing to let a table, and nothing else, say what a connective means. After that everything was computation. Equivalence became "same column", proof became "check every row", and De Morgan's laws became facts about small tables that can be used as algebra on large formulas. The reusable idea is that a claim about finitely many cases can be settled by listing the cases, and that a circuit or a Venn diagram proves something exactly when it is such a list in disguise. The [next lesson](@logic/implication) applies the same method to the connective that people most often get wrong: "if ... then".

**Check yourself.** Which formula is logically equivalent to $\lnot(P \lor Q)$?
Answer: $\lnot P \land \lnot Q$ "Not (at least one is true)" says both are false. The columns are both F, F, F, T.

**Recap.** - A statement is a sentence that is true or false. The connectives $\lnot$, $\land$, $\lor$ are defined by their truth tables, and $\lor$ is inclusive: true when at least one part is true.
- A formula with $n$ letters has a table with $2^n$ rows, computed column by column from the inside out.
- $A \equiv B$ means the same truth value in every row. A tautology is true in every row, a contradiction in none.
- Double negation: $\lnot\lnot P \equiv P$. De Morgan: $\lnot(P \land Q) \equiv \lnot P \lor \lnot Q$ and $\lnot(P \lor Q) \equiv \lnot P \land \lnot Q$. Each of $\land$, $\lor$ distributes over the other.
- Switch circuits (series is "and", parallel is "or") and Venn diagrams (regions are rows) are models of the tables.
- Every truth table has a formula in $\land$, $\lor$, $\lnot$: one conjunction for each true row, joined by "or". NAND alone can express all three.

## Problems

Problems 1 and 2 repeat the moves of the lesson. Problems 3 and 4 ask you to combine them. Problems 5 and 6 go further.

**Problem 1.** Compute the truth table of $P \land (\lnot P \lor Q)$ and find a shorter equivalent formula. Then get the same answer with the distributive law.

**Solution.** In the rows (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), (F, F) the column of $\lnot P \lor Q$ is T, F, T, T. Taking "and" with the column of $P$, which is T, T, F, F, gives T, F, F, F. That is the column of $P \land Q$. By the distributive law, $P \land (\lnot P \lor Q) \equiv (P \land \lnot P) \lor (P \land Q)$; the first bracket is a contradiction, and "F or $X$" has the value of $X$, leaving $P \land Q$.

**Problem 2.** Use De Morgan's laws to write the negation of each without a "not" in front of the whole thing. (a) "$n$ is even and $n$ is greater than 10." (b) "I will take the bus or I will walk." (c) $\lnot P \lor Q$.

**Solution.** (a) $\lnot(E \land G) \equiv \lnot E \lor \lnot G$: "$n$ is odd or $n$ is at most 10". (b) $\lnot(B \lor W) \equiv \lnot B \land \lnot W$: "I will not take the bus and I will not walk". (c) $\lnot(\lnot P \lor Q) \equiv \lnot\lnot P \land \lnot Q \equiv P \land \lnot Q$, using De Morgan and then double negation. Check (c) in the row $P$ true, $Q$ false: $\lnot P \lor Q$ is F, so its negation is T, and $P \land \lnot Q$ is $\text{T} \land \text{T}$, which is T.

**Problem 3.** A column on $P$, $Q$, $R$ is true exactly when an odd number of the three letters are true. Write its disjunctive normal form, and verify it in the rows (T, F, F) and (T, T, F).

**Solution.** The rows with an odd number of T's are (T, T, T), (T, F, F), (F, T, F) and (F, F, T). So the normal form is

$$
(P \land Q \land R) \lor (P \land \lnot Q \land \lnot R) \lor (\lnot P \land Q \land \lnot R) \lor (\lnot P \land \lnot Q \land R).
$$

In the row (T, F, F) the second conjunction is $\text{T} \land \text{T} \land \text{T}$, so the formula is T, as wanted. In the row (T, T, F) the first conjunction fails at $R$, the second at $\lnot Q$, and the third and fourth at $\lnot P$, so the formula is F, as wanted.

**Problem 4.** The connective **NOR** is defined by $P \downarrow Q = \lnot(P \lor Q)$. Express $\lnot P$, $P \lor Q$ and $P \land Q$ using $\downarrow$ alone, and conclude that NOR by itself is functionally complete.

**Solution.** *Not:* $P \downarrow P = \lnot(P \lor P) \equiv \lnot P$, because $P \lor P$ has the value of $P$. *Or:* $(P \downarrow Q) \downarrow (P \downarrow Q) \equiv \lnot(P \downarrow Q) = \lnot\lnot(P \lor Q) \equiv P \lor Q$. *And:* $(P \downarrow P) \downarrow (Q \downarrow Q) \equiv \lnot P \downarrow \lnot Q = \lnot(\lnot P \lor \lnot Q) \equiv \lnot\lnot P \land \lnot\lnot Q \equiv P \land Q$, by De Morgan and double negation. Since every truth table has a formula in $\land$, $\lor$, $\lnot$, and each of those can be rewritten with $\downarrow$, every truth table has a formula in $\downarrow$ alone.

**Problem 5.** Find the error. "Claim: $P \lor (Q \land R) \equiv (P \lor Q) \land R$. Proof: when all three letters are true both sides are true, and when all three are false both sides are false. So the two sides agree." Give a row in which the two sides differ, and state the correct law.

**Solution.** The proof checks two rows out of eight. Take $P$ true, $Q$ false, $R$ false. The left side is $\text{T} \lor (\text{F} \land \text{F})$, which is T. The right side is $(\text{T} \lor \text{F}) \land \text{F}$, which is F. So the claim is false. The correct law distributes $P$ to both parts: $P \lor (Q \land R) \equiv (P \lor Q) \land (P \lor R)$. In the same row the right side of that is $\text{T} \land \text{T}$, which is T.

**Problem 6.** Prove that $\{\land, \lor\}$ without $\lnot$ is not functionally complete. (Hint: what is the truth value of a formula built from letters with only $\land$ and $\lor$ in the row where every letter is true?)

**Solution.** We show that every formula built from letters using only $\land$ and $\lor$ is true in the row where all letters are true. Argue by [induction](@discrete-math/induction) on the number of connectives: prove it for formulas with none, and show that if it holds for all formulas with fewer than $k$ connectives then it holds for those with $k$. A formula with no connectives is a single letter, which is true in that row. A formula with $k \ge 1$ connectives is $A \land B$ or $A \lor B$, where $A$ and $B$ have fewer connectives, so both are true in that row, and then $A \land B$ and $A \lor B$ are true there too. Now the column of $\lnot P$ has F in the row where $P$ is true. No formula in $\land$ and $\lor$ alone has an F in the all-true row, so none has the table of $\lnot P$.

---

# If-then statements: converse and contrapositive

> When is "if P then Q" true? One table answers it, shows why the contrapositive says the same thing and the converse does not, and solves the four-card puzzle.

Series: Logic and Proof (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/logic/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/logic/implication/
Keywords: implication, conditional statement, converse, contrapositive, vacuous truth, necessary and sufficient, modus ponens, Wason selection task

[Figure 1, animation: Four cards, each with a letter on one side and a number on the other, showing A, K, 4 and 7. The rule to test says that a card with a vowel on one side has an even number on the other.]

Four cards lie on a table. Each has a letter on one side and a number on the other, and the sides you can see show A, K, 4 and 7. Someone makes a claim about these four cards: "If a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other." You want to find out whether the claim is true, and you want to turn over as few cards as possible.

**Pause and try.** Which cards must you turn over? Write your answer down before opening this one.

**Answer.** The A and the 7. Most people say "A and 4", or only "A". When the psychologist Peter Wason set this puzzle in the 1960s, fewer than one in ten of his subjects chose correctly, and the result has been repeated many times since. If you picked the 4 you are in good company, and the rest of this page is about why the 4 can tell you nothing while the 7 can sink the claim. We come back to the cards at the end.

The puzzle is hard because "if ... then" in conversation carries suggestions that are no part of what it says. To reason with it reliably we have to fix exactly when "if $P$ then $Q$" counts as true, in the way the [previous lesson](@logic/truth-tables) did for "and", "or" and "not". Recall the method. A statement is a sentence that is true (T) or false (F). A connective is defined by a truth table, which gives the truth value of the compound in each of the four combinations of truth values of $P$ and $Q$. Two compounds are logically equivalent, written $\equiv$, when their columns agree in every row.

## When is a promise broken?

Your aunt says: "If you pass the exam, then I will buy you a bike." Let $P$ be "you pass" and $Q$ be "she buys you a bike". There are four ways things can go. In which of them has she lied?

[Figure 2, steps: The four outcomes of the promise "if you pass the exam, I will buy you a bike". Only one outcome breaks the promise: you pass and no bike appears. The last column records, for each row, whether the promise was kept.]

  - step: You pass and you get the bike. The promise was kept.
  - step: You pass and there is no bike. This is the one outcome in which she lied.
  - step: You fail. Bike or no bike, she has not broken her word, because the promise only covered the case where you pass.
  - step: A statement is either true or false. The promise is false in one row, so it is true in the other three.
She lied in exactly one case: you passed and no bike came. If you failed, she is free to buy the bike anyway or to keep her money, and either way nobody can call her a liar. A statement has to be true or false, with nothing in between, so a promise that was not broken counts as true.

**Definition.** Let $P$ and $Q$ be statements. The **conditional** $P \to Q$, read "if $P$ then $Q$" or "$P$ implies $Q$", is false when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false, and true in the other three cases. $P$ is called the **hypothesis** and $Q$ the **conclusion**.

| $P$ | $Q$ | $P \to Q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | T |

In the bottom two rows, where the hypothesis is false, the conditional is said to be **vacuously true**. These rows bother everyone at first. They make "if $2 + 2 = 5$ then Paris is in Italy" a true statement. A table is a choice, and this choice needs defending. The promise was one argument. Here are two more that do not depend on it.

### The argument from general statements

Everyone accepts that this is true: *for every integer $n$, if $n$ is a multiple of 4, then $n$ is even.* A statement about every integer is true only if it holds for each one. So put some integers in and see which rows of the table they land in.

[Figure 3, animation: The integers 1 to 12 sorted by the truth values of P, "n is a multiple of 4", and Q, "n is even". Three of the four boxes fill up. The box for P true and Q false stays empty, and that empty box is all that the if-then statement claims.]

The number 8 is a multiple of 4 and even: row one. The number 6 is not a multiple of 4 but is even: row three. The number 7 is neither: row four. If the conditional were false in row three or in row four, the general statement would be false at $n = 6$ or at $n = 7$, and we would have to say that "multiples of 4 are even" is refuted by the number 7. Nobody wants that. The one row that no integer occupies is row two, and that is the row the statement forbids.

### The argument by elimination

Rows one and two are not in dispute: T, then F. There are four ways to complete the column, and three of them are something else that we already have.

| rows 3 and 4 | full column | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| F, F | T, F, F, F | $P \land Q$: "if" would mean "and" |
| F, T | T, F, F, T | unchanged when $P$ and $Q$ swap: "if $P$ then $Q$" would mean "if $Q$ then $P$" |
| T, F | T, F, T, F | the column of $Q$ alone: the hypothesis would do nothing |
| T, T | T, F, T, T | the definition |

"If" is weaker than "and", it has a direction, and its hypothesis matters. Only the last line keeps all three.

You might object that with $P$ false there is no connection between $P$ and $Q$ at all. That is correct, and the table never claimed one. The arrow says nothing about causes or reasons.

**Key idea.** $P \to Q$ makes exactly one claim: the combination "$P$ true, $Q$ false" does not occur. To refute it you must produce that combination, and nothing else will do.

In symbols this is two equivalences, both read off the columns:

$$
P \to Q \;\equiv\; \lnot P \lor Q, \qquad \lnot(P \to Q) \;\equiv\; P \land \lnot Q.
$$

The column of $\lnot P \lor Q$ is $\text{F} \lor \text{T}$, $\text{F} \lor \text{F}$, $\text{T} \lor \text{T}$, $\text{T} \lor \text{F}$, which is T, F, T, T. The second follows from the first by De Morgan's law, $\lnot(A \lor B) \equiv \lnot A \land \lnot B$.

**Pause and try.** Write the negation of "if it rains, then the match is canceled". Is it "if it rains, then the match is not canceled"?

**Answer.** The negation is "it rains and the match is not canceled", $R \land \lnot C$. The other sentence, $R \to \lnot C$, is a different statement: on a dry day both $R \to C$ and $R \to \lnot C$ are vacuously true, so one cannot be the negation of the other.

## A picture: one region inside another

Many conditionals are about a whole collection of things: all integers, all cards. For those there is a picture. Draw a region for the things that make $P$ true and another for those that make $Q$ true. "For every $x$, if $P$ holds for $x$ then $Q$ holds for $x$" says that no point lies inside the first region and outside the second, which means the first region sits inside the second.

[Figure 4, animation: A point moves around a box in which the region where P is true lies inside the region where Q is true. The table on the right highlights the row the point is in. It visits three rows, and it can never be in the row with P true and Q false.]

The picture also shows what the conditional does not say. There may be plenty of points in the outer region that are not in the inner one, where $Q$ is true and $P$ is false. Keep this picture in mind for the next two sections.

## Converse, inverse and contrapositive

From one conditional you can make three others by swapping the two parts, negating them, or both. Try all three on the statement about multiples of 4, for an integer $n$.

- Swap: "if $n$ is even, then $n$ is a multiple of 4." False at $n = 6$.
- Negate both: "if $n$ is not a multiple of 4, then $n$ is not even." False at $n = 6$.
- Swap and negate: "if $n$ is not even, then $n$ is not a multiple of 4." True for every $n$.

**Pause and try.** "If it is raining, then the ground is wet." Form the same three variations. Which of them must be true whenever the original is? For each one that need not be, describe a situation where the original is true and the variation is false.

**Answer.** Swap: "if the ground is wet, it is raining". Negate both: "if it is not raining, the ground is not wet". Both fail when a sprinkler is on under a clear sky, although the original still holds. Swap and negate: "if the ground is dry, then there is no rain". This one must be true whenever the original is, because rain on dry ground is exactly what the original rules out.

**Definition.** For the conditional $P \to Q$:

- its **converse** is $Q \to P$;
- its **inverse** is $\lnot P \to \lnot Q$;
- its **contrapositive** is $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$.

[Figure 5, steps: Truth tables of a conditional and its three variations. The contrapositive has the same column as the original. The converse and the inverse have a different column, which they share with each other.]

  - step: The original conditional is false only in row two.
  - step: The contrapositive is false only when not Q is true and not P is false, which is row two again. Same column.
  - step: The converse is false only when Q is true and P is false, which is row three. It disagrees with the original in rows two and three.
  - step: The inverse has the same column as the converse.
**Theorem.** Let $P$ and $Q$ be two letters standing for statements, and compare the following formulas by their columns.

- $P \to Q \equiv \lnot Q \to \lnot P$. A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive.
- $P \to Q$ is not equivalent to its converse $Q \to P$, and not equivalent to its inverse $\lnot P \to \lnot Q$: the columns differ in rows two and three.
- $Q \to P \equiv \lnot P \to \lnot Q$. The converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other.

**Proof.** A conditional is false in exactly one row, the one where its hypothesis is true and its conclusion false.

(1) $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$ is false exactly when $\lnot Q$ is true and $\lnot P$ is false, that is, when $Q$ is false and $P$ is true. That is the row where $P \to Q$ is false. The two columns have their single F in the same row, so they are equal.

(2) $Q \to P$ is false exactly when $Q$ is true and $P$ is false, which is row three. In row two, $P \to Q$ is F and $Q \to P$ is T, so they are not equivalent. $\lnot P \to \lnot Q$ is false exactly when $\lnot P$ is true and $\lnot Q$ is false, that is, $P$ false and $Q$ true: row three again. So the inverse also differs from $P \to Q$ in row two.

Non-equivalence means the columns differ in some row. It does not prevent a particular conditional and its converse from both being true, as happens in rows one and four.

(3) By the two computations in (2), the converse and the inverse both have their single F in row three.

In the picture of regions, the contrapositive says that everything outside the outer region is outside the inner one, which is the same drawing described from the outside. The converse says that the outer region sits inside the inner one, which is a different drawing.

## "Only if", "necessary", "sufficient", "if and only if"

English has several other ways of saying $P \to Q$, and they are easy to read backwards.

**Only if.** "You may vote only if you are at least 18" does not promise a vote to every adult. It says that voting without being 18 does not happen: if you vote ($V$), then you are at least 18 ($E$). So "$P$ only if $Q$" means $P \to Q$. The word "if" introduces the hypothesis, and the words "only if" introduce the conclusion.

**Sufficient and necessary.** When $P \to Q$ is true, we say $P$ is **sufficient** for $Q$, because having $P$ is enough to get $Q$. We also say $Q$ is **necessary** for $P$, because without $Q$ there is no $P$ (this is the contrapositive). Being a multiple of 4 is sufficient for being even and not necessary, as 6 shows. Being even is necessary for being a multiple of 4 and not sufficient. In the picture, the inner region is the sufficient condition and the outer region the necessary one.

**If and only if.** When both directions hold we say so with a new connective.

**Definition.** The **biconditional** $P \leftrightarrow Q$, read "$P$ if and only if $Q$" and abbreviated "iff", is $(P \to Q) \land (Q \to P)$. Its column is T, F, F, T: it is true exactly when $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth value. One also says that $P$ is **necessary and sufficient** for $Q$.

For example, an integer is even if and only if its last digit is even. To prove an "if and only if" you must prove two conditionals, one in each direction, and a common error is to prove one and stop.

## Valid and invalid arguments

An argument has premises and a conclusion. Its form is **valid** if the conclusion is true in every row of the truth table in which all the premises are true. Three forms involving a conditional come up constantly.

[Figure 6, image: Three argument forms tested on the truth table of P \to Q. The shaded rows are those where both premises are true, and the framed cells show the conclusion there. Modus ponens and modus tollens never lead from true premises to a false conclusion. Affirming the consequent does, in the row where P is false and Q is true.]

**Theorem.** (a) **Modus ponens** is valid: from $P \to Q$ and $P$, infer $Q$. (b) **Modus tollens** is valid: from $P \to Q$ and $\lnot Q$, infer $\lnot P$. (c) **Affirming the consequent** is invalid: from $P \to Q$ and $Q$, the conclusion $P$ does not follow.

**Proof.** (a) $P \to Q$ and $P$ are both true only in row one, and there $Q$ is true. (b) $P \to Q$ and $\lnot Q$ are both true only in row four, and there $P$ is false, so $\lnot P$ is true. (c) $P \to Q$ and $Q$ are both true in rows one and three. In row three $P$ is false. So there is a case with true premises and a false conclusion.

Modus tollens is modus ponens applied to the contrapositive. Affirming the consequent is modus ponens applied to the converse, which is why it fails. "If it rains the ground is wet; the ground is wet; so it rained" forgets the sprinkler. There is a fourth form, *denying the antecedent* (from $P \to Q$ and $\lnot P$, infer $\lnot Q$), which is invalid by the same row three.

## The four cards again

The rule on the table is $P \to Q$ with $P$: "the card has a vowel on its letter side" and $Q$: "the card has an even number on its number side". By the KEY statement, the only thing that can break the rule is a card that is a vowel and odd. So a card needs turning exactly when its hidden side could complete that combination.

[Figure 7, steps: The four-card puzzle solved. The A must be turned because an odd number behind it would break the rule. The 7 must be turned because a vowel behind it would break the rule. Nothing behind the K or the 4 can break it.]

  - step: The A is a vowel, so the rule makes a demand on its other side. Turn it over. Here the number is even and the rule survives, but an odd number would have broken it.
  - step: The K is a consonant. The rule says nothing about consonants, so no number behind it can break the rule. Leave it.
  - step: The 4 is even. Turn it anyway: a consonant. A vowel would have been fine too, so this card could never break the rule.
  - step: The 7 is odd. Turn it: a vowel. This card has a vowel on one side and an odd number on the other, and the rule is false.
Go through the cards as rows of the table. The A has $P$ true, so it is in row one or row two, and row two is the bad one: turn it. The K has $P$ false, so it is in row three or four, both vacuously true: leave it. The 4 has $Q$ true, so it is in row one or three, both true: leave it. The 7 has $Q$ false, so it is in row two or four, and row two is the bad one: turn it.

Turning the A is modus ponens, and turning the 7 is modus tollens. Choosing the 4 is affirming the consequent: it treats the rule as if it also said "an even number has a vowel behind it", which is the converse.

The difficulty is in the abstraction more than in the logic. In 1982 Richard Griggs and James Cox gave students the same puzzle as a bar scene: each card is a customer, with a drink on one side and an age on the other, showing beer, cola, 22 and 16, and the rule is "if a person is drinking beer, then the person must be over 19". About three quarters of their subjects correctly checked the beer drinker and the 16-year-old. The table for $\to$ is what everyone already uses when the content is familiar.

## Worked examples

**Worked example.** **Classify a claim.** "An integer whose last digit is 0 is divisible by 5." Write it as a conditional, form the converse and contrapositive, decide which are true, and describe the situation with "necessary" and "sufficient".

As a conditional about an integer $n$: if the last digit of $n$ is 0 ($P$), then $n$ is divisible by 5 ($Q$). It is true, since such an $n$ is a multiple of 10. The converse is "if $n$ is divisible by 5, then its last digit is 0", and $n = 15$ has $Q$ true and $P$ false, so the converse is false. The contrapositive is "if $n$ is not divisible by 5, then its last digit is not 0", true because the original is. So ending in 0 is sufficient for divisibility by 5 and not necessary, and divisibility by 5 is necessary for ending in 0 and not sufficient.

**Worked example.** **Proof by contrapositive.** Let $n$ be an integer. Show that if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even.

A direct attack starts from "$n^2 = 2k$" and has to extract information about $n$, which means taking a square root of something we know little about. The contrapositive starts from $n$ instead: *if $n$ is not even, then $n^2$ is not even.* An integer that is not even is odd, so $n = 2k + 1$ for some integer $k$. Then

$$
n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1,
$$

which is odd. The contrapositive is proved, and by part (1) of the theorem so is the original statement.

*Check:* $n^2 = 36$ gives $n = \pm 6$, even; and the odd numbers 3, 5, 7 have squares 9, 25, 49, all odd.

**Worked example.** **Testing for a tautology by hunting for the F.** Is $P \to (Q \to P)$ true in every row?

Instead of four rows, ask how it could be false. The outer conditional is false only if $P$ is true and $Q \to P$ is false. But $Q \to P$ is false only if $Q$ is true and $P$ is false. That needs $P$ to be true and false in the same row, which cannot happen. So no row makes it false, and it is a tautology. In words: if $P$ is true, then it is true whatever else you suppose.

## What the arrow does not mean

The arrow is not "causes" and not "and then". "If the moon is made of cheese, then $2 + 2 = 4$" is true, with no link between the parts. In mathematics this rarely does harm, because almost every conditional that matters sits inside a "for every": for every integer $n$, if ... then .... There the vacuous rows are the cases the theorem is not about, and the next lesson, on [quantifiers](@logic/quantifiers), makes that precise.

Parentheses matter more with $\to$ than with $\land$ or $\lor$. When $P$, $Q$, $R$ are all false, $(P \to Q) \to R$ is $\text{T} \to \text{F}$, which is F, while $P \to (Q \to R)$ is $\text{F} \to \text{T}$, which is T.

**Common mistake.** **Reading a conditional as its converse.** "If you have the flu, you have a fever. You have a fever, so you have the flu." The premise puts flu inside fever, and says nothing about how much of fever lies outside flu. Whenever you are tempted, look for the sprinkler: a case with $Q$ true and $P$ false.

**Common mistake.** **Negating by pushing "not" onto the conclusion.** The negation of "if $n$ is prime then $n$ is odd" is not "if $n$ is prime then $n$ is not odd". To deny a conditional you exhibit the forbidden combination: "$n$ is prime and $n$ is not odd", which holds for $n = 2$.

## Stepping back

One row of one table did all the work. A conditional forbids "hypothesis true, conclusion false" and forbids nothing else. From that came vacuous truth, the equivalence with the contrapositive, the failure of the converse, the two valid argument forms, and the answer to the cards. When a conditional confuses you, ask what would refute it.

**Check yourself.** Which statement is logically equivalent to "if a shape is a square, then it is a rectangle"?
Answer: If a shape is not a rectangle, then it is not a square. This is the contrapositive. Both statements forbid exactly one thing: a square that is not a rectangle.

**Recap.** - $P \to Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false. When $P$ is false it is vacuously true.
- $P \to Q \equiv \lnot P \lor Q$, and its negation is $P \land \lnot Q$.
- The contrapositive $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$ is equivalent to $P \to Q$. The converse $Q \to P$ and the inverse $\lnot P \to \lnot Q$ are equivalent to each other and not to $P \to Q$.
- "$P$ only if $Q$", "$P$ is sufficient for $Q$" and "$Q$ is necessary for $P$" all mean $P \to Q$. "$P$ if and only if $Q$" means both directions.
- Modus ponens ($P \to Q$, $P$, so $Q$) and modus tollens ($P \to Q$, $\lnot Q$, so $\lnot P$) are valid. Affirming the consequent ($P \to Q$, $Q$, so $P$) is not.
- To test a rule "if $P$ then $Q$", check the cases where $P$ is true and the cases where $Q$ is false.

## Problems

Problems 1 to 3 repeat the moves of the lesson, 4 to 6 combine them, and 7 and 8 go further.

**Problem 1.** Compute the column of $\lnot P \to Q$ and identify it as a connective you already know. Then translate "I will go unless it rains" using it.

**Solution.** In the rows (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), (F, F) the hypothesis $\lnot P$ is F, F, T, T. A conditional with a false hypothesis is true, so the first two rows give T. Row three is $\text{T} \to \text{T}$, which is T, and row four is $\text{T} \to \text{F}$, which is F. The column T, T, T, F is that of $P \lor Q$. "I will go unless it rains" says: if it does not rain, I will go, $\lnot R \to G$, which is $R \lor G$: it rains or I go.

**Problem 2.** For a triangle $T$, consider "if $T$ is equilateral, then $T$ is isosceles" (an isosceles triangle has at least two equal sides). State the converse, inverse, contrapositive and negation, and say which of the five statements are true for every triangle $T$.

**Solution.** Original: true for every triangle, since three equal sides include two equal sides. Converse: "if $T$ is isosceles, then $T$ is equilateral"; false for the triangle with sides 5, 5, 3. Inverse: "if $T$ is not equilateral, then $T$ is not isosceles"; false for the same triangle. Contrapositive: "if $T$ is not isosceles, then $T$ is not equilateral"; true for every triangle, being equivalent to the original. Negation: "$T$ is equilateral and $T$ is not isosceles"; false for every triangle.

**Problem 3.** Write each as a conditional $A \to B$, saying what $A$ and $B$ are. (a) "You get dessert only if you finish dinner." (b) "Passing the final is sufficient for passing the course." (c) "Oxygen is necessary for fire."

**Solution.** (a) "Only if" introduces the conclusion: if you get dessert, then you finished dinner. It does not promise dessert to everyone who finishes. (b) The sufficient condition is the hypothesis: if you pass the final, then you pass the course. (c) The necessary condition is the conclusion: if there is fire, then there is oxygen. Equivalently, by the contrapositive, no oxygen means no fire.

**Problem 4.** Four cards each have a number on one side and a letter on the other, and they show 3, 8, E and T. The rule is "if a card has an odd number on one side, then it has a vowel on the other". Which cards must be turned over to test the rule?

**Solution.** Here $P$ is "the number is odd" and $Q$ is "the letter is a vowel". The rule can be broken only by a card with an odd number and a consonant. The 3 has $P$ true: a consonant behind it would break the rule, so turn it. The 8 has $P$ false: leave it. The E has $Q$ true: whatever number is behind it, the rule holds for this card, so leave it. The T has $Q$ false: an odd number behind it would break the rule, so turn it. Answer: 3 and T.

**Problem 5.** Decide whether each argument is valid, and name its form. (a) "If the alarm rings, there is smoke or heat. The alarm is ringing. There is no smoke. So there is heat." (b) "If a number is divisible by 6, it is divisible by 3. The number 9 is divisible by 3. So 9 is divisible by 6."

**Solution.** (a) Valid. From $A \to (S \lor H)$ and $A$, modus ponens gives $S \lor H$. A true "or" needs at least one true part, and $S$ is false, so $H$ is true. (b) Invalid: this is affirming the consequent. Both premises are true and the conclusion is false, which no valid form allows.

**Problem 6.** Show that $P \to (Q \to R) \equiv (P \land Q) \to R$ without writing eight rows, by finding the rows where each side is false.

**Solution.** The left side is false exactly when $P$ is true and $Q \to R$ is false, and $Q \to R$ is false exactly when $Q$ is true and $R$ is false. So the left side is false in the single row $P$ true, $Q$ true, $R$ false. The right side is false exactly when $P \land Q$ is true and $R$ is false, which is the same row. The two columns have their only F in the same place, so they are equal.

**Problem 7.** Let $a$ and $b$ be integers. Prove by contrapositive: if $ab$ is odd, then $a$ is odd and $b$ is odd.

**Solution.** The contrapositive is: if it is not the case that both are odd, then $ab$ is not odd. By De Morgan's law, "not ($a$ odd and $b$ odd)" is "$a$ is even or $b$ is even". Suppose $a$ is even, say $a = 2k$. Then $ab = 2(kb)$ is even. If instead $b$ is even, $b = 2m$, then $ab = 2(am)$ is even. In both cases $ab$ is not odd, which proves the contrapositive and therefore the statement.

**Problem 8.** Prove that $\bigl((P \to Q) \land (Q \to R)\bigr) \to (P \to R)$ is a tautology. Then explain what is wrong with this chain: "If it is a dog, it is a mammal. If it is a cat, it is a mammal. So if it is a dog, it is a cat."

**Solution.** Suppose some row made the formula false. Then in that row the hypothesis $(P \to Q) \land (Q \to R)$ is true and the conclusion $P \to R$ is false. The second says $P$ is true and $R$ is false. Since $P \to Q$ is true and $P$ is true, $Q$ is true (modus ponens). Since $Q \to R$ is true and $Q$ is true, $R$ is true. But $R$ is false. No such row exists, so the formula is a tautology. The chain about dogs has premises $D \to M$ and $C \to M$, which do not have the shape $P \to Q$, $Q \to R$: the middle term $M$ is the conclusion of both. To chain them one would need $M \to C$, the converse of the second premise, and that is false.

---

# Quantifiers: for all, there exists, and negation

> Everyone loves someone" has two meanings. Quantifiers separate them, show how to negate each, and turn the epsilon-delta definition of a limit into a game.

Series: Logic and Proof (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/logic/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/logic/quantifiers/
Keywords: quantifiers, for all, there exists, universal quantifier, existential quantifier, negating quantifiers, order of quantifiers, epsilon delta definition

[Figure 1, animation: Two readings of "everyone loves someone" among four people. On the left each person loves somebody, a different somebody for different people. On the right there is one person whom all four love.]

"Everyone loves someone." Does that say each person has somebody they love, possibly a different somebody for each? Or does it say there is one particular person who is loved by all? English allows both, and the two claims are far apart: the first is true in most families, and the second is true of almost no group of people.

In conversation the ambiguity is harmless. In mathematics the same pair of readings sits inside the definition of a limit, and choosing the wrong one produces a definition that almost no function satisfies. So we need a notation that forces a choice, and rules for working with it.

This lesson leans on two earlier ones. From [truth tables](@logic/truth-tables): a statement is a sentence that is true or false; $\land$, $\lor$, $\lnot$ mean "and", "or", "not"; and De Morgan's laws say $\lnot(P \land Q) \equiv \lnot P \lor \lnot Q$ and $\lnot(P \lor Q) \equiv \lnot P \land \lnot Q$. From [implication](@logic/implication): $P \to Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false, so it is true whenever $P$ is false, and its negation is $P \land \lnot Q$.

## Predicates and the two quantifiers

The sentence "$x^2 < 30$" is not a statement, because it is neither true nor false until we know $x$. It becomes a statement when a value is put in: "$3^2 < 30$" is true and "$6^2 < 30$" is false. Such a sentence is called a predicate, and the values allowed for $x$ form its domain.

There is a second way to turn a predicate into a statement, which is to say *how many* values of the domain satisfy it. Take the domain $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ and check them one at a time.

[Figure 2, animation: The predicate x^2 < 30 tested on each element of the domain 1 to 6. It is true for five of them and false for 6. So "for all x" is false, with 6 as a counterexample, and "there exists x" is true, with 1 as a witness.]

**Definition.** A **predicate** $P(x)$ with **domain** $D$ is a sentence containing a variable $x$ that becomes a statement whenever $x$ is replaced by an element of $D$.

- The **universal** statement $\forall x \in D\; P(x)$, read "for all $x$ in $D$, $P(x)$", is true when $P(x)$ is true for every element $x$ of $D$. An element for which $P(x)$ is false is a **counterexample**.
- The **existential** statement $\exists x \in D\; P(x)$, read "there exists $x$ in $D$ such that $P(x)$", is true when $P(x)$ is true for at least one element $x$ of $D$. Such an element is a **witness**.

The symbols $\forall$ and $\exists$ are **quantifiers**.

Each clause matches the scan. One counterexample, $x = 6$, was enough to make the universal statement false, and five agreeing values could not save it. One witness was enough to make the existential statement true. On a finite domain a quantifier is a long connective: $\forall x\, P(x)$ is $P(1) \land P(2) \land \dots \land P(6)$, and $\exists x\, P(x)$ is $P(1) \lor P(2) \lor \dots \lor P(6)$.

The domain is part of the statement. "$\exists x\; (x^2 = 2)$" is false if $x$ ranges over the integers and true if it ranges over the real numbers. "$\forall x\; (x^2 \ge x)$" is true over the integers and false over the reals, where $x = \frac12$ is a counterexample. When the domain is not written, it must be clear from context.

Often we quantify over part of a domain, as in "every $x > 0$". This is shorthand with a fixed meaning, and the two quantifiers unpack differently:

$$
\forall x > 0\; Q(x) \text{ means } \forall x\,(x > 0 \to Q(x)), \qquad \exists x > 0\; Q(x) \text{ means } \exists x\,(x > 0 \land Q(x)).
$$

**Pause and try.** True or false? (a) $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\; (x^2 > 0)$. (b) $\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}\; (n^2 = n)$. (c) "Every unicorn in this room is purple", that is, $\forall x \in U\; \text{Purple}(x)$ where $U$ is the set of unicorns in the room, which is empty.

**Answer.** (a) False: $x = 0$ is a counterexample. (b) True: $n = 1$ is a witness, and so is $n = 0$. (c) True. A universal statement is false only if there is a counterexample, and an empty domain contains none. This is the vacuous truth of the conditional again, since the claim is "for every $x$, if $x$ is a unicorn in this room then $x$ is purple" and the hypothesis is always false. Over an empty domain every $\forall$ statement is true and every $\exists$ statement is false.

## How to say "no"

Someone claims that all swans are white. What must be the case for the claim to be false? A common first answer is "no swans are white", and it overshoots badly. The claim is refuted by one black swan in a lake of white ones.

On the finite example this is De Morgan's law at work on a long conjunction.

[Figure 3, steps: Negating "for all x, P(x)" on the domain 1 to 6. The universal statement is six statements joined by "and". Negating it turns every "and" into "or" and negates each piece, which is the statement "there exists x such that not P(x)".]

  - step: For all x, P(x) is six statements joined by AND. One false piece makes the whole thing false.
  - step: Negate it. By De Morgan's law the NOT lands on every piece, flipping each value, and each AND becomes OR.
  - step: The counterexample that made the universal statement false, x = 6, is the witness that makes the new statement true.
**Theorem.** (Negation of quantifiers.) For every predicate $P(x)$ with domain $D$:

$$
\lnot\,\forall x \in D\; P(x) \;\equiv\; \exists x \in D\; \lnot P(x), \qquad \lnot\,\exists x \in D\; P(x) \;\equiv\; \forall x \in D\; \lnot P(x).
$$

**Proof.** *First rule.* $\lnot \forall x\, P(x)$ is true exactly when $\forall x\, P(x)$ is false. By the definition of $\forall$ that happens exactly when $P(x)$ fails to be true for some element $x$ of $D$, that is, when $\lnot P(x)$ is true for at least one $x$. By the definition of $\exists$ this is exactly when $\exists x\, \lnot P(x)$ is true. The two sides are true in the same circumstances.

*Second rule.* Apply the first rule to the predicate $\lnot P(x)$: $\lnot \forall x\, \lnot P(x) \equiv \exists x\, \lnot\lnot P(x) \equiv \exists x\, P(x)$. Negating both sides gives $\forall x\, \lnot P(x) \equiv \lnot \exists x\, P(x)$.

When $D$ is finite, with $n$ elements, these rules are De Morgan's laws for $n$ statements, which follow from the two-statement laws by [induction](@discrete-math/induction) on $n$: peel off the last piece, apply the two-statement law, and use the case of $n - 1$ on the rest. When $D$ is infinite there is no table to check, and the argument from the definitions above is the whole proof. The rules are sometimes called the generalized De Morgan laws.

A restricted domain stays as it is under negation. For example $\lnot\,\forall x > 0\; Q(x)$ unpacks to $\lnot \forall x\,(x > 0 \to Q(x))$, which is $\exists x\, \lnot(x > 0 \to Q(x))$, which is $\exists x\,(x > 0 \land \lnot Q(x))$: there is a positive $x$ for which $Q$ fails. Only the quantifier and the predicate changed.

**Pause and try.** Negate each statement, and say which of the pair is true. (a) "Some prime number is even." (b) $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\; (x > 0 \to x^2 > x)$.

**Answer.** (a) "Every prime number is odd." The original is true, with witness 2, so the negation is false. (b) $\exists x \in \mathbb{R}\; (x > 0 \land x^2 \le x)$. Here the negation is true, with witness $x = \frac12$, since $\frac14 \le \frac12$. So the original is false.

## Two quantifiers: the order matters

Now we can separate the two readings of the opening sentence. Let the domain be four people, A, B, C and D, and let $L(x, y)$ mean "$x$ loves $y$". This predicate has two variables, and each needs a quantifier:

- $\forall x\, \exists y\; L(x, y)$: for every person $x$ there is a person $y$ whom $x$ loves.
- $\exists y\, \forall x\; L(x, y)$: there is a person $y$ whom every person $x$ loves.

To test them we need to know who loves whom. Here is one possibility.

[Figure 4, steps: A relation among four people, drawn as arrows from each person (left) to the people they love (right). Every person has an outgoing arrow, so the first statement is true. No person on the right receives arrows from all four, so the second is false, until one more arrow is added.]

  - step: Who loves whom: an arrow from x on the left to y on the right means x loves y. There are six arrows.
  - step: For all x there exists y: check that each person on the left has at least one arrow going out. All four do.
  - step: There exists y for all x: look for one person on the right who receives an arrow from all four. D comes closest, with three, but D does not love D.
  - step: Add one arrow, from D to D. Now D is loved by all four and the second statement is true as well.
With the six arrows of the first slide, $\forall x\, \exists y\; L(x, y)$ is true and $\exists y\, \forall x\; L(x, y)$ is false. The same relation, the same two quantifiers, and opposite truth values. So the order in which quantifiers are written is part of the meaning.

A grid makes the difference easy to see. Put $x$ down the side and $y$ across the top, and mark the cell $(x, y)$ when $L(x, y)$ is true.

[Figure 5, image: The same relation as a grid, before and after the arrow from D to D is added. "For all x there exists y" asks for a mark in every row. "There exists y for all x" asks for a column that is completely marked, which is a stronger demand.]

A full column puts a mark in every row, but marks in every row need not line up in one column. That is the content of the next theorem.

**Theorem.** Let $P(x, y)$ be a predicate with $x$ in a domain $D$ and $y$ in a domain $E$. If $\exists y\, \forall x\; P(x, y)$ is true, then $\forall x\, \exists y\; P(x, y)$ is true. The converse can fail.

**Proof.** Suppose $\exists y\, \forall x\; P(x, y)$. Take a witness $y_0$ in $E$, so that $P(x, y_0)$ is true for every $x$ in $D$. To prove $\forall x\, \exists y\; P(x, y)$, let $x$ be any element of $D$. Then $P(x, y_0)$ is true, so $y_0$ is a witness for $\exists y\; P(x, y)$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, the universal statement holds. For the failure of the converse, the six-arrow relation above is an example: there $\forall x\, \exists y\; L(x, y)$ is true and $\exists y\, \forall x\; L(x, y)$ is false.

### The same thing with real numbers

Over the real numbers, compare $\forall x\, \exists y\; (y > x)$ with $\exists y\, \forall x\; (y > x)$. It helps to read them as a game between you and me, with the moves made in the order the quantifiers are written. A $\forall$ is your move: you pick the value, trying to make me fail. An $\exists$ is my move. Whoever moves later can see the earlier moves.

[Figure 6, animation: Two games on the number line. Top: you pick x, then I pick y = x + 1, which is always larger, so "for all x there exists y > x" is true. Bottom: I must fix y first, and then you move x past it, so "there exists y larger than all x" is false.]

In the first game I move second and answer your $x$ with $y = x + 1$. That is a winning strategy, so $\forall x\, \exists y\; (y > x)$ is true. In the second I must name one $y$ before you move, and you reply with $x = y$. To prove it false properly, negate it with the theorem, one quantifier at a time:

$$
\lnot\, \exists y\, \forall x\; (y > x) \;\equiv\; \forall y\, \lnot \forall x\; (y > x) \;\equiv\; \forall y\, \exists x\; (y \le x),
$$

and this is true, with $x = y$ as the witness for each $y$.

**Key idea.** Read a string of quantifiers from left to right as moves in a game between a defender, who wants the statement to come out true, and an opponent: each $\forall$ is the opponent's choice, each $\exists$ is the defender's, and later choices may depend on earlier ones. The statement is true exactly when the defender has a winning strategy. To negate the statement, change every $\forall$ to $\exists$, every $\exists$ to $\forall$, and negate the predicate at the end.

The game is a way of reading the definitions and adds nothing to them: "for every $x$ there is a $y$" says exactly that whatever $x$ is chosen, a suitable $y$ can be found afterwards. One caution. Two quantifiers of the *same* kind may be swapped freely, since $\forall x\, \forall y$ and $\forall y\, \forall x$ both say "for all pairs", and likewise for $\exists$. Only a $\forall$ next to an $\exists$ is sensitive to order.

## The limit definition as a game

The best known sentence with three alternating quantifiers is the definition of a [limit](@calculus/limits). Let $a$ be a real number and let $f$ be a function defined at every point of some open interval containing $a$, except possibly at $a$ itself. Then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means

$$
\forall \varepsilon > 0\;\; \exists \delta > 0\;\; \forall x\;\; \bigl(0 < |x - a| < \delta \;\to\; |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\bigr).
$$

The calculus lesson writes the last part as "$0 < |x - a| < \delta$ implies $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$". The word "implies" there carries a silent "for every $x$", which is the third quantifier, and $x$ ranges over the points where $f$ is defined.

As a game: you choose a tolerance $\varepsilon$. I answer with a distance $\delta$, which may depend on your $\varepsilon$. You then choose any $x$. I win if the conditional holds, which means that either your $x$ is not within $\delta$ of $a$ (or equals $a$), and the conditional is vacuously true, or else $f(x)$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $L$. The limit is $L$ exactly when I have a strategy that wins against every $\varepsilon$.

Take $f(x) = 2x + 1$, $a = 1$ and $L = 3$. Then $|f(x) - 3| = |2x - 2| = 2|x - 1|$, so my strategy is $\delta = \varepsilon / 2$: if $|x - 1| < \delta$ then $|f(x) - 3| < 2\delta = \varepsilon$.

[Figure 7, animation: The limit game for f(x) = 2x + 1 at a = 1 with L = 3. You shrink the horizontal band of half-height \varepsilon around 3. The piece of the graph over my window sticks out of the band until I answer by shrinking the window to half-width \delta = \varepsilon / 2.]

The order $\forall \varepsilon\, \exists \delta$ is the first reading of "everyone loves someone": each $\varepsilon$ gets its own $\delta$. Swap the two and you get $\exists \delta > 0\; \forall \varepsilon > 0\; \forall x\,(\dots)$, which demands one window that works for every tolerance at once. That forces $|f(x) - L|$ to be smaller than every positive number, so $f(x) = L$ exactly throughout the window. Even $2x + 1$ fails this. The definition of a limit depends on the order of its quantifiers.

**Pause and try.** Write out the negation of the limit definition: what does it mean that $L$ is *not* the limit of $f(x)$ as $x \to a$? Remember that $\forall \varepsilon > 0$ and $\exists \delta > 0$ keep their restrictions, and that the negation of $A \to B$ is $A \land \lnot B$.

**Answer.** $$
\exists \varepsilon > 0\;\; \forall \delta > 0\;\; \exists x\;\; \bigl(0 < |x - a| < \delta \;\land\; |f(x) - L| \ge \varepsilon\bigr).$$ There is a tolerance that cannot be met: however small a window is proposed, it contains a point $x \ne a$ at which $f(x)$ is at least $\varepsilon$ away from $L$.
$$

In the negated game the roles are exchanged. Now I move first, with a single $\varepsilon$, and I must beat every $\delta$ you offer. Let $f(x) = 1$ for $x > 0$ and $f(x) = -1$ for $x < 0$, and suppose you claim that $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 1$.

[Figure 8, steps: Refuting the claim that a step function has limit 1 at 0. I choose the tolerance 1. Whatever window you offer, I pick the point halfway to its left edge, where the function is -1, which is a distance 2 from the claimed limit.]

  - step: The function is -1 to the left of 0 and 1 to the right. The claim is that its limit at 0 is 1.
  - step: To refute the claim I move first, with tolerance 1. The band runs from 0 to 2, and the left half of the graph is outside it.
  - step: You offer the window of half-width 1. I pick x = -0.5, inside the window, where the function is -1.
  - step: You try a narrower window, 0.4. I pick x = -0.2. No window can work, because every window reaches a little to the left of 0.
Written as a proof: take $\varepsilon = 1$. Let $\delta > 0$ be arbitrary and put $x = -\delta/2$. Then $0 < |x - 0| = \delta/2 < \delta$, and $|f(x) - 1| = |-1 - 1| = 2 \ge 1$. This establishes $\exists \varepsilon\, \forall \delta\, \exists x\,(\dots)$, the negation of the claim. Notice the shape of the proof: one $\varepsilon$ exhibited, an arbitrary $\delta$ handled, and an $x$ produced that depends on $\delta$.

## Worked examples

**Worked example.** **Translate, then negate.** "Every real number has a real cube root."

The sentence speaks of every number $x$ and promises a root $y$ for it: $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\; \exists y \in \mathbb{R}\; (y^3 = x)$. The root depends on the number, so $\exists y$ comes second. The negation flips both quantifiers and negates the equation: $\exists x \in \mathbb{R}\; \forall y \in \mathbb{R}\; (y^3 \ne x)$, "some real number is the cube of nothing". The original is true (the witness for $x = 8$ is $y = 2$, for $x = -1$ it is $y = -1$, and in general $y = \sqrt[3]{x}$), so the negation is false. With the order swapped, $\exists y\, \forall x\; (y^3 = x)$ would say that one number is the cube root of everything, which is false.

**Worked example.** **All four combinations on a small domain.** Let $x$ and $y$ range over $\{1, 2, 3\}$ and let $P(x, y)$ be "$x + y = 4$". Decide $\forall x\, \exists y$, $\exists y\, \forall x$, $\exists x\, \exists y$ and $\forall x\, \forall y$.

The true pairs are $(1, 3)$, $(2, 2)$ and $(3, 1)$. In a grid they form a diagonal: one mark in each row, one in each column.

- $\forall x\, \exists y\; P$: every row has a mark, namely $y = 4 - x$. True.
- $\exists y\, \forall x\; P$: needs a full column. Each column has one mark out of three. False.
- $\exists x\, \exists y\; P$: needs one mark anywhere. True, for instance $(2, 2)$.
- $\forall x\, \forall y\; P$: needs every cell marked. False, for instance $1 + 1 \ne 4$.

**Worked example.** **Negating to prove something.** A function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is *bounded* if $\exists M \in \mathbb{R}\; \forall x \in \mathbb{R}\; (|f(x)| \le M)$. Show that $f(x) = x^2$ is not bounded.

We must prove the negation, $\forall M\, \exists x\; (|f(x)| > M)$. In game terms the opponent now picks $M$ and we answer with $x$, so our $x$ may depend on $M$. Let $M$ be any real number and take $x = |M| + 1$. Then $x \ge 1$, so $x^2 \ge x = |M| + 1 > |M| \ge M$. Hence $|f(x)| = x^2 > M$.

*Check:* for $M = 100$ this gives $x = 101$ and $x^2 = 10201 > 100$; for $M = -5$ it gives $x = 6$ and $36 > -5$.

## Common mistakes and edge cases

**Common mistake.** **Negating "all" as "none".** The negation of "all the lights are on" is "at least one light is off", not "all the lights are off". With three lights on and one off, both "all on" and "all off" are false, and a statement and its negation can never be false together.

**Common mistake.** **Letting $\delta$ depend on $x$.** In a limit proof the quantifiers come in the order $\varepsilon$, $\delta$, $x$. The $\delta$ is chosen before $x$ is known, so it may be built from $\varepsilon$ and $a$ but never from $x$. A "proof" that says "take $\delta = |x - a| + 1$" has quietly changed the statement to $\forall \varepsilon\, \forall x\, \exists \delta$, which is true of every function and says nothing.

Two edge cases. Over an empty domain $\forall x\, P(x)$ is true and $\exists x\, P(x)$ is false, so "for all" does not imply "there exists" unless the domain has at least one element. And "there exists" means *at least one*: if you want exactly one, say "there exists a unique $x$", which is the conjunction of $\exists x\, P(x)$ with $\forall x\, \forall y\,\bigl((P(x) \land P(y)) \to x = y\bigr)$.

## Stepping back

The hard part was noticing that English hides two things a mathematical sentence must show: which variables are "all" and which are "some", and in what order they are chosen. Once those are written down, truth is a matter of who can win a game, and negation is a mechanical exchange of the two players. Nearly every definition in analysis, including continuity, convergence and boundedness, is a short string of quantifiers, and reading one comes down to asking who moves when.

**Check yourself.** What is the negation of "every student has read some book on the list"?
Answer: Some student has read no book on the list. $\lnot\,\forall s\, \exists b\; R(s, b) \equiv \exists s\, \forall b\; \lnot R(s, b)$: both quantifiers flip and the predicate is negated.

**Recap.** - A predicate $P(x)$ becomes a statement when $x$ is given a value from the domain, or when it is quantified: $\forall x\, P(x)$ (true for every $x$) or $\exists x\, P(x)$ (true for at least one).
- One counterexample refutes a $\forall$. One witness proves an $\exists$. The domain is part of the statement.
- Negation: $\lnot \forall x\, P(x) \equiv \exists x\, \lnot P(x)$ and $\lnot \exists x\, P(x) \equiv \forall x\, \lnot P(x)$. With several quantifiers, flip each one and negate the predicate.
- Order matters between $\forall$ and $\exists$. $\exists y\, \forall x\, P$ implies $\forall x\, \exists y\, P$, and not conversely.
- Game reading: $\forall$ is the opponent's move and $\exists$ is the defender's, in the order written.
- $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ is $\forall \varepsilon > 0\, \exists \delta > 0\, \forall x\,(0 < |x - a| < \delta \to |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon)$. Its negation is $\exists \varepsilon > 0\, \forall \delta > 0\, \exists x\,(0 < |x - a| < \delta \land |f(x) - L| \ge \varepsilon)$.

## Problems

Problems 1 to 3 repeat the moves of the lesson, 4 to 6 combine them, and 7 and 8 go further.

**Problem 1.** Decide whether each statement is true, giving a witness, a counterexample or a short reason. (a) $\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}\; (n^2 \ge n)$. (b) $\exists x \in \mathbb{R}\; (x^2 < x)$. (c) $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\; \exists y \in \mathbb{R}\; (xy = 1)$. (d) $\exists y \in \mathbb{R}\; \forall x \in \mathbb{R}\; (xy = 0)$.

**Solution.** (a) True. If $n \le 0$ then $n^2 \ge 0 \ge n$. If $n \ge 1$ then $n^2 = n \cdot n \ge n \cdot 1 = n$. Every integer is in one of the two cases. (b) True, with witness $x = \frac12$: $\frac14 < \frac12$. (c) False: $x = 0$ is a counterexample, since $0 \cdot y = 0 \ne 1$ for every $y$. (d) True, with witness $y = 0$: $x \cdot 0 = 0$ for every $x$.

**Problem 2.** Negate each statement, moving the negation all the way in. (a) $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\; (x^2 \ne 2)$. (b) $\exists n \in \mathbb{N}\; \forall m \in \mathbb{N}\; (m \le n)$. (c) $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\; (x > 2 \to x^2 > 4)$. For (b), say which of the statement and its negation is true.

**Solution.** (a) $\exists x \in \mathbb{R}\; (x^2 = 2)$. (b) $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\; \exists m \in \mathbb{N}\; (m > n)$. The original says there is a largest natural number. The negation is true, with witness $m = n + 1$ for each $n$, so the original is false. (c) $\exists x \in \mathbb{R}\; (x > 2 \land x^2 \le 4)$, using the fact that the negation of $A \to B$ is $A \land \lnot B$.

**Problem 3.** On the domain $\{A, B, C\}$ the relation $L$ consists of exactly the pairs $(A, B)$, $(B, B)$ and $(C, A)$. Decide the truth of $\forall x\, \exists y\; L(x, y)$, $\exists y\, \forall x\; L(x, y)$, $\exists x\, \forall y\; L(x, y)$ and $\forall y\, \exists x\; L(x, y)$.

**Solution.** Draw the grid with rows $x$ and columns $y$: row A has a mark in column B, row B in column B, row C in column A. (1) Every row has a mark, so $\forall x\, \exists y\; L$ is true. (2) A full column is needed: column B has marks from A and B but not C, and columns A and C have fewer. False. (3) A full row is needed, and every row has only one mark. False. (4) Every column needs a mark, and column C has none. False.

**Problem 4.** Consider "for every positive real number there is a smaller positive real number". Write it with quantifiers and decide whether it is true. Then swap the two quantifiers, say in words what the new statement claims, and decide whether it is true.

**Solution.** $\forall x > 0\; \exists y > 0\; (y < x)$. True: given $x$, take $y = x/2$, which is positive and less than $x$. Swapped: $\exists y > 0\; \forall x > 0\; (y < x)$, "there is a positive real number smaller than every positive real number". This is false. Its negation is $\forall y > 0\; \exists x > 0\; (y \ge x)$, which is true with $x = y$.

**Problem 5.** Play the limit game for $f(x) = 3x - 1$ at $a = 2$ with $L = 5$: give a strategy for choosing $\delta$ from $\varepsilon$ and prove that it wins.

**Solution.** We have $|f(x) - 5| = |3x - 6| = 3|x - 2|$. Strategy: given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\delta = \varepsilon / 3$. Now let $x$ be any number with $0 < |x - 2| < \delta$. Then $|f(x) - 5| = 3|x - 2| < 3\delta = \varepsilon$. The conditional holds for every $x$, so $\forall \varepsilon > 0\, \exists \delta > 0\, \forall x\,(\dots)$ is true and $\lim_{x \to 2}(3x - 1) = 5$. For instance, against $\varepsilon = 0.03$ the reply is $\delta = 0.01$.

**Problem 6.** "There are infinitely many primes" can be written $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\; \exists p \in \mathbb{N}\; (p > n \land p \text{ is prime})$. Write its negation with the negation moved all the way in, and say in words what the negation claims.

**Solution.** Flip both quantifiers and negate the predicate with De Morgan's law: $\exists n \in \mathbb{N}\; \forall p \in \mathbb{N}\; (p \le n \lor p \text{ is not prime})$. By the equivalence $\lnot A \lor B \equiv A \to B$, the bracket can also be written "$p$ is prime $\to p \le n$". In words: there is a number $n$ such that every prime is at most $n$, that is, the primes are bounded above. (Euclid proved that this negation is false.)

**Problem 7.** Use the negated definition to prove that $\lim_{x \to 1} (2x + 1)$ is not $3.5$.

**Solution.** We need $\exists \varepsilon > 0\; \forall \delta > 0\; \exists x\; (0 < |x - 1| < \delta \land |2x + 1 - 3.5| \ge \varepsilon)$. Choose $\varepsilon = 0.25$. Let $\delta > 0$ be arbitrary, and pick any $x$ with $0 < |x - 1| < \delta$ and also $|x - 1| < 0.1$ (for instance $x = 1 + \min(\delta, 0.1)/2$). Then $|(2x + 1) - 3| = 2|x - 1| < 0.2$, so $2x + 1$ lies between $2.8$ and $3.2$, and its distance from $3.5$ is more than $0.3$, which is at least $0.25$. Both parts of the conjunction hold.

**Problem 8.** Let $f(x) = 1$ for $x > 0$ and $f(x) = -1$ for $x < 0$. The lesson showed that 1 is not the limit of $f$ at 0. Prove that *no* real number $L$ is: write the statement "$f$ has no limit at 0" with quantifiers, and prove it.

**Solution.** "$f$ has a limit at 0" is $\exists L\, \forall \varepsilon > 0\, \exists \delta > 0\, \forall x\,(0 < |x| < \delta \to |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon)$. Its negation is

$$
\forall L\;\; \exists \varepsilon > 0\;\; \forall \delta > 0\;\; \exists x\;\; \bigl(0 < |x| < \delta \land |f(x) - L| \ge \varepsilon\bigr).
$$

Let $L$ be any real number and choose $\varepsilon = 1$. Let $\delta > 0$ be arbitrary. Consider the two points $x_1 = \delta/2$ and $x_2 = -\delta/2$; both satisfy $0 < |x| < \delta$, and $f(x_1) = 1$, $f(x_2) = -1$. If both $|1 - L| < 1$ and $|-1 - L| < 1$ held, the triangle inequality would give $2 = |1 - (-1)| \le |1 - L| + |L - (-1)| < 2$, which is impossible. So at least one of $|f(x_1) - L| \ge 1$, $|f(x_2) - L| \ge 1$ holds, and we choose $x$ to be that point. Notice the order of dependence: $\varepsilon$ did not depend on $L$ here, but $x$ depended on both $\delta$ and $L$, as the quantifiers allow.

---

# Proof by contradiction: why √2 is not a fraction

> No fraction squares to exactly 2. To prove it, assume one does and follow the assumption until it breaks. That method is proof by contradiction.

Series: Logic and Proof (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/logic/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/logic/proof-by-contradiction/
Keywords: proof by contradiction, square root of 2 is irrational, irrational numbers, infinite descent, well-ordering principle, infinitely many primes, Euclid's proof, contrapositive vs contradiction

[Figure 1, animation: A square floor of side 17 holds 289 cells. Two square tiles of side 12 hold 288 between them. In opposite corners they overlap in 49 cells and leave two corners of 25 cells bare, so the tiles fall one cell short.]

A square floor 17 units on a side has area 289. Two square tiles 12 units on a side have a combined area of 288. If the two numbers agreed we would have $17^2 = 2 \times 12^2$, which says $\left(\frac{17}{12}\right)^2 = 2$, and the fraction $\frac{17}{12}$ would be the square root of 2. It misses by one part in 289, and with all the whole numbers there are to choose from it seems certain that some other pair closes the gap.

No pair does, and this has been known for well over two thousand years. The puzzle is how anyone could know it, since there are infinitely many fractions and checking them one at a time never ends. A proof has to deal with every fraction at once. The method that does so is to suppose that a fraction with square 2 exists and to reason from that supposition until it produces something impossible.

Three earlier facts are used below. From [truth tables](@logic/truth-tables): a statement is either true or false, and $Q \land \lnot Q$ is false whatever $Q$ is. From [implication](@logic/implication): $P \to Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false, and it is equivalent to its contrapositive $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$.
