So $f$ is not surjective, and no bijection exists; $B$ is also infinite, so it is uncountable. (b) Two sequences are equal only when all their terms agree, by definition. The elements of $B$ are the sequences themselves, not numbers represented by them, so two different sequences are never the same element. (c) List the strings by length, and within each length in dictionary order: the empty string, then $0, 1$, then $00, 01, 10, 11$, and so on. There are $2^k$ strings of length $k$, a finite number, so every string is reached after finitely many steps and appears once.

**Problem 6.** A student argues: "The rationals between 0 and 1 are uncountable. Take any list of them, and form the diagonal number $x$. It is not on the list. So no list is complete." Find the error. Then explain what, if anything, the argument does prove about $x$.

**Solution.** The diagonal construction produces a real number $x$ that is not on the list. To contradict "the list contains every rational in $(0,1)$" one would need $x$ to be rational, and nothing in the construction provides that. So there is no contradiction. In fact the rationals in $(0, 1)$ are countable, so a complete list exists, and for that list the argument proves that $x$ is irrational: $x$ is a real number in $(0, 1)$ different from every rational in $(0, 1)$.

**Problem 7.** (a) Let $S$ and $T$ be countably infinite sets with no element in common. Prove that $S \cup T$ is countably infinite. (b) Deduce that the set of irrational numbers is uncountable.

**Solution.** (a) Let $s_1, s_2, \dots$ and $t_1, t_2, \dots$ be lists of $S$ and $T$ in which each element appears once. Interleave them: $s_1, t_1, s_2, t_2, \dots$, that is, $h(2k - 1) = s_k$ and $h(2k) = t_k$. Every element of $S \cup T$ is some $s_k$ or some $t_k$, so it appears. No element appears twice, because the $s_k$ are distinct, the $t_k$ are distinct, and no $s_k$ equals a $t_j$ since the sets are disjoint. So $h$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ to $S \cup T$. (b) Suppose, for contradiction, that the set $I$ of irrational numbers is countable. It is not finite: the numbers $\sqrt 2 + n$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ are all irrational (if $\sqrt 2 + n$ were a rational $r$, then $\sqrt 2 = r - n$ would be rational) and all different. So $I$ is countably infinite. The set $\mathbb{Q}$ is countably infinite, and $\mathbb{Q}$ and $I$ have no element in common. By part (a), $\mathbb{R} = \mathbb{Q} \cup I$ is countably infinite. But $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable. This contradiction shows that $I$ is uncountable. In this sense almost all real numbers are irrational.

---

# Position, velocity and acceleration: reading motion graphs

> Slope turns a position graph into velocity and velocity into acceleration; area goes back. The constant-acceleration equations come from one trapezoid.

Series: Physics (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/physics/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/physics/motion-graphs/
Keywords: position velocity acceleration, motion graphs, position-time graph, velocity-time graph, area under velocity graph, kinematic equations, constant acceleration, displacement

[Figure 1, animation: A car's 20 seconds on a straight, flat road, played at double speed. The curve records its position, measured in meters from where it started, against time.]

The graph above records where a car was during twenty seconds on a straight road. From the graph alone, try to say when the car was moving fastest, when it was standing still, and when it was going backward.

The tempting answer to the first question is "at the top", because that is where the graph is highest. But the height of this graph is the car's position, and between 12 and 14 seconds, where the graph is highest, the car is parked 96 meters down the road. The road is flat the whole way; the hill exists only in the graph.

**Pause and try.** Watch the animation again and commit to answers. During which stretch of time is the car fastest? When is it stopped? When is it reversing? For each, say what feature of the *graph* told you.

**Answer.** It is fastest from 4 s to 8 s, where the graph climbs most steeply. It is stopped from 12 s to 14 s, where the graph is flat. It reverses from 14 s to 20 s, where the graph falls. In every case the information is in how steep the graph is and which way it tilts, and none of it is in how high the graph is.

## Position needs an origin and a direction

To graph a motion we first have to turn "where the car is" into a number. Pick one point on the road and call it the origin. Pick one of the two directions along the road and call it positive. Every number that follows depends on these two choices, so a careful solution states them at the start. Here the origin is the place where the car starts, and the positive direction is the way it first drives.

**Definition.** For an object moving along a straight line with a chosen origin and positive direction, its **position** $x(t)$ at time $t$ is its distance from the origin, in meters (m), taken as positive on the positive side of the origin and negative on the other side. Time $t$ is in seconds (s). The **displacement** from time $t_1$ to time $t_2$ is the change in position,

$$
\Delta x = x(t_2) - x(t_1),
$$

which can have either sign. The **distance traveled** is the total length of path covered, which is never negative.

The symbol $\Delta$ is read "change in". For our car, $x(0) = 0$ m, $x(12) = 96$ m and $x(20) = 72$ m. Its displacement over the whole trip is $72 - 0 = +72$ m, but the distance it traveled is $96 + 24 = 120$ m, because it drove 96 m forward and then 24 m back.

## Velocity is the slope of the position graph

Start where the motion is simplest. From 4 s to 8 s the graph is a straight line from 24 m up to 72 m, so the car covers 48 m in 4 s:

$$
\frac{72 \text{ m} - 24 \text{ m}}{8 \text{ s} - 4 \text{ s}} = 12 \text{ m/s}.
$$

On the graph this is rise over run, the [slope](@algebra/slope-and-lines) of the line, and it comes with units: meters on the vertical axis divided by seconds on the horizontal axis.

**Definition.** The **average velocity** of an object from time $t_1$ to time $t_2$ (with $t_2 \neq t_1$) is

$$
v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1},
$$

measured in meters per second (m/s). On a position graph it is the slope of the straight line joining the two points.

Now try the same recipe on the first four seconds. The car goes from 0 m to 24 m, an average of 6 m/s. That number is correct and unsatisfying, because the graph is curved there: the car began at rest and was doing 12 m/s by the end. What we want is the velocity at one moment, say at $t = 3$ s. An average needs an interval, so we use intervals that start at 3 s and get shorter.

[Figure 2, steps: Slopes read off the car's position graph. On a straight stretch one slope describes the whole stretch; on a curved stretch the slope over a shrinking interval settles toward the velocity at a single moment.]

  - step: From 4 s to 8 s the graph is straight: 48 m in 4 s, a slope of 12 m/s.
  - step: From 3 s to 4 s, on the curved part, the car covers 10.5 m: an average of 10.5 m/s.
  - step: Shrink the interval to a tenth of a second: from 3 s to 3.1 s the slope is 9.15 m/s.
  - step: From 12 s to 14 s the graph is flat. The slope is 0: the car is parked.
  - step: From 16 s to 18 s the graph falls 12 m in 2 s. The slope is negative: the car is backing up.
Over the intervals from 3 s to 4 s, to 3.5 s and to 3.1 s the average velocities are 10.5, 9.75 and 9.15 m/s. They are heading for 9, and we can see why. During the first four seconds this car's position is $x = 1.5t^2$ meters (we will derive that formula below), so from $t = 3$ to $t = 3 + h$ the average velocity is

$$
\frac{1.5(3+h)^2 - 1.5(3)^2}{h} = \frac{9h + 1.5h^2}{h} = 9 + 1.5h \text{ m/s}.
$$

The leftover $1.5h$ can be made as small as we like by shortening the interval, and the only number the averages approach is 9. That number is what we mean by the velocity at $t = 3$ s.

**Definition.** The **instantaneous velocity** $v(t)$ is the value approached by the average velocity over intervals containing $t$ as their length shrinks to zero, when there is such a value. On the position graph it is the slope of the tangent line at time $t$. The **speed** is the magnitude $|v(t)|$.

**Note.** If you know calculus: this is the derivative, $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, and [What is a derivative?](@calculus/what-is-a-derivative) makes "approached by" precise. Nothing below needs more than slopes.

Velocity carries a sign, and the sign means direction. A positive slope says the car moves in the positive direction, a negative slope says it moves the other way, and zero slope says it is at rest. That settles the opening questions: steepest climb from 4 s to 8 s ($v = 12$ m/s), flat from 12 s to 14 s ($v = 0$), falling from 14 s to 20 s ($v < 0$, with $v = -6$ m/s on the straight part).

If we read the slope at every moment and plot it, we get a second graph. Then we can do the same thing to that graph and get a third.

[Figure 3, animation: The same trip at double speed with three graphs drawn in step: position, the slope of the position graph (velocity), and the slope of the velocity graph (acceleration).]

## Acceleration is the slope of the velocity graph

The velocity graph of this trip is made of straight pieces, which is what makes it a good first example. Look at the first one. In 4 s the velocity rises from 0 to 12 m/s, so the car gains 3 m/s of velocity every second. A rate of "meters per second, per second" is written m/s².

**Definition.** The **average acceleration** from $t_1$ to $t_2$ is $a_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v(t_2) - v(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}$, in m/s². The **instantaneous acceleration** $a(t)$ is the value it approaches as the interval shrinks to zero around $t$: the slope of the velocity graph at time $t$.

Reading the slope of each straight piece gives the whole trip in one table.

| Time (s) | Velocity (m/s) | Acceleration (m/s²) | What the car is doing |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 to 4 | 0 up to 12 | $+3$ | speeding up, forward |
| 4 to 8 | 12 | 0 | cruising forward |
| 8 to 12 | 12 down to 0 | $-3$ | slowing down, forward |
| 12 to 14 | 0 | 0 | parked |
| 14 to 16 | 0 down to $-6$ | $-3$ | speeding up, backward |
| 16 to 18 | $-6$ | 0 | cruising backward |
| 18 to 20 | $-6$ up to 0 | $+3$ | slowing down, backward |

[Figure 4, image: The car's velocity graph (top) with a slope triangle on each sloping piece, and its acceleration graph (bottom) on the same time axis. Each level of the lower graph is the slope of the piece above it.]

Two rows of the table deserve a second look. From 14 s to 16 s the acceleration is negative and the car is speeding up. From 18 s to 20 s the acceleration is positive and the car is slowing down. Acceleration says which way the velocity is changing, and whether that makes the car faster or slower depends on which way it is already going. The rule that covers all seven rows is this: an object speeds up when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign, and slows down when they have opposite signs.

**Common mistake.** **"Negative acceleration means slowing down."** It is tempting because the first example anyone meets is a car braking while it moves in the positive direction. But a car reversing harder and harder has $v < 0$ and $a < 0$, and its speed is increasing. Compare the signs of $v$ and $a$ before you say "speeding up" or "slowing down".

## Going back: area under the velocity graph

Slopes took us from position to velocity. Suppose now that only the velocity graph survived, and we want to recover how far the car went.

Where the velocity is constant this is easy. From 4 s to 8 s the car does 12 m/s for 4 s, so $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t = 12 \times 4 = 48$ m. On the velocity graph, 12 is the height of a rectangle and 4 is its width, so the displacement is the rectangle's area. The units agree: (m/s) × s = m.

During the first four seconds the velocity is changing, and there is no single height to multiply by. So we cut the time into short strips and treat the velocity as constant within each one. We can do this honestly in two ways. If the car's velocity stays between 3 m/s and 6 m/s during some second, it travels at least 3 m and at most 6 m in that second. Using the lowest velocity in every strip gives a total that is too small, and using the highest gives one that is too large.

**Pause and try.** Cut the first 4 s into four strips of 1 s. The velocity is $v = 3t$, so it is 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12 m/s at $t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$. Find the too-small total and the too-large total. Then guess the exact displacement.

**Answer.** Too small: $(0 + 3 + 6 + 9) \times 1 = 18$ m. Too large: $(3 + 6 + 9 + 12) \times 1 = 30$ m. The truth is somewhere between, and the midpoint, 24 m, is the natural guess. The figure tests it.

[Figure 5, steps: The first four seconds of the velocity graph cut into strips. The blue rectangles use the lowest velocity in each strip and the grey caps raise them to the highest, so the true displacement is trapped between the two totals.]

  - step: Four strips of 1 s: the displacement is between 18 m and 30 m.
  - step: Eight strips: between 21 m and 27 m.
  - step: Sixteen strips: between 22.5 m and 25.5 m.
  - step: Sixty-four strips: between 23.625 m and 24.375 m. Both totals close in on 24 m, the area of the triangle under the line.
With $n$ strips the two totals work out to $24 - 24/n$ and $24 + 24/n$ meters. The true displacement lies between them for every $n$, and so does the area of the triangle under the line, since the blue staircase fits inside the triangle and the capped one covers it. Two numbers that are both trapped in an interval of width $48/n$, for every $n$, cannot differ. So the displacement in the first four seconds equals the triangle's area exactly: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \text{ s} \times 12 \text{ m/s} = 24$ m, which is where the graph put the car at $t = 4$ s.

To be clear about the status of that argument: for a velocity graph that is a straight line, we have proved that displacement equals area, given one physical fact: over any interval, the displacement is at least the lowest velocity times the duration and at most the highest velocity times the duration. For a curved velocity graph the same trapping works, but showing that the two totals always close in on a single number takes more care; that is the subject of [integrals](@calculus/integrals) and the [fundamental theorem of calculus](@calculus/fundamental-theorem).

One more point before we use it. From 14 s to 20 s the velocity is negative, and $v\,\Delta t$ is negative for every strip, so the region between the graph and the time axis counts as negative there. Displacement is a **signed area**: regions above the axis add and regions below it subtract.

[Figure 6, steps: Signed area under the car's velocity graph, accumulated from the start of the trip, rebuilds the position graph. Area above the time axis is blue and counts as positive; area below is gold and counts as negative.]

  - step: For the first 4 s the area under the velocity graph is a triangle: 24 m.
  - step: From 4 s to 8 s a rectangle adds 12 times 4, or 48 m. The car is at 72 m.
  - step: Braking from 8 s to 12 s adds another triangle of 24 m: 96 m in all.
  - step: While the car is parked the velocity is zero and no area is added.
  - step: From 14 s to 20 s the velocity is negative. That area is -24 m, and the car ends at 72 m.
**Key idea.** On a position graph, the slope is the velocity. On a velocity graph, the slope is the acceleration, and the signed area between the graph and the time axis from $t_1$ to $t_2$ is the displacement $x(t_2) - x(t_1)$.

Notice what area cannot tell you: it gives the *change* in position, so to know where the car is you need its starting position as well. The same argument one level up shows that the signed area under an acceleration graph is the change in velocity.

## Constant acceleration: four equations from one trapezoid

Many motions have a stretch of constant acceleration: a car braking steadily, a ball in the air. For those the velocity graph is one straight line, the area under it is a trapezoid, and everything can be written as a formula.

**Pause and try.** A car moving at 4 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. Sketch its velocity graph and find its displacement from the area, by splitting the region under the line into a rectangle and a triangle.

**Answer.** The velocity climbs from 4 m/s to $4 + 2 \times 5 = 14$ m/s. The rectangle is 4 m/s tall and 5 s wide: 20 m. The triangle on top is 5 s wide and $14 - 4 = 10$ m/s tall: $\tfrac12 \times 5 \times 10 = 25$ m. Displacement: 45 m.

[Figure 7, image: The velocity graph for a car that starts at 4 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. The rectangle is the distance it would cover at its starting velocity; the triangle is the extra distance gained by speeding up.]

Replace the numbers with letters and the same picture gives the general result.

**Theorem.** (Constant-acceleration equations.) Suppose an object moves along a line with constant acceleration $a$ throughout the time interval from $0$ to $t$, and has position $x_0$ and velocity $v_0$ at time 0. Then its velocity $v$ and position $x$ at time $t$ satisfy

- $v = v_0 + at$,
- $x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^2$,
- $x - x_0 = \tfrac{1}{2}(v_0 + v)\,t$,
- $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,(x - x_0)$.

**Proof.** (1) Constant acceleration means the velocity graph is a straight line of slope $a$. Its slope between times 0 and $t$ is $(v - v_0)/t = a$, so $v = v_0 + at$.

(2) The displacement $x - x_0$ is the signed area between the velocity graph and the time axis from 0 to $t$, as shown above for straight-line graphs. Split that region at the height $v_0$. Below is a rectangle of width $t$ and height $v_0$, with signed area $v_0 t$. Above is a triangle of width $t$ and height $v - v_0 = at$, with signed area $\tfrac{1}{2}\,t\,(at) = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. (If $v_0$ or $a$ is negative, the corresponding piece lies below its base line and counts as negative, which is what the formulas $v_0 t$ and $\tfrac12 at^2$ give.) Adding, $x - x_0 = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

(3) Substitute $at = v - v_0$ from (1) into (2): $x - x_0 = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}(v - v_0)t = \tfrac{1}{2}(v_0 + v)t$.

(4) If $a \neq 0$, (1) gives $t = (v - v_0)/a$. Put this into (3): $x - x_0 = \dfrac{(v_0 + v)(v - v_0)}{2a} = \dfrac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2a}$, and multiply by $2a$. If $a = 0$ then $v = v_0$ and (4) reads $v^2 = v_0^2$, which is true.

Check the units of (2): $v_0 t$ is (m/s)(s) = m and $\tfrac12 at^2$ is (m/s²)(s²) = m, so every term is a length. In (4) every term is in m²/s². A formula whose terms have different units is wrong.

Each equation leaves out one of the quantities $x - x_0$, $v$, $a$, $t$, and that tells you which to reach for: (4) has no $t$ in it, so it answers "how far" questions when nobody has told you how long.

The first four seconds of our car are the case $x_0 = 0$, $v_0 = 0$, $a = 3$ m/s², where (2) gives $x = 1.5t^2$, the formula we borrowed earlier. Another case is worth recognizing. An object falling freely near the Earth's surface, with air resistance neglected, has a constant downward acceleration of magnitude $g \approx 9.8$ m/s². Dropped from rest, it falls $\tfrac12 g t^2 = 4.9t^2$ meters in $t$ seconds, which rounds to the $5t^2$ used for the falling ball in the calculus lesson linked above.

## Worked examples

**Worked example.** **Braking distance.** A car traveling at 25 m/s (90 km/h) brakes with a constant acceleration of magnitude 7 m/s², typical of hard braking on a dry road. How far does it travel before stopping? What if it starts at 50 m/s?

Take the direction of travel as positive, so $v_0 = 25$ m/s, $v = 0$ and $a = -7$ m/s². We want a distance and have no time, so we use (4): $0 = v_0^2 + 2a\,\Delta x$, which gives

$$
\Delta x = \frac{-v_0^2}{2a} = \frac{-(25)^2}{2(-7)} = \frac{625}{14} \approx 44.6 \text{ m}.
$$

At 50 m/s the same formula gives $2500/14 \approx 178.6$ m. Doubling the speed multiplied the stopping distance by four, because $v_0$ enters squared.

*Check* with the graph: braking takes $t = 25/7 \approx 3.57$ s, and the area of the triangle under the velocity line is $\tfrac12 \times 3.57 \times 25 \approx 44.6$ m. At double the speed the triangle is twice as tall and twice as wide.

**Worked example.** **A ball thrown straight up.** A ball leaves a hand 2 m above the ground moving upward at 15 m/s. Neglect air resistance. How high does it get, when does it land, and how fast is it moving when it does?

Set the origin at the ground and take up as positive. Gravity pulls downward, so $a = -9.8$ m/s² for the whole flight, on the way up as well as on the way down. With $y$ for height, $y_0 = 2$ m and $v_0 = +15$ m/s.

*Highest point.* The ball is at its highest when it stops rising, that is, when $v = 0$. From (1), $0 = 15 - 9.8t$, so $t = 1.53$ s. From (4), $0 = 15^2 + 2(-9.8)(y - 2)$, so $y = 2 + 225/19.6 = 13.5$ m.

*Landing.* We need the time when $y = 0$. From (2), $0 = 2 + 15t - 4.9t^2$, and the quadratic formula gives

$$
t = \frac{15 \pm \sqrt{15^2 + 4(4.9)(2)}}{2(4.9)} = \frac{15 \pm 16.25}{9.8},
$$

so $t = 3.19$ s or $t = -0.13$ s. The flight starts at $t = 0$, so the landing is at 3.19 s. Then $v = 15 - 9.8 \times 3.19 = -16.3$ m/s: it lands moving downward at 16.3 m/s.

*Check* with (4), which does not use the time: $v^2 = 15^2 + 2(-9.8)(0 - 2) = 264.2$, so $|v| = 16.3$ m/s.

[Figure 8, animation: The thrown ball in real time, with its height graph and velocity graph. The velocity falls along one straight line of slope -9.8 m/s² for the whole flight and passes through zero at the top.]

At the top of the flight the velocity is zero and the acceleration is still $-9.8$ m/s². If both were zero the ball would stay there.

**Common mistake.** **Reading the graph as a picture of the path.** The height graph of the thrown ball is an arch, and the ball went straight up and straight down. The car's position graph has a hill, and the road is flat. A motion graph has time on its horizontal axis, so its shape shows how one quantity changed, and never the shape of the route. Read the axes first.

## Where the equations stop working

The four equations were proved for one stretch of constant acceleration, and they fail the moment that hypothesis does. Apply (2) blindly to the car's whole trip with the first phase's numbers, $x = \tfrac12 (3)(20)^2$, and you get 600 m; the car is actually at 72 m. For a motion with several phases, use the equations one phase at a time, feeding the final position and velocity of each phase into the next as its $x_0$ and $v_0$, or go back to slopes and areas, which do not need the acceleration to be constant.

Free fall is the other place to be careful. Air resistance grows with speed, so a real falling object's acceleration shrinks as it speeds up. For a ball thrown across a room the effect is too small to notice. For a skydiver it dominates: the model $v = 9.8t$ predicts 98 m/s after ten seconds, while a real skydiver in a spread position levels off near 55 m/s.

Finally, our car's acceleration jumps from $+3$ to 0 at $t = 4$ s. The velocity graph has a corner there, so its slope, and with it the acceleration, has no single value at that instant. Real cars change acceleration over a few tenths of a second, which rounds the corners and changes the distances very little.

**Check yourself.** A ball thrown straight up is at the highest point of its flight. Taking up as positive and neglecting air resistance, what are its velocity and acceleration at that instant?
Answer: $v = 0$ and $a = -9.8$ m/s² The ball has stopped rising, so $v = 0$, and gravity gives it the same downward acceleration at every moment of the flight.

**Recap.** - Position $x(t)$ needs a stated origin and positive direction. Displacement $\Delta x$ is signed; distance traveled is not.
- Velocity is the slope of the position graph (m/s). Acceleration is the slope of the velocity graph (m/s²). Both carry signs that depend on the chosen positive direction.
- An object speeds up when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign and slows down when they have opposite signs.
- Displacement is the signed area under the velocity graph.
- For constant acceleration only: $v = v_0 + at$, $x = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac12 at^2$, $x - x_0 = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)t$, $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)$.
- Free fall without air resistance is constant acceleration of magnitude $g \approx 9.8$ m/s², directed downward.

The next lesson, on [Newton's second law](@physics/newtons-second-law), asks what sets the acceleration in the first place, and the answer is force.

## Problems

Use $g = 9.8$ m/s² and neglect air resistance unless told otherwise. State your origin and positive direction in every solution.

**Problem 1.** Using the car of this lesson, find its average velocity from $t = 2$ s to $t = 10$ s. (You will need $x(2)$ and $x(10)$; get them from the constant-acceleration equations.)

**Solution.** During the first phase $x = 1.5t^2$, so $x(2) = 6$ m. The third phase starts at $t = 8$ s with $x_0 = 72$ m, $v_0 = 12$ m/s and $a = -3$ m/s²; two seconds into it, $x = 72 + 12(2) + \tfrac12(-3)(2)^2 = 90$ m. So $v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{90 - 6}{10 - 2} = 10.5$ m/s. As a check, the area under the velocity graph from 2 s to 10 s is two trapezoids of $\tfrac12(6 + 12)(2) = 18$ m each and a rectangle of 48 m: 84 m in total.

**Problem 2.** A cyclist riding at 4 m/s accelerates uniformly to 10 m/s over 3 s and then holds that velocity for 5 s. Find her acceleration during the first 3 s and her total displacement over the 8 s.

**Solution.** Take her direction of travel as positive. Acceleration: $a = (10 - 4)/3 = 2$ m/s². The area under the velocity graph is a trapezoid followed by a rectangle. Trapezoid: $\tfrac12(4 + 10)(3) = 21$ m. Rectangle: $10 \times 5 = 50$ m. Total displacement: 71 m.

**Problem 3.** At what times is the lesson's car exactly 84 m from its starting point?

**Solution.** The position rises to 96 m and comes back to 72 m, so it passes 84 m twice. *On the way out:* at $t = 8$ s the car is at 72 m, so 84 m is reached during the braking phase, where $x = 72 + 12u - 1.5u^2$ with $u = t - 8$. Setting this equal to 84 gives $1.5u^2 - 12u + 12 = 0$, that is, $u^2 - 8u + 8 = 0$, so $u = 4 \pm 2\sqrt2$. Only $u = 4 - 2\sqrt2 \approx 1.17$ lies within the phase ($0 \le u \le 4$), so $t \approx 9.17$ s. *On the way back:* at $t = 16$ s the car is at $96 - 6 = 90$ m and then moves at $-6$ m/s, so it reaches 84 m one second later, at $t = 17$ s.

**Problem 4.** A driver traveling at 30 m/s sees an obstacle 80 m ahead. Her reaction time is 0.8 s, during which the car keeps its velocity, and then she brakes at a constant 7.5 m/s². (a) What total distance would the car need to stop? (b) How fast is it moving when it reaches the obstacle?

**Solution.** Positive in the direction of travel, origin where she first sees the obstacle. (a) During the reaction time the car covers $30 \times 0.8 = 24$ m. Braking from 30 m/s to rest: $0 = 30^2 + 2(-7.5)\Delta x$, so $\Delta x = 900/15 = 60$ m. Total: 84 m, which is 4 m more than she has. (b) Braking begins at $x = 24$ m, leaving $80 - 24 = 56$ m. Then $v^2 = 30^2 + 2(-7.5)(56) = 900 - 840 = 60$, so $v \approx 7.7$ m/s. The last 4 m of the stopping distance would have removed the final 7.7 m/s.

**Problem 5.** For each statement, say whether it is true or false, and give an example from this lesson that supports your answer. (a) If an object's velocity is zero at some instant, its acceleration is zero at that instant. (b) If an object's acceleration is zero over an interval, it is at rest. (c) If an object's acceleration is positive, its speed is increasing.

**Solution.** (a) False. The thrown ball at the top of its flight has $v = 0$ and $a = -9.8$ m/s². (b) False. From 4 s to 8 s the car has $a = 0$ and moves steadily at 12 m/s; zero acceleration means constant velocity, and rest is only the special case $v = 0$. (c) False. From 18 s to 20 s the car has $a = +3$ m/s² and $v < 0$, and its speed drops from 6 m/s to 0. Speed increases only when $a$ and $v$ have the same sign.

**Problem 6.** A speeding car passes a parked police car at a constant 24 m/s. At that instant the police car starts from rest with constant acceleration 3 m/s². (a) When and where does the police car draw level? (b) How fast is it going then? (c) Explain the answer to (b) using the two velocity graphs, without equations.

**Solution.** Origin at the parked police car, positive along the road, $t = 0$ when the speeder passes. (a) Speeder: $x = 24t$. Police: $x = \tfrac12(3)t^2 = 1.5t^2$. They are level when $1.5t^2 = 24t$, so $t = 0$ (the start) or $t = 16$ s, at $x = 24 \times 16 = 384$ m. (b) $v = 3 \times 16 = 48$ m/s, exactly twice the speeder's velocity. (c) Both cars have the same displacement at the moment they are level, so the areas under their velocity graphs from 0 to that time are equal. The speeder's is a rectangle of height 24; the police car's is a triangle on the same base. A triangle has half the area of a rectangle with the same base and height, so to match the rectangle the triangle must be twice as tall: 48 m/s.

**Problem 7.** Galileo found that a ball starting from rest with constant acceleration covers distances in successive equal time intervals in the ratio $1 : 3 : 5 : 7 : \dots$ Prove it. Then explain it from the velocity graph.

**Solution.** Let the intervals have length $\tau$ and the acceleration be $a$, with $x_0 = 0$ and $v_0 = 0$. At the end of the $n$th interval $t = n\tau$ and $x = \tfrac12 a n^2\tau^2$. The distance covered during the $n$th interval is therefore

$$
\tfrac12 a\tau^2\bigl(n^2 - (n-1)^2\bigr) = \tfrac12 a\tau^2\,(2n - 1).
$$

For $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$ the factor $2n - 1$ is $1, 3, 5, 7$. On the velocity graph, a line through the origin, cut the region under the line at $t = \tau, 2\tau, 3\tau, \dots$ The first piece is a triangle of area $\tfrac12 a\tau^2$. Each later piece is a trapezoid that can be tiled by copies of that triangle: the $n$th strip is a rectangle of height $(n-1)a\tau$, which is $2(n-1)$ triangles, with one more triangle on top, making $2n - 1$.

**Problem 8.** (a) Prove that for motion with constant acceleration, the average velocity over any time interval equals the instantaneous velocity at the middle instant of that interval. (b) Show with the lesson's car that this can fail when the acceleration is not constant over the interval.

**Solution.** (a) Let the interval run from $t_1$ to $t_2$ with velocities $v_1$ and $v_2$ at its ends. Equation (3), applied with the clock started at $t_1$, gives $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_1 + v_2)(t_2 - t_1)$, so $v_{\text{avg}} = \tfrac12(v_1 + v_2)$. The velocity at the middle instant $t_m = \tfrac12(t_1 + t_2)$ is, by equation (1), $v_1 + a\,(t_m - t_1) = v_1 + \tfrac12 a(t_2 - t_1) = v_1 + \tfrac12(v_2 - v_1) = \tfrac12(v_1 + v_2)$. (b) Take the interval from 0 s to 8 s. The average velocity is $72/8 = 9$ m/s. The middle instant is $t = 4$ s, when the velocity is 12 m/s. They differ because the acceleration changed from 3 m/s² to 0 at $t = 4$ s, so the velocity graph over this interval is not a single straight line.

# Newton's second law, F = ma: what force really does

> Forces change an object's velocity; none is needed to keep it moving. Newton's three laws, free-body diagrams, the incline and the Atwood machine in full.

Series: Physics (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/physics/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/physics/newtons-second-law/
Keywords: Newton's second law, F = ma, net force, free-body diagram, Newton's laws of motion, block on an incline, Atwood machine, weight versus mass

[Figure 1, animation: Three pucks pushed off at 2 m/s across carpet, a wood floor and ice, in real time. The arrow on each puck is its velocity. The smoother the surface, the more slowly the velocity is lost.]

Give a puck a shove across a carpet and it stops within half a meter. Aristotle looked at motions like that one and drew the obvious conclusion: things move only while something pushes them, and stop when the pushing stops. For two thousand years this was physics.

Now give the same shove on a wood floor, and then on ice. The puck goes one meter, then nearly seven. Nothing about the puck or the shove changed; only the surface did. Galileo asked what the sequence is heading toward: on a surface with no friction at all, the puck would have no reason ever to stop. If that is right, Aristotle had it backward: the carpet is what stops the puck, and nothing at all is needed to keep it going.

## Without a net force, velocity does not change

In the animation each puck loses velocity at a steady rate, and that rate is set by the surface: 4.9 m/s every second on the carpet, 1.96 on the wood, 0.29 on the ice. (These follow from friction coefficients of 0.5, 0.2 and 0.03; we will see how below.) As the friction force shrinks toward zero, so does the rate at which velocity is lost. The limiting case is Newton's first law.

It needs one piece of vocabulary. A **force** is a push or a pull on one object by another: it has a size, measured in newtons (N), and a direction, so it is a vector. When several forces act on one object, their vector sum is the **net force**.

**Key idea.** **Newton's first law.** There are frames of reference, called **inertial frames**, in which an object with zero net force on it moves with constant velocity: at rest if it was at rest, and in a straight line at steady speed otherwise.

The clause about frames is needed. Watch a ball on the floor of a bus as the bus brakes: the ball rolls forward with no force pushing it. The law has not failed. A braking bus is not an inertial frame, and the law makes no claim there. For most purposes the ground is inertial to good accuracy, and every problem below is described from the ground.

Notice what the law says about the puck on carpet. Its velocity changes, so the net force on it cannot be zero, and the friction force is the only horizontal force around. Force is linked to the *change* of velocity. The next step is to find out exactly how.

## The same push on different masses

Here is an experiment that can be done on an air-hockey table, where friction is negligible. Pull a puck with a spring held at a fixed stretch, so that the pull is constant, and record the motion. Then change the puck, or pull with two identical springs side by side for double the force.

[Figure 2, animation: Three pucks on a frictionless table, each pulled by the same constant 2 N force, in real time. A dot is left behind every half second. The pucks' masses are 0.5 kg, 1 kg and 2 kg.]

The dots spread out, so each puck is speeding up, and a measurement of the spacing shows that each one has a constant acceleration (the slope of its velocity graph; see [the previous lesson](@physics/motion-graphs)). Here are the values such an experiment gives.

| Force (N) | Mass of puck (kg) | Acceleration (m/s²) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.5 | 4 |
| 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 4 |

**Pause and try.** Find the pattern in the table. Then predict the acceleration of a 4 kg puck pulled with 2 N, and of a 1.5 kg puck pulled with 6 N.

**Answer.** For a fixed puck, doubling the force doubles the acceleration (rows 4, 2 and 5). For a fixed force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration (rows 1 to 3). Both are covered by $a = F/m$: every row has acceleration equal to force divided by mass. The predictions are $2/4 = 0.5$ m/s² and $6/1.5 = 4$ m/s².

[Figure 3, image: Acceleration against force for the three pucks. Each puck's points lie on a straight line through the origin, and the slope of the line is 1 divided by the puck's mass.]

## Newton's second law

**Key idea.** **Newton's second law.** In an inertial frame, an object of constant mass $m$ acted on by forces with vector sum $\vec F_{\text{net}}$ has acceleration $\vec a$ given by

$$
\vec F_{\text{net}} = m\,\vec a.
$$

Mass is in kilograms (kg), acceleration in m/s², and force in newtons, where $1 \text{ N} = 1 \text{ kg·m/s}^2$.

Each clause connects to something we have seen. "Net" is there because the puck on carpet responds to the total of the forces on it. The acceleration points along the net force, which is why friction, pointing backward, slows the puck. And $m$ measures how hard the object is to accelerate: the 2 kg puck needs twice the force of the 1 kg puck for the same acceleration. This resistance to acceleration is called **inertia**, and mass is its measure.

You might object that the law is circular: we measure force by the acceleration it causes and then announce that force causes acceleration. Part of the law is indeed a definition, since it fixes the size of the newton. But the table contains facts that no definition could force on nature: two identical springs give exactly twice the acceleration of one, and two identical pucks stuck together accelerate exactly half as much as one. Forces add, masses add, and one equation relates them. That is the experimental content, and it has been confirmed to high precision for everyday objects.

The law also answers the opening question precisely. What a force produces is acceleration, the rate of change of velocity. With zero net force the acceleration is zero and the velocity stays whatever it was, which is the first law again.

## Several forces add as vectors

The second law is a vector equation. Suppose a 2 kg puck on the frictionless table is pushed with 3 N toward the east and, at the same time, 4 N toward the north. It does not accelerate at $7/2$ m/s².

[Figure 4, steps: A 2 kg puck seen from above, pushed by 3 N to the east and 4 N to the north. The two forces add tip to tail, and the puck accelerates along their sum.]

  - step: Two pushes act on a 2 kg puck seen from above: 3 N east and 4 N north.
  - step: Slide the second arrow to the tip of the first. Forces add tip to tail, as displacements do.
  - step: The arrow from start to finish is the net force: 5 N, pointing 53 degrees north of east.
  - step: The puck accelerates along the net force at 5 N / 2 kg = 2.5 m/s². Here is its first second.
Forces combine the way displacements do, tip to tail (the lesson on [vectors](@linear-algebra/vectors) explains this addition in detail). Here the two pushes are perpendicular, so the Pythagorean theorem gives the size of the sum, $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$ N, and the acceleration is $5/2 = 2.5$ m/s² along that diagonal.

In practice we rarely draw the triangle. We choose perpendicular $x$ and $y$ axes, describe each force by its components along them, and use the second law once per axis:

$$
\sum F_x = m a_x, \qquad \sum F_y = m a_y.
$$

For the puck, $a_x = 3/2 = 1.5$ m/s² and $a_y = 4/2 = 2$ m/s², and $\sqrt{1.5^2 + 2^2} = 2.5$ m/s² as before.

## Weight is a force; mass is not

Near the Earth's surface, every object dropped in a vacuum falls with the same acceleration, $g \approx 9.8$ m/s² downward. Read through the second law, that fact tells us the force of gravity on an object of mass $m$: it must have magnitude $mg$.

**Definition.** The **weight** of an object is the gravitational force on it. Near the Earth's surface it has magnitude $W = mg$, with $g \approx 9.8$ m/s² (equivalently 9.8 N/kg), and points straight down.

A 2 kg block has a weight of $2 \times 9.8 = 19.6$ N. Its mass is a property of the block and is 2 kg anywhere. Its weight depends on where it is: on the Moon, where $g$ is 1.62 m/s², the same block weighs 3.2 N and is exactly as hard to shove sideways as on Earth.

## Forces come in pairs

A book lying on a table has weight, yet it does not accelerate, so some other force must balance its weight. The table pushes up on it. A force that a surface exerts at right angles to itself is called a **normal force** ("normal" meaning perpendicular).

Where there is a force there are always two objects, and the third law says the interaction is symmetric.

**Key idea.** **Newton's third law.** If object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force on A of equal magnitude and opposite direction. The two forces are of the same kind and act on *different* objects.

The book pushes down on the table as hard as the table pushes up on the book. The Earth pulls the book down with 19.6 N, say, and the book pulls the Earth up with 19.6 N. The Earth's acceleration in response is that force divided by $6 \times 10^{24}$ kg, which is why nobody notices it.

**Common mistake.** **"Action and reaction cancel, so nothing can move."** They are equal and opposite, but they act on different objects, and the second law is applied to one object at a time. Only forces on the *same* object are added. In particular, the book's weight and the normal force on it are not a third-law pair: both act on the book. They happen to be equal here because the book's acceleration is zero, and in an accelerating elevator they are not equal.

## Free-body diagrams: the method

Almost every mechanics problem is solved by the same procedure, and it is worth following it rigidly until it is automatic.

- Choose one object.
- Draw it alone, and draw an arrow for every force exerted *on* it by something else: its weight, plus one force for each thing touching it (surfaces, strings, hands). This drawing is a **free-body diagram**.
- Choose axes, with one of them along the direction of the acceleration if you know it.
- Split each force into components along the axes.
- Write $\sum F = ma$ for each axis and solve.
- Check units, and check a special case where you know the answer.

The standard first test of the method is a block sliding down a ramp. Take a 2 kg block on a frictionless ramp tilted at $30°$.

**Pause and try.** Before working it out, predict: is the block's acceleration down the ramp equal to $g$, half of $g$, or something else? And will a heavier block slide down faster?

**Answer.** The figure and derivation below give exactly half of $g$ for a $30°$ ramp, 4.9 m/s², because only half of the weight points along the ramp. The mass cancels, so a heavier block has the same acceleration.

[Figure 5, steps: The free-body diagram of a 2 kg block on a frictionless ramp tilted at 30 degrees, built one step at a time. The weight is split into a part along the ramp and a part pressing into it.]

  - step: Isolate the block. Everything else matters only through the forces it exerts on the block.
  - step: Gravity pulls straight down with the block's weight: 2 kg times 9.8 m/s², or 19.6 N.
  - step: The ramp pushes on the block at right angles to its surface. This is the normal force N.
  - step: Tilt the axes: x points down the ramp and y points out of it. The block can only move along x.
  - step: Split the weight along the axes: 9.8 N down the ramp and 17.0 N into the ramp.
  - step: Out of the ramp the forces cancel, so N = 17.0 N. Down the ramp, 9.8 N is left unbalanced: the net force.
The one piece of geometry in that figure is the angle between the weight and the $y$ axis. Tilting a ramp by $\theta$ from the horizontal tilts its perpendicular by the same $\theta$ from the vertical, so the weight makes angle $\theta$ with the perpendicular. Its component along the perpendicular is therefore $mg\cos\theta$, and its component along the ramp is $mg\sin\theta$.

A real ramp also has friction. For a block that is sliding, the friction force is found by experiment to be roughly proportional to the normal force, $f = \mu_k N$, directed against the sliding, where the number $\mu_k$ (the **coefficient of kinetic friction**) depends on the two surfaces. This is an empirical rule that holds well for dry solids, and it is a model, with nothing like the standing of Newton's laws.

**Theorem.** (Block on an incline.) A block of mass $m$ slides down a fixed ramp that makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal, where $0° < \theta < 90°$. Assume the frame is inertial and the only forces on the block are its weight, the normal force, and kinetic friction $f = \mu_k N$ (take $\mu_k = 0$ for a frictionless ramp). Then the normal force and the block's acceleration down the ramp are

$$
N = mg\cos\theta, \qquad a = g\,(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta).
$$

**Proof.** Take $x$ down the ramp and $y$ perpendicularly out of it. The forces on the block have components: weight, $(mg\sin\theta,\ -mg\cos\theta)$; normal force, $(0,\ N)$; friction, $(-\mu_k N,\ 0)$, since the block slides in the $+x$ direction and friction opposes that.

The block stays on the surface, so its $y$ coordinate does not change and $a_y = 0$. The second law along $y$ gives $N - mg\cos\theta = 0$, so $N = mg\cos\theta$.

Along $x$: $mg\sin\theta - \mu_k N = ma$. Substituting $N$ gives $mg\sin\theta - \mu_k mg\cos\theta = ma$, and dividing by $m$ gives $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.

The checks from step 6: $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ and $\mu_k$ are pure numbers, so $a$ has the units of $g$. With no friction, a flat ramp ($\theta \to 0°$) gives $a \to 0$ and a vertical one ($\theta \to 90°$) gives $a \to g$, free fall. And the mass has cancelled, for the same reason all objects fall together: a heavier block is pulled harder and is harder to accelerate, in the same proportion.

For our block at $30°$ with no friction, $a = 9.8 \times 0.5 = 4.9$ m/s². With $\mu_k = 0.2$, the friction force is $0.2 \times 17.0 = 3.4$ N and $a = 9.8\,(0.5 - 0.2 \times 0.866) = 3.2$ m/s². If friction is strong enough that $\mu_k > \tan\theta$, the formula gives a negative $a$: a block already sliding down slows, and once it stops it is no longer sliding, so the theorem no longer describes it.

[Figure 6, animation: A 2 kg block on a ramp whose angle sweeps from 10 to 80 degrees. The weight (orange) never changes; its part along the ramp grows with the angle while its part pressing into the ramp shrinks.]

[Figure 7, animation: Two identical blocks released from rest on 30 degree ramps, in real time, each sliding 5 m. Without friction the acceleration is 4.9 m/s²; with a friction coefficient of 0.2 it is 3.2 m/s², and the block arrives a third of a second later.]

We can now account for the opening figure. A puck on a level surface has $N = mg$, so friction is $\mu_k mg$ and the puck's acceleration is $-\mu_k g$: $-4.9$ m/s² for $\mu_k = 0.5$, $-0.29$ m/s² for $\mu_k = 0.03$.

## Worked examples

**Worked example.** **A scale in an elevator.** A 60 kg person stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator. What does the scale read when the elevator accelerates upward at 1.5 m/s²?

A scale reports the force pressing on it, which by the third law equals the normal force $N$ it exerts on the person. So we need $N$. *Object:* the person. *Forces on the person:* weight $mg = 60 \times 9.8 = 588$ N down, and $N$ up. *Axis:* up is positive, and $a = +1.5$ m/s². The second law gives $N - mg = ma$, so

$$
N = m(g + a) = 60 \times 11.3 = 678 \text{ N}.
$$

A scale marked in kilograms divides by 9.8 and shows 69.2 kg. The person's weight is still 588 N; the floor has to push harder than that to accelerate them upward.

*Checks.* With $a = 0$ (at rest, or moving at steady speed in either direction) $N = mg$, the usual reading. With $a = -g$, a cut cable, $N = 0$: the scale reads zero while the weight is unchanged.

A harder problem has two objects tied together. In an **Atwood machine** two masses hang from a string that passes over a pulley. Take $m_1 = 3$ kg and $m_2 = 2$ kg, released from rest.

**Pause and try.** The heavier mass will fall and the lighter one rise. Before reading on, decide: is the tension in the string equal to the heavier weight (29.4 N), equal to the lighter weight (19.6 N), or somewhere between? Use the second law on each mass to justify your choice.

**Answer.** Between. The 3 kg mass accelerates downward, so the net force on it is downward and the string must pull up with *less* than 29.4 N. The 2 kg mass accelerates upward, so the string must pull up with *more* than 19.6 N. The example finds the value.

**Worked example.** **The Atwood machine.** Find the acceleration of the masses and the tension in the string.

*Assumptions.* The string has negligible mass and does not stretch; the pulley has negligible mass and turns without friction. Then the tension $T$ is the same along the whole string, and the two masses always have equal speeds, so their accelerations have the same magnitude $a$.

*Mass 1 (3 kg), taking down as positive since it moves down.* Forces: weight $m_1 g$ down, tension $T$ up.

$$
m_1 g - T = m_1 a.
$$

*Mass 2 (2 kg), taking up as positive since it moves up.* Forces: tension $T$ up, weight $m_2 g$ down.

$$
T - m_2 g = m_2 a.
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates $T$: $(m_1 - m_2)\,g = (m_1 + m_2)\,a$, so

$$
a = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g = \frac{1}{5} \times 9.8 = 1.96 \text{ m/s}^2.
$$

Then from the second equation, $T = m_2(g + a) = 2 \times 11.76 = 23.5$ N, between the two weights as predicted. In general $T = \dfrac{2 m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g$.

*Checks.* Equal masses give $a = 0$ and $T = mg$: balance. If $m_2 = 0$ then $a = g$ and $T = 0$: mass 1 falls freely. The formula for $a$ is a ratio of masses times $g$, so its units are m/s².

[Figure 8, animation: The Atwood machine with 3 kg and 2 kg masses, released from rest, in real time. The string pulls up on both masses with the same 23.5 N, which is less than the left weight and more than the right one, so the left mass accelerates down and the right one up at 1.96 m/s².]

## Where the laws apply

Each hypothesis in the second law marks a boundary. The frame must be inertial: inside the braking bus, or on a spinning carousel, objects accelerate with no force on them, and the law has to be supplemented before it can be used there. The object is treated as a single point with one acceleration; a block that tips or a wheel that spins needs more than this lesson. The mass must stay constant, which rules out a rocket burning its fuel. And at speeds near that of light, about $3 \times 10^8$ m/s, the law itself gives way to special relativity. For cars, balls and planets it is accurate far beyond what you can measure in a school laboratory.

**Common mistake.** **"The normal force equals the weight."** It does for an object at rest on a level floor with nothing else pushing on it, and students carry $N = mg$ everywhere. On the $30°$ ramp $N = mg\cos\theta = 17.0$ N, less than the 19.6 N weight. In the rising elevator $N$ was 678 N against a weight of 588 N. The normal force is whatever the second law requires perpendicular to the surface, so find it from the free-body diagram each time.

**Check yourself.** A book lies at rest on a table. The Earth pulls down on the book. Which force is the third-law partner of that pull?
Answer: The book's upward gravitational pull on the Earth The pair is "Earth pulls book" and "book pulls Earth": the same two objects with the roles swapped, the same kind of force, equal in size and opposite in direction.

**Recap.** - First law: in an inertial frame, zero net force means constant velocity. Motion needs no force; a change of motion does.
- Second law: $\vec F_{\text{net}} = m\vec a$ for an object of constant mass in an inertial frame, with $1 \text{ N} = 1 \text{ kg·m/s}^2$. Use it one axis at a time.
- Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different objects, so the pair never cancels on one object.
- Weight is the force $mg$ and changes with location; mass is the measure of inertia and does not.
- Method: one object, a free-body diagram of the forces on it, axes, components, $\sum F = ma$ per axis, checks.
- Sliding down an incline: $N = mg\cos\theta$ and $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$, whatever the mass.

The next lesson, on [projectile motion](@physics/projectile-motion), applies the two component equations to a ball in flight, where the only force is gravity.

## Problems

Use $g = 9.8$ m/s². Draw a free-body diagram for every problem that involves forces on an object.

**Problem 1.** A 1200 kg car experiences a net forward force of 3000 N. Find its acceleration, the time it takes to go from rest to 25 m/s, and the distance covered in that time.

**Solution.** $a = F_{\text{net}}/m = 3000/1200 = 2.5$ m/s². From $v = at$: $t = 25/2.5 = 10$ s. Distance: $\tfrac12 at^2 = \tfrac12(2.5)(10)^2 = 125$ m. Units check for the first step: N/kg = (kg·m/s²)/kg = m/s².

**Problem 2.** A 6.5 kg sled on frictionless ice is pulled by two ropes: 5 N toward the east and 12 N toward the north. Find the magnitude and direction of its acceleration.

**Solution.** The forces are perpendicular, so the net force has magnitude $\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = 13$ N. Its direction is $\tan^{-1}(12/5) \approx 67.4°$ north of east. The acceleration is $13/6.5 = 2$ m/s² in that direction. By components: $a_x = 5/6.5 = 0.769$ and $a_y = 12/6.5 = 1.846$ m/s², and $\sqrt{0.769^2 + 1.846^2} = 2.0$ m/s².

**Problem 3.** An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg. Find her weight on the Earth and on the Moon ($g_{\text{Moon}} = 1.62$ m/s²). On which is it harder to push her horizontally from rest to 1 m/s on a frictionless floor in one second?

**Solution.** On Earth $W = 70 \times 9.8 = 686$ N; on the Moon $W = 70 \times 1.62 = 113$ N. The horizontal push needs $F = ma = 70 \times 1 = 70$ N in both places, because the push has to overcome her inertia, which is her mass, and her mass is 70 kg everywhere. Weight is vertical and does not enter the horizontal equation.

**Problem 4.** A crate slides down a $20°$ ramp with $\mu_k = 0.15$. Find its acceleration. If it starts from rest, how fast is it moving after sliding 2 m?

**Solution.** $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) = 9.8\,(0.3420 - 0.15 \times 0.9397) = 9.8 \times 0.2011 = 1.97$ m/s². With constant acceleration from rest, $v^2 = 2a\,\Delta x = 2 \times 1.97 \times 2 = 7.88$, so $v = 2.81$ m/s. The mass was not given and is not needed.

**Problem 5.** A block slides down a ramp with $\mu_k = 0.3$ at constant velocity. What is the angle of the ramp? Would a heavier block also slide at constant velocity on it?

**Solution.** Constant velocity means $a = 0$, so $\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta = 0$, that is, $\tan\theta = \mu_k = 0.3$ and $\theta = 16.7°$. The mass does not appear in the condition, so any block with the same $\mu_k$ slides at constant velocity on this ramp: the pull along the ramp and the friction force are both proportional to $m$.

**Problem 6.** A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator, and the scale reads 52 kg. Find the elevator's acceleration. Can you tell whether the elevator is going up or down?

**Solution.** The scale's reading means the normal force is $N = 52 \times 9.8 = 509.6$ N. With up positive, $N - mg = ma$ gives $a = N/m - g = 509.6/60 - 9.8 = 8.49 - 9.8 = -1.31$ m/s². The acceleration is 1.31 m/s² downward. That does not fix the direction of motion: the elevator could be moving down and speeding up, or moving up and slowing down. Force determines acceleration, and the velocity can be anything.

**Problem 7.** Two blocks sit touching on a frictionless table: 4 kg on the left, 2 kg on the right. A horizontal 12 N force pushes on the left block toward the right. (a) Find the acceleration. (b) Find the force the 4 kg block exerts on the 2 kg block. (c) Repeat (b) if the 12 N force instead pushes on the right block toward the left. Why do the answers differ?

**Solution.** (a) The blocks move together, so treat them as one 6 kg object. The only horizontal external force is 12 N, and $a = 12/6 = 2$ m/s². (b) Now isolate the 2 kg block. The only horizontal force on it is the contact force $C$ from the 4 kg block, so $C = 2 \times 2 = 4$ N. Check with the 4 kg block: by the third law the 2 kg block pushes back on it with 4 N, so the net force is $12 - 4 = 8$ N, and $8/4 = 2$ m/s². (c) The acceleration is again 2 m/s², now to the left. Isolate the 4 kg block: the only horizontal force on it is the contact force, so $C = 4 \times 2 = 8$ N. The contact force is whatever is needed to accelerate the block that the hand is *not* touching, and in (c) that block has twice the mass.

**Problem 8.** "A horse pulls on a cart. By the third law the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. The two forces cancel, so the horse can never get the cart moving." Find the error, and explain with the second law how the cart, and the horse, do accelerate.

**Solution.** The two forces named act on different objects: the horse's pull acts on the cart, and the cart's pull acts on the horse. Forces are added only when they act on the same object, so these two never appear in the same sum and cannot cancel. *The cart:* the horizontal forces on it are the horse's forward pull $P$ and backward friction and rolling resistance $f_c$. It accelerates forward when $P > f_c$. *The horse:* the horizontal forces on it are the cart's backward pull, of magnitude $P$, and the forward force $F_g$ that the ground exerts on its hooves. (The horse pushes backward on the ground; by the third law the ground pushes forward on the horse.) It accelerates forward when $F_g > P$. So both accelerate provided $F_g > P > f_c$. On frictionless ice $F_g = 0$ and the horse could not start the cart, which shows that the ground's push, and not the third-law pair in the argument, is what decides the matter.

---

# Projectile motion: dropped and fired bullets land together

> Gravity acts only on the vertical part of a projectile's motion. From that come the parabola, the time of flight, the range, and why 45 degrees goes farthest.

Series: Physics (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/physics/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/physics/projectile-motion/
Keywords: projectile motion, range formula, time of flight, maximum height, trajectory equation, 45 degree launch angle, independence of horizontal and vertical motion, complementary angles

[Figure 1, animation: Two balls leave a ledge 4.9 m high at the same instant, shown at half speed: one is dropped and one is fired sideways at 6 m/s. A ring marks each ball every tenth of a second, and the rings stay level with each other all the way down.]

A rifle is held level, 1.5 m above flat ground, and fired. At the instant the bullet leaves the barrel, a second bullet is dropped from the same height. One of them is moving at 400 m/s and will come down two hundred meters away; the other falls at your feet. Which hits the ground first?

**Pause and try.** Commit to an answer and a reason before reading on: the dropped bullet, the fired bullet, or neither.

**Answer.** Neither. With air resistance ignored they land at the same instant, about 0.55 s after release. Most people pick the dropped bullet, feeling that the fired one's speed should hold it up for a while. The animation above runs the same experiment with slower balls, and the rest of the lesson explains why forward speed gives no protection against falling.

## What the strobe picture shows

In the animation the two balls leave a ledge 4.9 m high. Read the heights of the rings. After 0.2 s both balls have fallen 0.20 m; after 0.4 s, 0.78 m; after 0.6 s, 1.76 m; after 1.0 s, 4.9 m, and both are on the ground. These are the distances $\tfrac12 g t^2 = 4.9t^2$ that a body dropped from rest falls in $t$ seconds, where $g = 9.8$ m/s² is the acceleration of free fall. The fired ball falls exactly as if it had been dropped.

Now read the fired ball's horizontal positions: 1.2 m, 2.4 m, 3.6 m, and 6 m at landing. It covers 0.6 m in every tenth of a second, which is a steady 6 m/s, exactly as if gravity were absent.

So the fired ball seems to be doing two simple things at once: moving sideways at constant velocity, and falling like a dropped ball. Neither motion takes any notice of the other. That is a strong claim, and a picture of one experiment does not prove it. Newton's second law does.

## Why the two motions are independent

The [second law](@physics/newtons-second-law) says that the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration, and that this holds separately along each of two perpendicular axes: $\sum F_x = ma_x$ and $\sum F_y = ma_y$. Take $x$ horizontal, in the direction the ball is fired, and $y$ vertically upward.

Once the ball is in the air, and if we neglect air resistance, exactly one force acts on it: its weight, of magnitude $mg$, straight down. Whatever threw the ball stopped pushing when the ball left it. The weight has no horizontal component, so

$$
0 = m a_x \quad\text{and}\quad -mg = m a_y, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad a_x = 0, \quad a_y = -g.
$$

Look at what each equation contains. The vertical one says the vertical velocity changes at the rate $-g$, and it mentions neither the horizontal position nor the horizontal velocity. A ball moving sideways at 6 m/s, a bullet moving at 400 m/s and a ball not moving sideways at all obey the same vertical equation, and if they start with the same height and the same vertical velocity (zero), they have the same height at every later moment. The horizontal equation says the horizontal velocity never changes, and it does not mention the vertical motion.

**Key idea.** With gravity as the only force, a projectile's horizontal motion has constant velocity and its vertical motion has constant acceleration $-g$, and neither affects the other. The only thing the two motions share is the clock.

The independence is a consequence of this particular force, and it is worth knowing how it could fail. If the force on the ball had a horizontal part that depended on the vertical motion, the two equations would be tied together. Air resistance does exactly that, as we will see at the end.

[Figure 2, animation: A ball kicked at 20 m/s, 60 degrees above the ground, in real time. Its shadow on the ground (blue) moves at a constant 10 m/s; its shadow on the wall (orange) rises and falls like a ball thrown straight up at 17.3 m/s. A dot is left every half second.]

## The equations of a projectile

To use the idea we need the two one-dimensional motions as formulas. Both are motions with constant acceleration, and for those the [earlier lesson on motion graphs](@physics/motion-graphs) derived, from the area under a velocity graph, that an object starting at position $x_0$ with velocity $v_0$ and constant acceleration $a$ has

$$
v = v_0 + at, \qquad x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2.
$$

We also need the starting velocity along each axis. A launch at speed $v_0$ and angle $\theta$ above the horizontal is an arrow of length $v_0$ tilted at $\theta$. It is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose horizontal side is $v_0\cos\theta$ and whose vertical side is $v_0\sin\theta$; those two sides are the horizontal and vertical components of the launch velocity.

**Theorem.** (Projectile motion.) A point object is launched at time $t = 0$ from the origin with speed $v_0$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. Take $x$ horizontal in the direction of launch and $y$ vertically up. Assume the frame is inertial and that the only force on the object is its weight $mg$, with $g$ constant (no air resistance, and a region small enough that the ground is flat and gravity uniform). Then while it is in flight, its velocity components (in m/s) and coordinates (in m) at time $t$ (in s) are

$$
v_x = v_0\cos\theta, \qquad v_y = v_0\sin\theta - g t,
$$

$$
x = (v_0\cos\theta)\,t, \qquad y = (v_0\sin\theta)\,t - \tfrac12 g t^2.
$$

**Proof.** The second law along each axis gives $a_x = 0$ and $a_y = -g$, as shown above; both are constant. Apply the constant-acceleration equations to the $x$ coordinate with starting position 0, starting velocity $v_0\cos\theta$ and acceleration 0: $v_x = v_0\cos\theta$ and $x = (v_0\cos\theta)t$. Apply them to the $y$ coordinate with starting position 0, starting velocity $v_0\sin\theta$ and acceleration $-g$: $v_y = v_0\sin\theta - gt$ and $y = (v_0\sin\theta)t - \tfrac12 g t^2$.

The fired ball of the opening is the case $\theta = 0$, launched from height 4.9 m: $x = 6t$ and the height is $4.9 - 4.9t^2$, which is zero at $t = 1$ s whatever the 6 is replaced by.

Here is a more typical case, the one in the last animation: a ball kicked from the ground at $v_0 = 20$ m/s and $\theta = 60°$. Its velocity components at launch are $20\cos 60° = 10$ m/s and $20\sin 60° = 17.3$ m/s. The vertical motion decides how long it stays up. It rises until $v_y = 0$, which happens when $17.3 - 9.8t = 0$, at $t = 1.77$ s, and by then it has climbed to $y = 17.3(1.77) - 4.9(1.77)^2 = 15.3$ m. It returns to the ground when $y = 0$ again: $t\,(17.3 - 4.9t) = 0$ gives $t = 3.53$ s, twice the time to the top. All that while it has been moving sideways at 10 m/s, so it lands $10 \times 3.53 = 35.3$ m away.

**Pause and try.** Repeat the calculation for the same kick speed at a lower angle: $v_0 = 20$ m/s and $\theta = 30°$. Find the time of flight, the greatest height and the landing distance. Compare the landing distance with the $60°$ kick.

**Answer.** The components swap: $v_x = 20\cos 30° = 17.3$ m/s and $v_y = 20\sin 30° = 10$ m/s at launch. Top of the flight: $10 - 9.8t = 0$, so $t = 1.02$ s, at height $10(1.02) - 4.9(1.02)^2 = 5.1$ m. Landing: $t = 2.04$ s, at $x = 17.3 \times 2.04 = 35.3$ m. The low kick is in the air for less time and rises a third as high, and it lands in the same place as the high one. The reason comes out of the general formulas below.

## The path is a parabola

There is a second way to read the equation $y = (v_0\sin\theta)t - \tfrac12 gt^2$, and it makes the shape of the path visible. The first term alone is where the ball would be if gravity were switched off: moving along its line of aim at a steady $v_0$. The second term is the distance a dropped ball falls in the same time.

[Figure 3, steps: The 30 degree kick at 20 m/s. Without gravity the ball would move along its line of aim; with gravity it is below that line by the distance a dropped ball falls in the same time.]

  - step: With gravity switched off the ball would follow its line of aim at a steady 20 m/s, covering 10 m every half second.
  - step: Gravity puts it below that line by the distance a dropped ball falls in the same time: 1.2 m, 4.9 m, 11.0 m and 19.6 m.
  - step: The actual positions lie on one smooth curve, the path of the ball. It lands just after 2 s.
To get the curve as an equation in $x$ and $y$ alone, eliminate the clock. From the horizontal motion $t = x/(v_0\cos\theta)$, which is allowed when $\cos\theta \neq 0$, that is, when the launch is not straight up. Substituting into $y$:

$$
y = (v_0\sin\theta)\frac{x}{v_0\cos\theta} - \frac{g}{2}\left(\frac{x}{v_0\cos\theta}\right)^2 = x\tan\theta - \frac{g}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}\,x^2.
$$

This has the form $y = bx - cx^2$ with $c > 0$, the equation of a parabola opening downward. The first term, $x\tan\theta$, is the line of aim, and the second is the fall below it.

[Figure 4, image: The 60 degree kick at four moments a quarter of the flight apart. The horizontal part of the velocity (blue) is the same every time; the vertical part (orange) shrinks, vanishes at the top and reverses.]

## Time of flight, height and range

The two worked kicks followed the same three steps, so we can run those steps once with letters. The results hold for a projectile that lands at the height it was launched from.

**Theorem.** (Level-ground formulas.) Under the assumptions of the projectile theorem, with $0° < \theta < 90°$, suppose the projectile lands at its launch height. Then

- its time of flight is $T = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$;
- its greatest height is $H = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, reached at time $T/2$;
- its range (horizontal distance to the landing point) is $R = \dfrac{2v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$;
- for a fixed launch speed $v_0$, the range is greatest at $\theta = 45°$, where $R = v_0^2/g$, and the launch angles $\theta$ and $90° - \theta$ give equal ranges.

**Proof.** (1) The projectile is at launch height when $y = 0$: $t\,(v_0\sin\theta - \tfrac12 g t) = 0$. The root $t = 0$ is the launch, and the other is $T = 2v_0\sin\theta/g$.

(2) While $v_y > 0$ the height is increasing and while $v_y < 0$ it is decreasing, so the greatest height occurs when $v_y = 0$: $t = v_0\sin\theta/g = T/2$. Then

$$
H = (v_0\sin\theta)\frac{v_0\sin\theta}{g} - \frac{g}{2}\,\frac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{g^2} = \frac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}.
$$

(3) The horizontal velocity is constant, so $R = (v_0\cos\theta)\,T = 2v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g$.

(4) We must find the largest value of the product $\sin\theta\cos\theta$. For any angle, $(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 \ge 0$. Expanding and using $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ gives $1 - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \ge 0$, so $\sin\theta\cos\theta \le \tfrac12$, with equality exactly when $\sin\theta = \cos\theta$. Between $0°$ and $90°$ that happens only at $\theta = 45°$. So $R \le v_0^2/g$, with equality only at $45°$. For the second claim, $\sin(90° - \theta) = \cos\theta$ and $\cos(90° - \theta) = \sin\theta$, so replacing $\theta$ by $90° - \theta$ swaps the two factors of the product and leaves $R$ unchanged.

Since $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta$ (the double-angle identity), the range is often written $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$. A units check: $v_0^2/g$ is (m²/s²)/(m/s²) = m, and the trigonometric factors are pure numbers, so $R$ and $H$ are lengths; $v_0/g$ is (m/s)/(m/s²) = s, so $T$ is a time.

**Note.** If you know calculus, part 4 is a one-line [optimization](@calculus/optimization): the derivative of $\sin 2\theta$ is $2\cos 2\theta$, which is zero at $\theta = 45°$.

The proof of part 4 also says *why* $60°$ and $30°$ tied. Range is horizontal speed times time aloft, and time aloft is proportional to vertical launch speed. The $60°$ kick has vertical speed 17.3 and horizontal speed 10; the $30°$ kick has them the other way round. The product is the same. At $45°$ the two components are equal, and a product of two numbers whose squares have a fixed sum is largest when the numbers are equal.

**Pause and try.** A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at angles of $15°$, $30°$, $45°$, $60°$ and $75°$. Before watching the next animation, rank the five landing distances, and say which kick is in the air longest.

**Answer.** $45°$ lands farthest, at $20^2/9.8 = 40.8$ m. $30°$ and $60°$ tie at 35.3 m, and $15°$ and $75°$ tie at $40.8 \times \sin 30° = 20.4$ m. The $75°$ kick is in the air longest, 3.94 s, because time of flight depends only on the vertical launch speed.

[Figure 5, animation: Five balls kicked together at 20 m/s, at angles from 15 to 75 degrees, in real time. The 45 degree ball lands farthest, and the pairs 30 and 60 degrees, 15 and 75 degrees, come down at the same points at different times.]

[Figure 6, image: Range against launch angle for a launch speed of 20 m/s on level ground. The curve is symmetric about 45 degrees, where it peaks at 40.8 m; angles equally far from 45 degrees on either side give the same range.]

## Worked examples

**Worked example.** **The two bullets.** A bullet leaves a level rifle barrel 1.5 m above flat ground at 400 m/s. Neglecting air resistance, when and where does it land?

The vertical motion alone sets the time. Take the origin on the ground below the muzzle, with $y$ up. The bullet starts at $y_0 = 1.5$ m with zero vertical velocity, so $y = 1.5 - 4.9t^2$. Setting $y = 0$: $t = \sqrt{1.5/4.9} = 0.553$ s. The 400 m/s never entered, so a dropped bullet takes the same 0.553 s. Horizontally, $x = 400 \times 0.553 = 221$ m.

*Check.* Units: $\sqrt{\text{m}/(\text{m/s}^2)} = \text{s}$. A fall of 1.5 m in about half a second matches everyday experience of dropping something from chest height.

**Worked example.** **Hitting a target.** A ball is kicked from the ground at 20 m/s. At what angle should it be launched to land 30 m away on level ground?

We know $R$ and $v_0$ and want $\theta$, so we use the range formula in its double-angle form: $\sin 2\theta = gR/v_0^2 = 9.8 \times 30/400 = 0.735$. Between $0°$ and $180°$ two angles have this sine: $2\theta = 47.3°$ and $2\theta = 180° - 47.3° = 132.7°$. So $\theta = 23.7°$ or $\theta = 66.3°$, a low shot and a high shot. They add to $90°$, as part 4 of the theorem requires.

The two differ in time of flight: $T = 2(20)\sin 23.7°/9.8 = 1.64$ s for the low shot and $2(20)\sin 66.3°/9.8 = 3.74$ s for the high one. *Check:* horizontal speed times time must be 30 m. Low shot: $20\cos 23.7° \times 1.64 = 30.0$ m.

**Worked example.** **A throw from a cliff.** A stone is thrown from the edge of a cliff 20 m above the sea, at 15 m/s and $40°$ above the horizontal. When and where does it hit the water, and how fast is it moving?

The landing point is below the launch point, so the level-ground formulas do not apply, and we go back to the component equations. Origin at the base of the cliff, $y$ up. Launch components: $v_x = 15\cos 40° = 11.49$ m/s and $v_{y0} = 15\sin 40° = 9.64$ m/s. The height is $y = 20 + 9.64t - 4.9t^2$. Setting $y = 0$ and using the quadratic formula,

$$
t = \frac{9.64 + \sqrt{9.64^2 + 4(4.9)(20)}}{9.8} = \frac{9.64 + 22.02}{9.8} = 3.23 \text{ s},
$$

where we kept the positive root. Then $x = 11.49 \times 3.23 = 37.1$ m from the base of the cliff. At impact $v_y = 9.64 - 9.8 \times 3.23 = -22.0$ m/s and $v_x$ is still 11.49 m/s, so the speed is $\sqrt{11.49^2 + 22.0^2} = 24.8$ m/s.

*Check.* The vertical motion satisfies $v_y^2 = v_{y0}^2 + 2(-g)(\Delta y)$ with $\Delta y = -20$ m, so $v_y^2 = 93.0 + 392 = 485.0$ and $|v_y| = 22.0$ m/s.

[Figure 7, animation: The stone thrown from the 20 m cliff at 15 m/s and 40 degrees, in real time. Its speed drops to 11.5 m/s at the top of the path, where only the horizontal velocity is left, and reaches 24.8 m/s at the water.]

**Common mistake.** **"At the top of its path the ball stops."** A ball thrown straight up does stop for an instant at the top. A projectile launched at an angle does not: only its vertical velocity is zero there, and it is still moving horizontally at $v_0\cos\theta$. The stone above never moves slower than 11.5 m/s. Its acceleration at the top is $g$ downward, the same as everywhere else on the path.

**Common mistake.** **"The force of the throw carries it forward."** It is tempting to draw a forward force on a ball in flight, because the ball is moving forward. The hand stopped pushing at release, and motion at constant velocity needs no force. After release the free-body diagram contains the weight and nothing else.

## What air resistance changes

Every result above assumed that gravity is the only force. For a shot put, or a ball tossed across a room, that is accurate to a percent or so. For a fast, light object it is not. Air resistance is a force directed against the velocity, and for a ball at sporting speeds its size grows roughly as the square of the speed.

[Figure 8, image: A baseball hit at 45 m/s and 45 degrees: the parabola it would follow with no air, and a path computed with air resistance proportional to the square of the speed, for a ball whose terminal speed is 40 m/s. The table above the plot gives the range and the peak height of each path, and a dot marks each peak.]

Four things change, and each can be read off the figure or the force.

- **The range and the height shrink.** In this model the baseball's range drops from 207 m to about 111 m. Real fly balls hit this hard travel about 120 m.
- **The path is no longer symmetric.** The ball loses horizontal velocity all the way along, so it comes down more steeply than it went up, and the highest point is past the middle of the range.
- **The best angle is below $45°$.** A flatter launch spends less time fighting the air. For this model the greatest range is at about $40°$.
- **The two motions are no longer independent.** The drag force points against the velocity and its size depends on the total speed, so the vertical equation now contains the horizontal velocity. A fast horizontal bullet feels a larger vertical drag while it falls than a dropped one does, and it lands slightly later. The dropped and fired bullets land together only in the model without air.

The model has other boundaries. The ground was taken to be flat and $g$ constant; for an artillery shell that travels tens of kilometers, or a rocket, the Earth's curvature and the weakening of gravity with height both matter. And if the launch and landing heights differ, as in the cliff example, the component equations still hold but the level-ground formulas, and with them the $45°$ rule, do not.

**Check yourself.** A soccer ball is kicked at an angle and air resistance is negligible. At the highest point of its path, which statement is true?
Answer: Its velocity is horizontal and its acceleration is $g$ downward $v_y = 0$ at the top, so the velocity is $v_0\cos\theta$ along the horizontal. The only force is the weight, so the acceleration is $g$ downward, as at every point of the flight.

**Recap.** - With gravity the only force, $a_x = 0$ and $a_y = -g$. The horizontal motion has constant velocity, the vertical motion is free fall, and they share only the time.
- From the origin: $x = (v_0\cos\theta)t$, $y = (v_0\sin\theta)t - \tfrac12 gt^2$, $v_x = v_0\cos\theta$, $v_y = v_0\sin\theta - gt$.
- The path is the parabola $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}x^2$: the line of aim minus a free fall.
- Landing at launch height: $T = 2v_0\sin\theta/g$, $H = v_0^2\sin^2\theta/(2g)$, $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$.
- On level ground the range is greatest at $45°$, and $\theta$ and $90° - \theta$ give the same range.
- Air resistance shortens and steepens the path, lowers the best angle, and couples the two motions.

In the cliff example the landing speed could have been found without the angle at all. The next lesson, on [conservation of energy](@physics/energy-conservation), explains why.

## Problems

Use $g = 9.8$ m/s² and neglect air resistance unless a problem says otherwise.

**Problem 1.** A ball rolls off the edge of a table 1.2 m high at 2.5 m/s. How long is it in the air, and how far from the foot of the table does it land?

**Solution.** Origin on the floor below the edge, $y$ up, $x$ along the ball's direction. Vertically the ball starts at 1.2 m with $v_y = 0$: $0 = 1.2 - 4.9t^2$, so $t = \sqrt{1.2/4.9} = 0.495$ s. Horizontally $x = 2.5 \times 0.495 = 1.24$ m.

**Problem 2.** A ball is kicked from level ground at 18 m/s and $35°$. Find its time of flight, range and greatest height.

**Solution.** $v_0\sin\theta = 18 \times 0.5736 = 10.32$ m/s and $v_0\cos\theta = 18 \times 0.8192 = 14.74$ m/s. $T = 2(10.32)/9.8 = 2.11$ s. $R = 14.74 \times 2.11 = 31.1$ m (the formula $18^2\sin 70°/9.8$ gives the same). $H = 10.32^2/(2 \times 9.8) = 5.44$ m.

**Problem 3.** For the kick in the previous problem, find the ball's speed at the top of its path, and its speed and direction of motion at the instant it lands.

**Solution.** At the top $v_y = 0$, so the speed is $v_x = 14.74$ m/s. At landing $t = T$, and $v_y = v_0\sin\theta - gT = v_0\sin\theta - 2v_0\sin\theta = -v_0\sin\theta = -10.32$ m/s, while $v_x = 14.74$ m/s. The speed is $\sqrt{14.74^2 + 10.32^2} = 18$ m/s, the launch speed, and the direction is $35°$ below the horizontal. On level ground a projectile lands with its launch speed, at its launch angle mirrored downward.

**Problem 4.** A stone thrown horizontally from the top of a cliff hits the sea 2.0 s later, 24 m from the base of the cliff. Find the speed of the throw, the height of the cliff, and the stone's speed and direction at impact.

**Solution.** Horizontal: $24 = v_0 \times 2.0$, so $v_0 = 12$ m/s. Vertical: the stone falls $\tfrac12(9.8)(2.0)^2 = 19.6$ m, the height of the cliff.
