# Supply and demand: where a price comes from

> Line up buyers by what they would pay and sellers by what they would accept. The price where the two counts match is the one that leaves nobody turned away.

Series: Economics (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/supply-and-demand/
Keywords: supply and demand, equilibrium price, market clearing price, demand curve, willingness to pay, price ceiling shortage, shift in demand vs quantity demanded

[Figure 1, animation: Eight buyers (blue staircase) and eight sellers (orange staircase) of one used textbook. As the price moves, the number who want to buy and the number who want to sell change. They are equal, at five each, only for prices between $50 and $55.]

Tickets for a 2000-seat concert go on sale at \$80 and are gone within a minute. By the afternoon the same seats are listed on resale sites at \$320. People blame greed, or bots, or a ticketing website that buckled. There is a plainer diagnosis, and to reach it we need to know where a price comes from in the first place.

So leave the concert for a few minutes and take a market small enough to count on your fingers. A calculus course requires a particular textbook. Eight students need a used copy, and eight students who finished the course last term each have one to sell. The copies are in the same condition, so nobody cares which one they get. What will a copy sell for?

## Eight buyers and what each would pay

Ask each buyer privately for the most she would pay before giving up and making do with the library copy.

| Buyer | Ana | Ben | Cho | Dev | Eli | Fay | Gus | Hoa |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Would pay up to | \$55 | \$95 | \$35 | \$75 | \$25 | \$85 | \$45 | \$65 |

**Definition.** A buyer's **willingness to pay** for one unit of a good is the highest price at which she would still choose to buy it. We assume she buys when the price is at or below this number and does not buy when it is above.

The number reflects her alternatives as much as her taste. Ben may be no keener on calculus than Eli; perhaps he has no time to sit in the library. All the model needs is the number itself.

**Pause and try.** If copies cost \$60, which of the eight would buy? How many would buy at \$30?

**Answer.** At \$60 the buyers are those willing to pay at least 60: Ben (95), Fay (85), Dev (75) and Hoa (65), so four copies. At \$30 everyone buys except Eli (25), so seven copies.

Answering that question took a search through the table. Sorting the buyers from highest willingness to pay to lowest turns the search into reading a graph.

[Figure 2, steps: Each bar is one buyer, as tall as the most that buyer would pay. Sorted from tallest to shortest, the tops of the bars form the demand curve: at any price, the number of bars reaching that height is the number of copies buyers want.]

  - step: The eight buyers in the order of the table: Ana, Ben, Cho, Dev, Eli, Fay, Gus, Hoa.
  - step: Sort them from the highest willingness to pay to the lowest.
  - step: Trace the tops of the bars. This staircase is the demand curve.
  - step: Read it sideways. At a price of 60 dollars, four bars are tall enough: four copies are wanted.
**Definition.** The **quantity demanded** at a price $p$, written $Q_d(p)$, is the number of units that buyers want to buy at that price. **Demand** is the whole relationship between price and quantity demanded: the function $p \mapsto Q_d(p)$, or its graph, the **demand curve**.

The two terms sound alike and mean different things, and a later section depends on the difference. "Quantity demanded" is a single number, such as 4 copies at \$60. "Demand" is the entire staircase.

One oddity of the graph is a convention you will meet everywhere in economics: price goes on the vertical axis even though it is the input. To use the curve, start from a price on the left edge, move across until you hit the staircase, and read the quantity below.

## Eight sellers and what each would accept

Each seller also has a private number: the lowest price she would take. Below it she would sooner keep the book. Call that her **cost** of selling. The eight sellers' costs are \$10, \$20, \$30, \$40, \$50, \$60, \$70 and \$80, and a seller sells when the price is at or above her cost.

[Figure 3, image: The eight sellers sorted from the lowest cost to the highest. The tops of the bars form the supply curve: at any price, the number of bars no taller than the price is the number of copies offered.]

The **quantity supplied** $Q_s(p)$ is the number of units sellers want to sell at price $p$, and **supply** is the whole relationship. This staircase climbs, because a higher price satisfies more sellers.

Before putting the two staircases together, here is what has been assumed. Every statement that follows is a statement about this model.

- **One homogeneous good.** The copies are interchangeable, so only the price matters.
- **Unit trades.** Each buyer wants one copy and each seller has one.
- **Price-taking.** There is one going price, and each person decides only whether to trade at it. Nobody thinks she can move it alone.
- **Everything else fixed.** Willingness to pay and costs stay put while we vary the price. Economists say *ceteris paribus*, "other things equal".
- **Voluntary trade.** Nobody can be made to buy or sell.

## The price at which the two counts agree

**Pause and try.** Someone posts a notice: "used calculus books, \$30 each". Count the buyers who want a copy at that price and the sellers willing to part with one. Who ends up disappointed? Then look for a price at which nobody would be.

**Answer.** At \$30, seven buyers want a copy (all but Eli) and three sellers are willing (costs 10, 20, 30). Only three trades can happen, so four buyers who wanted a book at \$30 go without. At \$50 the willing buyers are Ben, Fay, Dev, Hoa and Ana, and the willing sellers are those with costs 10 to 50: five and five. Any price from \$50 to \$55 gives the same two lists.

| Price | \$20 | \$30 | \$40 | \$50 | \$60 | \$70 | \$80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quantity demanded | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| Quantity supplied | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| Copies traded | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 |

The last row is the smaller of the two above it. Since nobody can be forced to trade, the scarcer side decides how many trades happen. Trade is largest at \$50, the one column in which the counts agree.

[Figure 4, steps: The book market at three prices. The red bar is the gap between the number of copies wanted and the number offered. Only between $50 and $55 is there no gap.]

  - step: At 30 dollars, seven copies are wanted and three are offered. Four willing buyers go without.
  - step: At 72 dollars, seven copies are offered and three are wanted. Four willing sellers find no buyer.
  - step: At 52 dollars, five are wanted and five are offered. Everyone who wants to trade can.
A price of \$30 would not last, because four buyers are shut out, and at least one of them is willing to pay \$65 or more, because only three of the seven hopefuls (Ana, Gus and Cho) have a willingness to pay below that. Say it is Hoa. She would gladly pay \$45 to the seller whose cost is \$40, and that seller would gladly accept. Both are better off than under the posted price, where neither trades. So the \$30 price is broken by a buyer who offers more. At \$72 the pressure runs the other way. Four willing sellers find no buyer, and at least one of them has a cost of \$40 or less. She offers her copy for \$60, and Hoa, who would not pay \$72, takes it. At \$52 no such deal exists. The buyers left out value the book at \$45 or less, the sellers left out need \$60 or more, and no price pleases both.

**Definition.** A **market-clearing price**, or **equilibrium price**, is a price $p$ with $Q_d(p) = Q_s(p)$. The common quantity is the **equilibrium quantity**. At a price where $Q_d(p) > Q_s(p)$ there is a **shortage** of $Q_d - Q_s$ units, and where $Q_s(p) > Q_d(p)$ there is an **excess supply** of $Q_s - Q_d$ units.

What we noticed in the table holds for any lists of numbers.

**Theorem.** Suppose $n$ buyers each want one unit and have willingness to pay $v_1 > v_2 > \dots > v_n$, and $n$ sellers each have one unit and costs $c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_n$, with no $v_i$ equal to any $c_j$. A buyer wants to trade at price $p$ when $v_i \ge p$, a seller when $c_j \le p$, and nobody can be forced to trade. Let $q^*$ be the number of indices $j$ with $v_j > c_j$.

- If $Q_d(p) = Q_s(p)$, the common value is $q^*$, everyone who wants to trade at $p$ can, and no buyer and seller who are left out could both gain by trading with each other at any price.
- If $Q_d(p) \ne Q_s(p)$, at least $|Q_d(p) - Q_s(p)|$ people who want to trade at $p$ cannot.
- If fewer than $q^*$ trades take place, some buyer and some seller are both left out even though the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the seller's cost.

**Proof.** The differences $v_j - c_j$ decrease as $j$ grows, so $v_j > c_j$ exactly when $j \le q^*$.

*Part 1.* Let $k = Q_d(p) = Q_s(p)$. The willing buyers are buyers $1$ to $k$ and the willing sellers are sellers $1$ to $k$, so they can be paired off and all of them trade. For $j \le k$ we have $v_j \ge p \ge c_j$, and since no value equals a cost, $v_j > c_j$; hence $k \le q^*$. If $k < n$, buyer $k+1$ is unwilling and so is seller $k+1$, which means $v_{k+1} < p < c_{k+1}$ and therefore $k + 1 > q^*$. (If $k = n$ then $q^* \le n = k$ anyway.) So $k = q^*$. Finally, anyone left out has $v_i < p$ or $c_j > p$, so a left-out buyer and a left-out seller have $v_i < c_j$. A trade between them at a price $r$ helps both only if $c_j \le r \le v_i$, and no such $r$ exists.

*Part 2.* Each trade uses one willing buyer and one willing seller, so at most $\min(Q_d, Q_s)$ trades occur, and at least $|Q_d - Q_s|$ people on the longer side are left over.

*Part 3.* If fewer than $q^*$ trades occur, at least one of buyers $1, \dots, q^*$ does not trade; call her buyer $i$. Likewise some seller $j \le q^*$ does not trade. Then $v_i \ge v_{q^*} > c_{q^*} \ge c_j$, so any price between $c_j$ and $v_i$ would leave both better off.

Match the parts to the book market. There $q^* = 5$, because $v_5 = 55 > c_5 = 50$ while $v_6 = 45 < c_6 = 60$. Part 2 is the four disappointed buyers at \$30. Part 3 is Hoa and the \$40 seller: at any price below $c_5 = 50$ fewer than five sellers are willing, at any price above $v_5 = 55$ fewer than five buyers are, and in both cases a trade that would help two people goes unmade.

**Key idea.** At a market-clearing price, the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer, everyone who wants to trade at that price does, and no buyer and seller who are left out could both gain from a deal with each other. At any other price the scarcer side sets the amount traded and somebody willing is turned away.

Be clear about the status of these claims. The theorem compares prices; it is arithmetic inside the model and it is proved. The claim that real prices *move* to the clearing level is a claim about behavior, and the model contains no mechanism for it. The Hoa story makes it plausible. The evidence is experimental. In classroom markets that Vernon Smith reported in 1962, and in many repetitions since, students were given private values and costs like our table and allowed to call out bids and offers, and trading prices typically settled near the clearing price within a few rounds.

## From staircases to curves

Eight buyers left a \$5 range of clearing prices. That slack is an artifact of the small numbers.

[Figure 5, steps: The same market with 8, 80 and 800 traders on each side, their values and costs spread evenly over the same ranges. As the steps shrink, the staircases become indistinguishable from two straight lines that cross at $50.]

  - step: Eight on each side: steps of 10 dollars, and any price from 50 to 55 dollars clears the market.
  - step: Eighty on each side: steps of 1 dollar. The clearing prices run only from 50 to 50.50 dollars.
  - step: Eight hundred on each side: steps of 10 cents, and 500 copies trade at a price within a nickel of 50 dollars.
With 800 traders on each side the staircases are, to within a few cents, the straight lines

$$
Q_d = 1000 - 10P \quad (20 \le P \le 100), \qquad Q_s = 10P \quad (0 \le P \le 80),
$$

where $P$ is the price in dollars and quantities are copies per term. The coefficients are [slopes](@algebra/slope-and-lines): each extra dollar on the price loses 10 buyers and brings in 10 sellers. This is why economists draw demand and supply as smooth curves. A curve is a staircase with too many steps to see.

**Worked example.** **Find the clearing price and quantity in the campus market.**

We want the price at which the two quantities agree, so set $Q_d = Q_s$:

$$
1000 - 10P = 10P \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1000 = 20P \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P = 50.
$$

Then $Q = 10 \times 50 = 500$ copies. This is a pair of linear equations in two unknowns, solved by substitution as in [systems of equations](@algebra/systems-of-equations), and the solution is the point where the two lines cross.

*Check.* On the demand side, $1000 - 10 \times 50 = 500$ as well. At \$40 there would be a shortage of $600 - 400 = 200$ copies, and at \$60 an excess supply of $600 - 400 = 200$.

## A change in demand is not a change in quantity demanded

Next term the course enrolls more students, and at every price 200 more copies are wanted than before. Nothing about the sellers has changed.

**Pause and try.** The new demand is $Q_d = 1200 - 10P$ and supply is still $Q_s = 10P$. Find the new clearing price and quantity. Did the quantity supplied change? Did supply?

**Answer.** $1200 - 10P = 10P$ gives $P = 60$ and $Q = 600$. The quantity supplied rose from 500 to 600 copies, because the higher price satisfies 100 more sellers. Supply, the relationship $Q_s = 10P$, is exactly what it was.

[Figure 6, animation: Demand rises by 200 copies at every price, so the demand line slides to the right. The supply line does not move. The crossing point climbs along the supply line from $50 and 500 copies to $60 and 600 copies.]

Here the distinction from earlier does its work.

**Definition.** A **change in quantity demanded** is a movement along a fixed demand curve, caused by a change in the good's own price. A **change in demand** is a shift of the whole curve, a different quantity at every price, caused by something the curve was holding fixed: the number of buyers, their incomes or tastes, the prices of related goods, what they expect. The same two phrases apply to supply.

The rise in enrollment was a change in demand. It caused a change in price, which caused a change in quantity supplied. Each curve answers "what if only the price changed?", so a price change can never shift either of them.

**Common mistake.** **"Demand went up, so the price rose; the higher price reduces demand; so the price falls back."** The second step uses "demand" for a movement along the curve. The higher price lowers the *quantity demanded* along the new curve, from 700 (what buyers would want at the old \$50) to 600, and that reduction is how the market gets to the new crossing point. Nothing pushes the curve back, so the price stays at \$60.

## A price ceiling

Suppose the student union, wanting books to be affordable, rules that no used copy may sell for more than \$30.

**Pause and try.** In the campus market, how many copies are wanted at \$30, and how many are offered? How many students who would have bought a book at the clearing price of \$50 now cannot get one?

**Answer.** $Q_d = 1000 - 300 = 700$ and $Q_s = 300$. There is a shortage of 400 copies. Only 300 copies trade. Of the 500 students who would have bought at \$50, at least 200 go without, and more than 200 if some of the 300 copies go to students outside that group. Trade has fallen by 200 copies even though 200 more students now want one.

[Figure 7, animation: A legal maximum price is lowered from $50 to $30. Sellers offer fewer copies and buyers want more, and the shortage (red) widens to 400 copies.]

**Definition.** A **price ceiling** is a legal maximum price. It is **binding** if it lies below the market-clearing price. A ceiling at or above the clearing price changes nothing in this model.

The 300 students who get a book pay \$20 less than before, and they are better off. But the price no longer decides who those 300 are. Something else has to: who saw the notice first, who knows a seller, who is willing to slip the seller an extra \$20. And since fewer than $q^* = 500$ trades take place, part 3 of the theorem applies. Some student who would pay more than \$50 has no book while an owner who would sell for \$35 keeps hers, and the rule forbids the trade that would help both.

Now return to the concert. The hall has 2000 seats whatever the price, so supply is a vertical line. Suppose the number of tickets fans want is $Q_d = 10000 - 25P$.

[Figure 8, image: The concert. Supply is 2000 seats at any price. At the $80 face price fans want 8000 tickets, a shortage of 6000. The price at which exactly 2000 are wanted is $320.]

**Worked example.** **The sell-out.** The clearing price solves $10000 - 25P = 2000$, so $25P = 8000$ and $P = 320$. At the face price of \$80, the quantity demanded is $10000 - 25 \times 80 = 8000$. The face price is a ceiling the promoter imposed on herself, 8000 fans chase 2000 seats, and the seats go to whoever clicks fastest. Among the 6000 left out are fans willing to pay far more than \$80, and among the lucky 2000 there may be some who value the seat at \$100. By the reasoning of part 3, trades between them benefit both, and the resale market is where those trades happen, at about \$320: four times the face price.

So nothing broke. A price set well below the clearing level produces a shortage as a matter of arithmetic, and a shortage produces a scramble and a second market. The demand numbers here are invented to fit the story, and the model is silent on *why* a promoter would choose \$80. Loyalty to fans, fear of looking greedy and the hope of selling merchandise have all been proposed, and deciding among them takes evidence.

## What the model leaves out

Each assumption fails somewhere. Used cars are not homogeneous, and a buyer who cannot judge quality behaves differently from Ben. A town with one employer or one pharmacy has a trader who sets the price and knows it. And "other things equal" is a discipline: every prediction has the form "if only this changes, then that follows". The model is also silent about whether a clearing price is fair. Eli, who could pay only \$25, has no book at \$52, and whether that is acceptable is a question the arithmetic cannot answer.

**Check yourself.** A frost in Brazil raises the price of coffee. Tea is a substitute for coffee. In the market for tea, what happens?
Answer: Demand for tea rises, so the price and quantity of tea both rise The price of a related good is one of the things the tea demand curve holds fixed. When it changes, the curve shifts right, and the crossing point moves up along the supply curve.

The hard part of this lesson was keeping a number apart from a curve. A price selects one point on each curve, a clearing price is where those points coincide, and events outside the market move a whole curve and drag the crossing point with it. [The next lesson](@economics/elasticity) asks how strongly quantity responds to price, which decides whether a seller who raises her price ends up with more revenue or less.

**Recap.** - Willingness to pay is the highest price at which a buyer still buys; a seller's cost is the lowest price she accepts. Sorting buyers and sellers by these numbers gives the demand and supply curves.
- Quantity demanded is a number at one price. Demand is the whole curve. The same goes for supply.
- A market-clearing price has $Q_d(p) = Q_s(p)$. At any other price the scarcer side sets the amount traded, someone willing is turned away, and if trade falls short of $q^*$ a trade that would help both sides goes unmade.
- With straight lines, find the equilibrium by setting $Q_d = Q_s$ and solving.
- A change in the good's own price moves along the curves. A change in anything else shifts a curve.
- A binding price ceiling creates a shortage and leaves something other than price to decide who is served.
- The model assumes a homogeneous good, price-taking traders and other things equal. That prices move to the clearing level is an empirical claim, supported by market experiments.

## Problems

The first three repeat the lesson's moves, the next three combine them, and the last two ask for an argument.

**Problem 1.** Five buyers would pay up to \$12, \$10, \$9, \$7 and \$4 for a concert poster. Five sellers would accept no less than \$3, \$5, \$6, \$8 and \$11. Find $q^*$, the quantity demanded and supplied at \$7.50, and all market-clearing prices.

**Solution.** Compare in order: $12 > 3$, $10 > 5$, $9 > 6$, but $7 < 8$. So $q^* = 3$. At \$7.50 the willing buyers are those at 12, 10 and 9, and the willing sellers are those at 3, 5 and 6, so $Q_d = Q_s = 3$ and \$7.50 clears the market. The counts stay at three and three for every price above 7 and below 8. At exactly \$7 the fourth buyer is also willing ($Q_d = 4$), and at exactly \$8 the fourth seller is ($Q_s = 4$), so the clearing prices are those strictly between \$7 and \$8.

**Problem 2.** Demand for a brand of notebook is $Q_d = 600 - 20P$ and supply is $Q_s = 40P - 120$, with $P$ in dollars and quantities in notebooks per week. Find the equilibrium.

**Solution.** Set $600 - 20P = 40P - 120$. Then $720 = 60P$, so $P = 12$, and $Q = 600 - 240 = 360$. Check with supply: $40 \times 12 - 120 = 360$.

**Problem 3.** In the notebook market of the previous problem, a ceiling of \$9 is imposed. Find the shortage and the number traded. What would a ceiling of \$15 do?

**Solution.** At \$9, $Q_d = 600 - 180 = 420$ and $Q_s = 360 - 120 = 240$. The shortage is 180 notebooks and 240 are traded, down from 360. A ceiling of \$15 is above the clearing price of \$12, so it is not binding and the market stays at \$12 and 360.

**Problem 4.** For each event, say whether it is a change in demand, in quantity demanded, in supply or in quantity supplied in the used-textbook market: (a) the professor makes the book optional; (b) the price falls from \$50 to \$45 and more students buy; (c) a campus bookstore starts paying \$10 more for returned copies, so owners are less eager to sell to students; (d) after (a), fewer owners bother to sell.

**Solution.** (a) A change in demand: fewer copies are wanted at every price, so the curve shifts left. (b) A change in quantity demanded: a movement along the demand curve caused by the book's own price. (c) A change in supply: every owner's cost of selling to a student rises, so fewer are offered at each price and the curve shifts left. (d) A change in quantity supplied: the fall in demand lowers the price, and sellers move down along an unchanged supply curve.

**Problem 5.** A **price floor** is a legal minimum price. In the campus market ($Q_d = 1000 - 10P$, $Q_s = 10P$), a floor of \$70 is imposed. Find the quantity traded and the excess supply. Who is left disappointed?

**Solution.** At \$70, $Q_d = 1000 - 700 = 300$ and $Q_s = 700$. Buyers are the scarcer side, so 300 copies trade and the excess supply is 400. The disappointed are 400 owners willing to sell at \$70 who find no buyer. Trade is 300, the same as under the \$30 ceiling: a price on either side of \$50 reduces trade, because one side or the other withdraws.

**Problem 6.** In the campus market, enrollment adds 200 buyers at every price and, in the same term, a graduating class adds 200 sellers at every price. Find the new equilibrium and explain why the direction of the price change could not have been predicted from the directions of the shifts alone.

**Solution.** The new curves are $Q_d = 1200 - 10P$ and $Q_s = 10P + 200$. Setting them equal, $1000 = 20P$, so $P = 50$ and $Q = 700$. The price is unchanged and the quantity is up by 200. More demand pushes the price up, more supply pushes it down, and here the two pushes are equal. If supply had risen by 100 instead, $1100 = 20P$ gives $P = 55$; if by 300, $P = 45$. Both shifts raise the quantity, so that direction is certain, but the price depends on their sizes.

**Problem 7.** A newspaper writes: "Rents rose this year because of higher demand for apartments. But as rents rise, demand will fall, and so rents will soon come back down." Find the error and say what the supply and demand model predicts.

**Solution.** The first sentence describes a shift of the demand curve to the right. The second uses "demand will fall" for the response of renters to a higher price, which is a fall in quantity demanded along the new curve. That movement is already part of the adjustment to the new crossing point; it does not shift the curve back. The model predicts that rents stay at the new, higher level until something else changes, for instance new building, which would be a shift in supply.

**Problem 8.** In the eight-student market, the price is capped at \$30 and the three sellers with costs 10, 20 and 30 sell. Define the gain from a trade as the buyer's willingness to pay minus the seller's cost. (a) Find the total gain if the three books go to Ben, Fay and Dev. (b) Find it if they go to Ana, Gus and Cho. (c) Find the total gain at a clearing price. (d) In case (b), describe a resale that benefits both parties.

**Solution.** The three sellers' costs total $10 + 20 + 30 = 60$. (a) $95 + 85 + 75 - 60 = 195$. (b) $55 + 45 + 35 - 60 = 75$. (c) At a clearing price the five highest-value buyers trade with the five lowest-cost sellers: $(95 + 85 + 75 + 65 + 55) - (10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 50) = 375 - 150 = 225$. The price itself does not appear, because what the buyer pays the seller receives. (d) Cho values her copy at \$35 and Ben would pay \$95. If Ben buys it from her for \$60, she gains \$25 and he gains \$35 compared with not trading. That resale is the concert's secondary market in miniature, and it moves the total from the outcome in (b) toward the one in (a). Even (a) falls short of 225, because under the cap only three books change hands.

# Elasticity: when raising the price lowers revenue

> Revenue is a rectangle under the demand curve. Elasticity compares percentage changes in quantity and price, and decides whether a price rise grows it.

Series: Economics (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/elasticity/
Keywords: price elasticity of demand, midpoint formula, elastic vs inelastic demand, total revenue test, point elasticity, unit elastic, elasticity vs slope

[Figure 1, animation: A cinema's demand curve (left) and its nightly revenue (right). Revenue is the area of the shaded rectangle, price times tickets sold. As the price climbs from $4 the rectangle grows, then shrinks. It is largest, $3000, at a price of $10.]

A cinema charges \$8 a ticket. It raises the price to \$10 and its nightly takings go up. A year later it raises the price again, from \$12 to \$14, and its takings go down. The hall, the films and the town are the same, and both increases were \$2. Why did the second one backfire?

To have numbers to work with, suppose the number of tickets the town buys per night at a price of $P$ dollars is

$$
Q = 600 - 30P, \qquad 0 \le P \le 20.
$$

One way such a formula arises, following [the lesson on supply and demand](@economics/supply-and-demand): 600 residents each have a highest price they would pay for a ticket, those prices are spread evenly between \$0 and \$20, and so each extra dollar loses 30 customers. This is the cinema's demand curve. It holds everything except the ticket price fixed, including incomes, the films on offer and the price of streaming at home.

| Price $P$ (dollars) | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tickets $Q$ | 480 | 420 | 360 | 300 | 240 | 180 | 120 |
| Revenue $P \times Q$ (dollars) | 1920 | 2520 | 2880 | 3000 | 2880 | 2520 | 1920 |

The table reproduces the story. From \$8 to \$10 revenue rises from \$2880 to \$3000, and from \$12 to \$14 it falls from \$2880 to \$2520.

## Revenue is a rectangle

**Definition.** A seller's **total revenue** is the money taken in: $R = P \times Q$, the price times the quantity sold at that price.

On the demand graph, a price $P$ and the quantity $Q$ sold at it are the height and the width of a rectangle with one corner at the origin and the opposite corner on the curve. Revenue is its area. A price rise makes the rectangle taller and narrower, and the area changes by the difference of two strips.

[Figure 2, steps: Raising the price trades one strip of revenue for another. The green strip is the extra $2 on every ticket still sold. The red strip is the tickets no longer sold, at the old price. From $8 the green strip is bigger; from $12 the red one is.]

  - step: At 8 dollars the cinema sells 360 tickets. Revenue is the area of the rectangle, 2880 dollars.
  - step: Raise the price to 10 dollars. Gained: 2 dollars more on each of 300 tickets. Lost: 60 tickets at 8 dollars each.
  - step: Start again at 12 dollars, where 240 tickets sell. Revenue is again 2880 dollars.
  - step: Raise the price to 14 dollars. Gained: 2 dollars more on each of 180 tickets. Lost: 60 tickets at 12 dollars each.
**Pause and try.** Before stepping to the last slide, compute both strips for the rise from \$12 to \$14 yourself. How many tickets are still sold, and what does each bring in extra? How many are lost, and what did each bring in before?

**Answer.** At \$14 the cinema sells 180 tickets, each bringing \$2 more than before: the gain is $2 \times 180 = 360$ dollars. It loses $240 - 180 = 60$ tickets that used to bring \$12 each: the loss is $12 \times 60 = 720$ dollars. The net change is $360 - 720 = -360$, matching $2520 - 2880$.

So the question "does a higher price raise revenue?" is a contest between two strips. The gain is the price change times the quantity that remains. The loss is the quantity change times the old price.

## Slope does not settle the contest

The natural first idea is that the outcome depends on how steep the demand curve is, meaning how many customers each extra dollar drives away. That idea fails on the spot, because the cinema's demand is a straight line. Its [slope](@algebra/slope-and-lines) is the same everywhere: 30 tickets lost per dollar, at \$8 and at \$12 alike.

Slope has a second defect. Its value depends on the units. Quote the price in cents and the same demand curve reads $Q = 600 - 0.3c$, with a slope of $0.3$ tickets per cent. Whether a price rise pays cannot depend on the currency unit, so the deciding quantity must be one that ignores units. Percentages do.

| Price change | Change in price | Change in tickets |
|---|---|---|
| \$8 to \$10 | $+2$ on 8, or $+25\%$ | $-60$ on 360, or $-16.7\%$ |
| \$12 to \$14 | $+2$ on 12, or $+16.7\%$ | $-60$ on 240, or $-25\%$ |

[Figure 3, image: Two $2 price rises on the same straight demand line. The slope triangles are identical, but as percentages the first is a large price rise with a small loss of customers, and the second is the reverse.]

Revenue is a product, and a product responds to proportional changes in its factors. At \$8 the price rose by a quarter while the audience shrank by a sixth, and the product grew. At \$12 the proportions were the other way round. The quantity we need is the ratio of the two percentages.

## Elasticity

Before defining that ratio, one flaw in ordinary percentages has to be repaired. Going from \$8 to \$10 is a rise of 25 percent, but going back from \$10 to \$8 is a fall of 20 percent, because the base changed. A measure of how responsive buyers are between two points on the curve should not depend on which point we call the start. The standard repair is to measure each change against the average of its two values.

**Definition.** Let $(P_1, Q_1)$ and $(P_2, Q_2)$ be two points on a demand curve, with all four numbers positive and $P_1 \ne P_2$. Write $\bar P = \frac12(P_1 + P_2)$ and $\bar Q = \frac12(Q_1 + Q_2)$ for the averages. The **price elasticity of demand** between the two points, by the **midpoint formula**, is

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{(Q_2 - Q_1)/\bar Q}{(P_2 - P_1)/\bar P}.
$$

Demand is **elastic** between the points if $|\varepsilon| > 1$, **inelastic** if $|\varepsilon| < 1$, and **unit elastic** if $|\varepsilon| = 1$.

The numerator is the proportional change in quantity and the denominator is the proportional change in price. Units cancel in each, so $\varepsilon$ is a pure number. On a downward-sloping demand curve the two changes have opposite signs, so $\varepsilon$ is negative; many books quote only its size, $|\varepsilon|$. For the cinema:

$$
\text{from \$8 to \$10:}\quad \varepsilon = \frac{-60/330}{2/9} = -\frac{9}{11} \approx -0.82, \qquad \text{from \$12 to \$14:}\quad \varepsilon = \frac{-60/210}{2/13} = -\frac{13}{7} \approx -1.86.
$$

**Pause and try.** Compute the midpoint elasticity for a price rise from \$9 to \$11 at the cinema, and the revenue at each of the two prices. What do you notice?

**Answer.** The quantities are $600 - 270 = 330$ and $600 - 330 = 270$, so $\bar Q = 300$ and $\bar P = 10$. Then $\varepsilon = \dfrac{-60/300}{2/10} = \dfrac{-0.2}{0.2} = -1$. The revenues are $9 \times 330 = 2970$ and $11 \times 270 = 2970$: no change at all, at an elasticity of exactly $-1$.

Demand was inelastic where the price rise paid, elastic where it backfired, and unit elastic where it made no difference. That is a theorem, and the midpoint averages are what make it exact.

**Theorem.** **(Revenue test.)** With the notation of the definition, let $R_1 = P_1 Q_1$ and $R_2 = P_2 Q_2$. Then

$$
R_2 - R_1 = (P_2 - P_1)\,\bar Q\,(1 + \varepsilon).
$$

So when the price rises along a downward-sloping demand curve, revenue rises if demand is inelastic between the two points, falls if it is elastic, and is unchanged if it is unit elastic.

**Proof.** Expand the two products

$$
(P_2 - P_1)(Q_1 + Q_2) = P_2 Q_1 + P_2 Q_2 - P_1 Q_1 - P_1 Q_2,
$$

$$
(Q_2 - Q_1)(P_1 + P_2) = P_1 Q_2 + P_2 Q_2 - P_1 Q_1 - P_2 Q_1.
$$

Adding them, the cross terms $P_2 Q_1$ and $P_1 Q_2$ cancel and the sum is $2P_2 Q_2 - 2P_1 Q_1$. Dividing by 2,

$$
R_2 - R_1 = (P_2 - P_1)\,\bar Q + (Q_2 - Q_1)\,\bar P.
$$

Factor $(P_2 - P_1)\bar Q$, which is not zero, out of the right side. The second term divided by it is $\dfrac{(Q_2 - Q_1)\bar P}{(P_2 - P_1)\bar Q}$, which is $\varepsilon$ by definition. That gives the formula. For a price rise, $(P_2 - P_1)\bar Q > 0$, so $R_2 - R_1$ has the sign of $1 + \varepsilon$: positive when $-1 < \varepsilon \le 0$, negative when $\varepsilon < -1$, zero when $\varepsilon = -1$.

The middle line of the proof is the two strips again, each measured at an average: $(P_2 - P_1)\bar Q$ is the gain from the higher price and $(Q_2 - Q_1)\bar P$ is the (negative) loss from the lost sales. As a check, $2 \times 330 \times (1 - \frac{9}{11}) = 120$ and $2 \times 210 \times (1 - \frac{13}{7}) = -360$, the two revenue changes in the table.

**Key idea.** Elasticity is the proportional change in quantity divided by the proportional change in price. A price rise increases revenue exactly when demand is inelastic over that stretch of the curve, $|\varepsilon| < 1$, and reduces it when demand is elastic, $|\varepsilon| > 1$.

The theorem assumed nothing about the shape of the demand curve. It holds for any two points with positive prices and quantities.

## Elasticity at a single price

The midpoint formula needs two points. Often we want the elasticity *at* a price, for small changes around it. Take the cinema's prices $P$ and $P + h$. The quantity changes by $-30h$, the average price is $P + \frac{h}{2}$, and the average quantity is $600 - 30P - 15h$, so

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{-30h}{600 - 30P - 15h} \cdot \frac{P + \frac h2}{h} = -30 \cdot \frac{P + \frac h2}{600 - 30(P + \frac h2)}.
$$

That is $-30$ times price over quantity, evaluated at the midpoint. As $h$ shrinks toward 0 it approaches $-30P/Q$.

**Definition.** For a straight-line demand curve $Q = a - bP$ with $a, b > 0$, the **point elasticity** at a price $P$ with $0 < P < a/b$ is

$$
\varepsilon(P) = -b \cdot \frac{P}{Q} = \frac{-bP}{a - bP}.
$$

(Optional, for readers who know [derivatives](@calculus/what-is-a-derivative): for any differentiable demand function $Q(P)$, the point elasticity is $\varepsilon(P) = Q'(P)\,P/Q(P)$, the limit of the midpoint formula as the two points merge. For a line, $Q'(P) = -b$.)

For the cinema, $\varepsilon(P) = -30P/(600 - 30P) = -P/(20 - P)$.

**Pause and try.** Compute the cinema's point elasticity at \$5, \$10 and \$15. The slope is the same at all three. What is changing?

**Answer.** $\varepsilon(5) = -5/15 \approx -0.33$, $\varepsilon(10) = -10/10 = -1$, and $\varepsilon(15) = -15/5 = -3$. The slope factor, $-30$, is fixed, but it is multiplied by $P/Q$. Moving up the line, $P$ grows and $Q$ shrinks, so a dollar becomes a smaller fraction of the price while 30 tickets become a larger fraction of the audience.

[Figure 4, animation: The point elasticity along the cinema's demand line. Its size is the price (orange part of the left edge) divided by the gap between the price and $20 (purple part). It is below 1 on the lower half of the line, exactly 1 at the middle, and grows without bound toward the top.]

This is why slope and elasticity must be kept apart. One straight line, with one slope, has every elasticity from nearly 0 at the bottom to arbitrarily large at the top.

**Common mistake.** **"A steep demand curve is inelastic and a flat one is elastic."** Steepness is slope, and slope changes with the units on the axes. Compare $Q = 100 - 2P$, which looks steep on a graph with price on the vertical axis, with $Q = 500 - 10P$, which looks flat. At $P = 40$ the first has $\varepsilon = -2 \times 40/20 = -4$ and the second has $\varepsilon = -10 \times 40/100 = -4$. The statement is true only in a limited form: of two demand curves *through the same point*, the flatter one is more elastic at that point, since they share $P/Q$ there.

For a straight line we can now say exactly where revenue peaks.

**Theorem.** Let demand be $Q = a - bP$ with $a, b > 0$, and consider prices $0 < P < a/b$. Then demand is inelastic for $P < \frac{a}{2b}$, unit elastic at $P = \frac{a}{2b}$ and elastic for $P > \frac{a}{2b}$. Revenue $R(P) = P(a - bP)$ is largest at the unit elastic price $P = \frac{a}{2b}$, the midpoint of the line, where it equals $\frac{a^2}{4b}$.

**Proof.** Since $a - bP > 0$ on this range, $|\varepsilon(P)| = \frac{bP}{a - bP} < 1$ exactly when $bP < a - bP$, that is, when $P < \frac{a}{2b}$. The same steps with $=$ and $>$ give the other two cases. For revenue, expand to check that

$$
\frac{a^2}{4b} - b\left(P - \frac{a}{2b}\right)^2 = \frac{a^2}{4b} - bP^2 + aP - \frac{a^2}{4b} = aP - bP^2 = R(P).
$$

The squared term is never negative and is zero only at $P = \frac{a}{2b}$, so $R(P) \le \frac{a^2}{4b}$ with equality only there.

For the cinema, $a = 600$ and $b = 30$: the peak is at $P = 10$ with $R = 360000/120 = 3000$, as in the table. Readers who know calculus can reach the same place for any demand curve: $R'(P) = Q + PQ'(P) = Q\,(1 + \varepsilon)$, which is zero where $\varepsilon = -1$, and [a maximum requires a zero slope](@calculus/optimization). One caution about what this result means. Maximum revenue is not maximum profit, since tickets also cost something to provide; [the next lesson](@economics/marginal-thinking) deals with that.

## Three special demand curves

A straight line passes through every elasticity. Three curves have the same elasticity everywhere, and they mark the limits of the definition.

[Figure 5, image: Demand curves with constant elasticity. A vertical curve: quantity ignores price. The curve Q = 2880/P: every rectangle under it has area 2880, so revenue never changes. A horizontal curve: any price above $10 loses every customer.]

A vertical demand curve has $Q_2 = Q_1$ for every price change, so $\varepsilon = 0$: demand is **perfectly inelastic**, and a price rise raises revenue in full proportion. On the curve $Q = 2880/P$ revenue is $P \times Q = 2880$ at every price, so by the revenue test $1 + \varepsilon = 0$ between any two of its points: it is unit elastic everywhere. A horizontal demand curve has no elasticity under our definition, because the definition requires $P_1 \ne P_2$. It is the limiting case of flatter and flatter curves, on which $|\varepsilon|$ grows without bound, and it is called **perfectly elastic**. A wheat farmer who is one of thousands faces demand of this kind: at the market price she can sell all she has, and a cent above it, nothing.

## What makes demand elastic

Elasticity is a property of buyers, and it has to be measured. The model does not tell us whether the demand for gasoline is elastic. Statistical studies do, and they find regular patterns. Demand tends to be more elastic when close substitutes exist (one brand of cereal against cereal in general), when the good takes a large share of the buyer's budget, and when buyers have more time to adjust.

[Figure 6, image: An illustration of the time horizon with made-up but typical numbers. Gasoline sells 100 million gallons a day at $4. If the price rises to $5, sales fall to 95 at first (elasticity about -0.2) and to 85 after some years (about -0.7), as drivers change cars and commutes.]

Surveys of the many studies of gasoline put its elasticity at roughly $-0.1$ to $-0.3$ in the short run (recent U.S. estimates are smaller, nearer $-0.05$) and two or three times that size over many years. Within a month a driver can only skip trips, but over several years she can buy a smaller car or move closer to work. These figures are estimates with wide error bands and they differ between places and periods. Treat any single quoted elasticity as approximate.

## Two applications

**Worked example.** **A good harvest that hurts farmers.** Suppose the demand for wheat is $Q = 130 - 10P$, with $Q$ in millions of bushels and $P$ in dollars per bushel, and suppose a harvest must be sold in the season it is grown, at whatever price clears the market. In a normal year the harvest is 100, so $100 = 130 - 10P$ gives $P = 3$ and farmers' revenue is $3 \times 100 = 300$ million dollars. In a bumper year the harvest is 110, so $P = 2$ and revenue is $2 \times 110 = 220$ million.

The reason is elasticity. Between the two points, $\varepsilon = \dfrac{10/105}{-1/2.5} = -\dfrac{5}{21} \approx -0.24$: demand is inelastic, so the price had to fall by a large proportion to sell a slightly larger crop. The revenue test, run for a price fall of 1, gives $(-1) \times 105 \times (1 - \frac{5}{21}) = -80$, the drop from 300 to 220.

*What is assumed.* The demand line is invented; the claim that demand for staple foods is inelastic is empirical and well supported. A single farmer still gains from her own good harvest, because her crop is too small to move the price. The loss appears only when everyone's crop is large at once.

[Figure 7, image: The wheat market in a normal year (100 million bushels at $3) and a bumper year (110 million at $2). Farmers gain the narrow green strip, 20 million dollars, and lose the wide red one, 100 million.]

**Worked example.** **Which goods to tax.** A state sells 100 million packs of cigarettes a year at \$8 a pack, of which \$3 is tax, so the tax raises 300 million dollars. It raises the tax to \$4. Assume for now that the shelf price rises by the full dollar, to \$9 (whether it would is the subject of [the lesson on taxes](@economics/surplus-and-taxes)), and that the elasticity of demand over this range is $-0.4$.

We want the new quantity $Q_2$. The proportional price change is $1/8.5 \approx 0.118$, so the proportional quantity change is $-0.4 \times 0.118 \approx -0.047$. Solving $\dfrac{Q_2 - 100}{(Q_2 + 100)/2} = -0.047$ gives $Q_2 \approx 95.4$. Tax revenue becomes $4 \times 95.4 \approx 382$ million dollars, up from 300.

Now run the same tax rise on a good with elasticity $-3$, for example gasoline in a small town whose neighbor does not tax it. The proportional quantity change is $-3 \times 0.118 \approx -0.353$, so $Q_2 \approx 70.0$, and tax revenue is $4 \times 70.0 = 280$ million: lower than before the increase. A tax collects reliably only where buyers do not easily leave.

**Check yourself.** A museum finds that the elasticity of demand for its tickets is about $-0.6$ around the current price. If the only goal is more ticket revenue, what should it do?
Answer: Raise the price Demand is inelastic, so the proportional loss of visitors is smaller than the proportional price rise, and revenue increases.

What took the work here was finding the right measure. Slope was the obvious candidate and failed twice, and the measure that survived is the one the revenue rectangle itself picks out: the ratio of proportional changes, with midpoint averages. The same ratio can be formed for supply, and in [the lesson on taxes](@economics/surplus-and-taxes) the two responsiveness measures together decide who bears a tax.

**Recap.** - Revenue $R = P \times Q$ is the area of a rectangle under the demand curve. A price rise adds a strip (higher price on remaining sales) and removes a strip (lost sales).
- Midpoint elasticity: $\varepsilon = \dfrac{(Q_2 - Q_1)/\bar Q}{(P_2 - P_1)/\bar P}$, a unit-free number, negative for demand. Elastic means $|\varepsilon| > 1$, inelastic $|\varepsilon| < 1$.
- Revenue test (proved, for any demand curve): $R_2 - R_1 = (P_2 - P_1)\bar Q(1 + \varepsilon)$. Raising price raises revenue exactly when demand is inelastic.
- Point elasticity on a line $Q = a - bP$ is $-bP/Q$. It runs from near 0 at low prices to unbounded at high ones, though the slope never changes.
- On a straight-line demand curve, revenue peaks at the midpoint, where $|\varepsilon| = 1$.
- How elastic a real demand is must be measured. Substitutes, budget share and time to adjust all raise it.

## Problems

The first three are direct computations, the next three need the theorems or an explanation, and the last two go further.

**Problem 1.** A café raises the price of a coffee from \$4 to \$5 and daily sales fall from 220 cups to 180. Compute the midpoint elasticity. Is demand elastic or inelastic over this range? Confirm with the revenues.

**Solution.** $\bar Q = 200$ and $\bar P = 4.5$. So $\varepsilon = \dfrac{-40/200}{1/4.5} = -0.2 \times 4.5 = -0.9$. Since $|\varepsilon| < 1$, demand is inelastic and the price rise should raise revenue. It does: $4 \times 220 = 880$ dollars before and $5 \times 180 = 900$ after. The revenue test gives the same change: $1 \times 200 \times (1 - 0.9) = 20$.

**Problem 2.** For the cinema, $Q = 600 - 30P$, find the point elasticity at prices of \$4, \$12 and \$16, and say in each case which way revenue moves if the price is raised slightly.

**Solution.** $\varepsilon(P) = -P/(20 - P)$. At \$4: $-4/16 = -0.25$, inelastic, revenue rises. At \$12: $-12/8 = -1.5$, elastic, revenue falls. At \$16: $-16/4 = -4$, elastic, revenue falls. This agrees with the table, where revenue climbs up to \$10 and declines after it.

**Problem 3.** Demand for a ferry crossing is $Q = 80 - 4P$ passengers per trip, with $P$ in dollars. Find the price that maximizes revenue, the revenue there, and the point elasticity at that price.

**Solution.** Here $a = 80$ and $b = 4$, so the revenue-maximizing price is $\frac{a}{2b} = 10$ dollars. Then $Q = 80 - 40 = 40$ and $R = 400$ dollars, which matches $\frac{a^2}{4b} = \frac{6400}{16} = 400$. The elasticity is $-4 \times 10/40 = -1$, as the theorem requires.

**Problem 4.** A city bus carries 9000 riders a day at a fare of \$2.00. The fare will rise to \$2.50, and studies suggest a midpoint elasticity of $-0.4$ over this range. Predict the direction of the change in fare revenue without computing, then estimate the new ridership and revenue.

**Solution.** Demand is inelastic, so by the revenue test a fare rise increases revenue. For the size: $\bar P = 2.25$, so the proportional price change is $0.5/2.25 = \frac{2}{9}$ and the proportional quantity change is $-0.4 \times \frac29 = -\frac{4}{45}$. Solve $\dfrac{Q_2 - 9000}{(Q_2 + 9000)/2} = -\dfrac{4}{45}$: this gives $45(Q_2 - 9000) = -2(Q_2 + 9000)$, so $47 Q_2 = 387000$ and $Q_2 \approx 8234$ riders. Revenue goes from $2 \times 9000 = 18000$ dollars to $2.5 \times 8234 \approx 20585$ dollars a day.

**Problem 5.** The cinema's demand in cents is $Q = 600 - 0.3c$, where $c$ is the price in cents. Find the slope and the point elasticity at a price of 1000 cents, and compare with the values in dollars. What does the comparison show?

**Solution.** The slope is $-0.3$ tickets per cent, against $-30$ tickets per dollar: a different number for the same curve. The elasticity is $-0.3 \times 1000 / (600 - 300) = -300/300 = -1$, the same as $\varepsilon(10) = -1$ in dollars. Changing the unit of price multiplies $P$ by 100 and divides the slope by 100, and the product $b \times P$ is untouched. Elasticity describes the buyers; slope describes the buyers and the choice of units together.

**Problem 6.** Rank these from least elastic demand to most elastic and justify the order: (a) gasoline, over the next month; (b) gasoline, over the next ten years; (c) gasoline from one particular station on a street with four stations.

**Solution.** Least to most elastic: (a), (b), (c). Over a month, drivers have almost no way to use less fuel, so quantity barely responds. Over ten years they can change cars, homes and jobs, so the same price rise removes more demand. One station among four faces a nearly perfect substitute a few meters away: a small price rise sends most of its customers next door, so its own demand is highly elastic even though the market's is not. The good is the same in all three; what differs is how easily buyers can avoid the higher price.

**Problem 7.** In the wheat example, $Q = 130 - 10P$. (a) Which harvest size would give farmers the largest total revenue, and what is that revenue? (b) Compare it with the normal harvest of 100. (c) Explain why no individual farmer would choose to grow less.

**Solution.** (a) Revenue as a function of price is $P(130 - 10P)$, which by the theorem peaks at $P = \frac{130}{20} = 6.5$ dollars, where $Q = 65$ million bushels and revenue is $6.5 \times 65 = 422.5$ million dollars. (b) A normal harvest of 100 earns 300 million. Farmers as a group would earn about 41 percent more by growing 35 percent less, because at 100 they are on the inelastic part of the demand curve. (c) Each farmer is a price-taker: her own output does not change the price, so every extra bushel she grows adds the full price to her revenue. The gain from a smaller total crop exists only if all restrict together, and each has a reason to break ranks.

**Problem 8.** Prove that on the demand curve $Q = k/P$, with $k > 0$, the midpoint elasticity between any two points is exactly $-1$, directly from the definition and without using the revenue test.

**Solution.** Let the points be $(P_1, k/P_1)$ and $(P_2, k/P_2)$ with $P_1 \ne P_2$. Then

$$
Q_2 - Q_1 = \frac{k}{P_2} - \frac{k}{P_1} = \frac{k(P_1 - P_2)}{P_1 P_2}, \qquad Q_1 + Q_2 = \frac{k(P_1 + P_2)}{P_1 P_2}.
$$

So $\dfrac{Q_2 - Q_1}{\bar Q} = \dfrac{2(Q_2 - Q_1)}{Q_1 + Q_2} = \dfrac{2(P_1 - P_2)}{P_1 + P_2}$, while $\dfrac{P_2 - P_1}{\bar P} = \dfrac{2(P_2 - P_1)}{P_1 + P_2}$. Their ratio is $\dfrac{P_1 - P_2}{P_2 - P_1} = -1$. This agrees with the revenue test: revenue is $k$ at every point, so $R_2 - R_1 = 0$ forces $1 + \varepsilon = 0$.

---

# Thinking at the margin: marginal cost and revenue

> The right question is what one more unit adds to revenue and to cost. Why averages mislead, why sunk costs drop out, and why profit peaks where MR meets MC.

Series: Economics (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/marginal-thinking/
Keywords: marginal cost, marginal revenue, MR = MC, profit maximization, sunk cost fallacy, average cost vs marginal cost, shutdown rule, price taker

[Figure 1, animation: A cake stall's revenue (blue) and cost (orange) for 0 to 6 cakes a day. The bar between them is the profit: red when cost is larger, green when revenue is. It is tallest at four cakes, where profit is $100.]

A flight with 150 seats costs an airline \$30,000 to operate, which is \$200 a seat. Ten minutes before the door closes there are ten empty seats, and a standby passenger offers \$80 for one of them. Selling a \$200 seat for \$80 looks like a way to lose \$120. The airline sells it, and the airline is right.

The \$200 figure answers the question "what did a seat cost on average?" The decision at the gate needs the answer to a different question: what changes if this one passenger boards? The crew, the fuel for the aircraft's own weight and the landing fee are paid whether or not seat 23C is occupied. Suppose one more passenger adds \$15 of fuel, catering and card fees. Then boarding the passenger adds \$80 of revenue and \$15 of cost, and the airline ends the day \$65 richer than if the seat had flown empty.

## Average cost and marginal cost answer different questions

Write $C(q)$ for the total cost of serving $q$ units, here passengers. For the flight, $C(q) = 30000 + 15q$ dollars.

**Definition.** For a total cost function $C(q)$ defined for $q = 0, 1, 2, \dots$:

- the **fixed cost** is $C(0)$, the cost that does not depend on $q$; the rest, $V(q) = C(q) - C(0)$, is the **variable cost**;
- the **average cost** of $q \ge 1$ units is $AC(q) = C(q)/q$;
- the **marginal cost** of the $q$-th unit is $MC(q) = C(q) - C(q - 1)$, the extra cost of producing $q$ units instead of $q - 1$.

With 140 seats sold, the average cost is $AC(140) = 30000/140 + 15 \approx 229$ dollars. The marginal cost of the 141st passenger is $C(141) - C(140) = 15$ dollars. Both are honest numbers. Only the second describes what the decision at the gate changes.

[Figure 2, image: The flight's average cost per passenger falls as more seats fill, but stays above $200. The cost of carrying one more passenger is $15 throughout. A standby offer of $80 is far below the average cost and far above the cost it causes.]

**Common mistake.** **"The seat costs \$200, so an \$80 fare loses \$120."** This compares the fare with a cost that is not at stake. Refusing the passenger does not save \$200; it saves \$15. The rule "never sell below average cost" would have the airline fly the seat empty and end the day \$65 poorer.

The two numbers are linked, and the link explains the graph. If the next unit costs less than the average so far, it pulls the average down, the way a low test score pulls down a grade average.

**Theorem.** For $q \ge 2$,

$$
AC(q) - AC(q-1) = \frac{MC(q) - AC(q-1)}{q}.
$$

So average cost falls from $q - 1$ to $q$ exactly when $MC(q) < AC(q-1)$, and rises exactly when $MC(q) > AC(q-1)$.

**Proof.** By the definitions, $C(q) = C(q-1) + MC(q)$ and $C(q-1) = (q-1)\,AC(q-1)$. So $C(q) = q\,AC(q-1) - AC(q-1) + MC(q)$. Dividing by $q$ gives $AC(q) = AC(q-1) + \dfrac{MC(q) - AC(q-1)}{q}$.

On the flight the marginal cost of \$15 is always below the average, so every extra passenger lowers the average and none of them ever brings it down to \$15.

## Sunk costs

The \$30,000 dropped out of the gate decision for a specific reason: by then it could not be changed.

**Definition.** A **sunk cost** is a cost that has already been paid or committed and cannot be recovered whatever is decided now.

A sunk cost appears in the result of every available option. When two options are compared by subtracting one result from the other, it cancels. With the standby passenger the day's result is $R + 80 - 30000 - 15 \times 141$, without her it is $R - 30000 - 15 \times 140$, and the difference is $80 - 15 = 65$ whatever the \$30,000 was.

"Fixed" and "sunk" are different properties. A fixed cost does not vary with quantity; a sunk cost can no longer be avoided at all. A week before departure the \$30,000 is fixed but not yet sunk, because the flight could still be canceled.

**Pause and try.** (a) At the gate, a tour group offers \$50 a seat for all ten empty seats. Accept? (b) A week earlier, only 60 seats are booked, at an average fare of \$250, no more bookings are expected, and canceling would avoid the entire \$30,000. Ignoring the cost of rebooking passengers, should the flight operate?

**Answer.** (a) Each seat adds \$50 of revenue and \$15 of cost, so accepting adds $10 \times 35 = 350$ dollars. Accept, although \$50 is a quarter of the average cost. (b) Now the \$30,000 is avoidable, so it counts. Operating brings in $60 \times 250 = 15000$ dollars and costs $30000 + 15 \times 60 = 30900$. Canceling is better by \$15,900. The same \$30,000 is ignored in (a) and decisive in (b), because only in (b) does the choice affect it.

**Common mistake.** **The sunk cost fallacy.** "I have already spent \$60 on this ticket, so I have to go," says someone who would now prefer to stay home. The \$60 is gone on both branches. The only live comparison is the evening at the concert against the evening at home. Businesses make the same error when they keep funding a failing project "because we have put so much into it".

## How many to make

The airline's question was about one unit. Most decisions are about how many. Mara sells large decorated cakes from a market stall. The stall fee is \$60 a day, paid in advance. Through experience she knows her demand: to sell $Q$ cakes in a day she can charge at most $P = 100 - 10Q$ dollars each. She charges every customer the same price, and she bakes to order, so nothing is wasted. She also knows her costs. She wants the largest profit.

| Cakes $q$ | Price | Revenue $R(q)$ | Cost $C(q)$ | Profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | | 0 | 60 | $-60$ |
| 1 | 90 | 90 | 80 | 10 |
| 2 | 80 | 160 | 95 | 65 |
| 3 | 70 | 210 | 115 | 95 |
| 4 | 60 | 240 | 140 | 100 |
| 5 | 50 | 250 | 185 | 65 |
| 6 | 40 | 240 | 250 | $-10$ |

Reading down the last column, the best plan is four cakes at \$60 each, for a profit of \$100. That settles this case. But the table hides why four is the answer, and it has to be rebuilt whenever anything changes. So ask the airline's question once per cake.

**Definition.** For revenue $R(q)$ and cost $C(q)$, **profit** is $\pi(q) = R(q) - C(q)$. The **marginal revenue** of the $q$-th unit is $MR(q) = R(q) - R(q-1)$, the extra revenue from selling $q$ units instead of $q - 1$.

**Pause and try.** Compute $MR(q)$ and $MC(q)$ for cakes 1 through 6 from the table. The fourth cake sells for \$60. Why is its marginal revenue not \$60?

**Answer.** $MR$: 90, 70, 50, 30, 10, $-10$. $MC$: 20, 15, 20, 25, 45, 65. To sell a fourth cake Mara must lower the price from \$70 to \$60 for every customer. She gains \$60 from the fourth cake and gives up \$10 on each of the three she would have sold anyway: $60 - 30 = 30$. These are the two strips from [the lesson on elasticity](@economics/elasticity).

[Figure 3, steps: Mara's decision one cake at a time. For each cake the blue bar is the revenue it adds and the orange bar is the cost it adds. Profit rises while blue is taller and falls once orange is.]

  - step: The first cake adds 90 dollars of revenue and 20 of cost. Profit goes from a loss of 60 to a gain of 10.
  - step: The second and third each add more revenue than cost. Profit rises to 65, then to 95.
  - step: The fourth adds 30 of revenue and 25 of cost. It is still worth baking, and profit reaches 100.
  - step: The fifth would add 10 of revenue and 45 of cost, cutting profit to 65. Stop at four.
Each cake changes profit by its marginal revenue minus its marginal cost: $+70$, $+55$, $+30$, $+5$, then $-35$ and $-75$. Starting from $-60$ and adding these up reproduces the profit column. The best quantity is where the additions stop being positive.

**Theorem.** **(Marginal rule.)** Let $R(q)$ and $C(q)$ be defined for $q = 0, 1, \dots, N$, with $\pi$, $MR$ and $MC$ as above.

- For every $q$, $\ \pi(q) = \pi(0) + \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{q} \bigl(MR(k) - MC(k)\bigr)$.
- Suppose there is a quantity $q^*$ such that $MR(k) > MC(k)$ for every $k \le q^*$ and $MR(k) < MC(k)$ for every $k > q^*$. Then $\pi(q^*) > \pi(q)$ for every $q \ne q^*$.

**Proof.** *Part 1.* For each $k \ge 1$,

$$
\pi(k) - \pi(k-1) = \bigl(R(k) - R(k-1)\bigr) - \bigl(C(k) - C(k-1)\bigr) = MR(k) - MC(k).
$$

Add these equations for $k = 1, \dots, q$. On the left, each $\pi(k)$ with $0 < k < q$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so the sum collapses to $\pi(q) - \pi(0)$.

*Part 2.* If $q < q^*$, then by part 1, $\pi(q^*) - \pi(q)$ is the sum of $MR(k) - MC(k)$ over $k = q+1, \dots, q^*$, and each term is positive. If $q > q^*$, then $\pi(q) - \pi(q^*)$ is the sum over $k = q^* + 1, \dots, q$, and each term is negative.

**Key idea.** Profit is the running total of marginal revenue minus marginal cost. When that difference changes sign only once, from positive to negative, the rule is: produce each unit whose added revenue is at least its added cost, and stop before the first unit that falls short. Profit peaks where the two meet.

The hypothesis in part 2, one switch from "revenue bar taller" to "cost bar taller", holds whenever $MR(k) - MC(k)$ decreases as $k$ grows. That is the usual case: selling more requires a lower price, and producing more eventually strains capacity. When it fails, part 1 still holds, and we will meet such a case below. If some unit has $MR(k) = MC(k)$ exactly, it leaves profit unchanged and both $k - 1$ and $k$ are best. When quantity varies continuously the switch always passes through such a point of equality, which is why the rule is quoted as "$MR = MC$".

Two rules of thumb that use averages fail on Mara's table. "Bake while the price exceeds average cost" keeps going to five cakes, where the price of \$50 is above $AC(5) = 37$; five cakes do make a profit, but \$35 less than four. "Make the quantity with the lowest average cost" picks four here, but only by coincidence: it ignores demand entirely.

[Figure 4, image: Mara's marginal cost (bars) and average cost (line) for each cake. While a bar is below the line the average falls, and once the bars rise above it the average rises, so the average is lowest, $35, at four cakes.]

The picture is the average-marginal theorem at work: $MC(4) = 25 < AC(3) \approx 38.3$, so the average falls to 35, and $MC(5) = 45 > AC(4) = 35$, so it rises to 37.

The stall fee plays no part in the quantity decision. It sits in $\pi(0) = -60$, the starting point of the sum in part 1, and in none of the terms.

[Figure 5, image: Mara's profit for each number of cakes when the stall fee is $60 (green) and when it is $100 (purple). The fee moves every point down by the same amount, so the best quantity is four in both cases.]

**Worked example.** **A change in fixed cost and a change in marginal cost.** Suppose the stall fee rises from \$60 to \$100. Every entry of the cost column rises by 40, no marginal cost changes, and the best quantity is still four; profit falls from 100 to 60. Now suppose instead that ingredients become \$10 dearer per cake. Every marginal cost rises by 10, to 30, 25, 30, 35, 55, 75. Marginal revenue minus marginal cost is now $60, 45, 20, -5, \dots$, so the fourth cake no longer pays and the best quantity is three. *Check:* at three cakes, revenue is 210 and cost is $115 + 30 = 145$, profit 65; at four, $240 - (140 + 40) = 60$.

## The same rule with calculus (optional)

If quantity can vary continuously, say cake sold by the kilogram, the differences become [derivatives](@calculus/what-is-a-derivative). Take $R(q) = 100q - 10q^2$ and $C(q) = 60 + 10q + 5q^2$. Marginal revenue is $R'(q) = 100 - 20q$ and marginal cost is $C'(q) = 10 + 10q$. Profit $\pi = R - C$ has $\pi'(q) = R'(q) - C'(q) = 90 - 30q$, which is zero at $q = 3$, and since $\pi''(q) = -30 < 0$ this is a maximum, by the reasoning in [the lesson on optimization](@calculus/optimization). There $R'(3) = C'(3) = 40$ and $\pi(3) = 210 - 135 = 75$.

[Figure 6, image: Smooth revenue and cost curves. The profit is the vertical gap between them. It is widest at q = 3, where the two tangent lines are parallel: revenue and cost are growing at the same rate, $40 per unit.]

The condition $R'(q) = C'(q)$ alone is not enough, for the same reason as in the discrete theorem: it also holds where profit is smallest, if marginal cost crosses marginal revenue from above.

## A seller who cannot choose the price

Mara had a demand curve of her own. Many sellers do not. A farmer selling wheat, or one of the students selling a used textbook in [the lesson on supply and demand](@economics/supply-and-demand), faces a going price that her own quantity is too small to move.

**Definition.** A **price-taker** is a seller who can sell any quantity at the market price $p$ and nothing at a higher price. For a price-taker $R(q) = pq$, so $MR(q) = p$ for every unit.

For a price-taker the marginal rule reads: produce every unit whose marginal cost is at most the price. When marginal cost is rising, production stops where $MC$ reaches $p$, which is the textbook condition $P = MC$. This is also where a supply curve comes from. In the supply-and-demand lesson each seller had a "cost", the lowest price she would accept, and the supply curve was those costs in increasing order. That cost is a marginal cost.

Suppose Mara switches to plain cakes that a supermarket buys at a fixed price, in any number, and her costs are the same as before.

[Figure 7, steps: Mara as a price-taker. Bars are the marginal cost of each cake and the blue line is the market price. She bakes the cakes whose bars lie below the line, as long as the revenue covers the variable cost.]

  - step: At a price of 40 dollars, the first four cakes each cost less than they bring in. Revenue 160, total cost 140, profit 20.
  - step: At 30 dollars she still bakes four. Revenue of 120 covers the variable cost of 80 but not the fee as well: a loss of 20.
  - step: At 17 dollars the best she could do is two cakes, which bring in 34 and cost 35. No quantity covers its variable cost, so she bakes nothing.
At \$40 the rule gives four cakes and a profit of $160 - 140 = 20$ dollars. At \$30 it still gives four, since $MC(4) = 25 \le 30 < MC(5) = 45$, but now revenue is 120 against a cost of 140. She loses \$20. Should she stay home?

**Pause and try.** The \$60 stall fee is paid in advance and is not refundable. At a price of \$30, compare Mara's result from baking four cakes with her result from baking none. What must revenue cover for baking to be worthwhile?

**Answer.** Baking four: $120 - 140 = -20$. Baking none: $0 - 60 = -60$. Baking is better by \$40, which is revenue of 120 minus the variable cost of 80. The fee is sunk, so it appears in both results and cancels. Baking is worthwhile exactly when revenue covers the variable cost.

In symbols, with a sunk fixed cost $F$ and variable cost $V(q)$: producing $q \ge 1$ units beats producing none exactly when $pq - V(q) - F \ge -F$, that is, when $p \ge V(q)/q$. The right side is the **average variable cost**, $AVC(q)$. So a price-taker should **shut down** when the price is below the smallest value of $AVC$, and otherwise produce where the marginal rule says.

**Worked example.** **Mara's shutdown price.** Her variable costs for 1 to 6 cakes are 20, 35, 55, 80, 125, 190, so $AVC$ is 20, 17.5, 18.3, 20, 25, 31.7. The minimum is \$17.50, at two cakes. At a price of \$18, two cakes bring in 36 against a variable cost of 35: she bakes, and loses \$59 instead of \$60. At \$17, two cakes bring in 34 against 35, and every other quantity does worse: she shuts down.

This is the case promised earlier in which the hypothesis of the marginal rule fails. At \$18, $MR - MC$ for the first three cakes is $-2, +3, -2$. The sign switches twice, because the second cake is cheaper to bake than the first. Stopping at the first negative term would give zero cakes, and the right answer is two. Part 1 of the theorem, the running total, still decides it: $-2 + 3 = +1 > 0$.

If the fee is not sunk, as when Mara is deciding whether to rent the stall next season, it counts, and the test becomes whether revenue covers *all* costs: $p \ge AC(q)$. Her lowest average cost is \$35. So at prices between \$17.50 and \$35 she operates today at a loss and does not renew.

## What the model assumes

The rule is a theorem about a seller who knows her revenue and cost schedules and wants maximum profit. Whether real firms behave this way is an empirical matter. Surveys since the 1930s have found many managers describing their pricing as a markup on average cost, while airline pricing systems are built on marginal reasoning of the kind in the opening. The airline example also leaned on an assumption: that the \$80 fare did not lower anyone else's fare. If regular customers learn to wait for last-minute bargains, the marginal revenue of the cheap seat is less than \$80, and the calculation has to include that.

**Check yourself.** A factory's lease costs \$10,000 a month and is paid for the year. This month it can make 500 chairs at a variable cost of \$30 each and sell them for \$40 each. What should it do?
Answer: Produce: revenue exceeds variable cost by \$5,000 Revenue is 20,000 and variable cost is 15,000. Producing loses 5,000 after the lease; not producing loses 10,000.

All of this came from one habit: compare the options that are open, and count only what differs between them. The average cost of a seat, the fee already paid and the money already spent on a ticket are the same on every branch, so they cancel. [The next lesson](@economics/surplus-and-taxes) uses marginal cost as the supply curve to ask how much buyers and sellers gain from a market, and what a tax does to that gain.

**Recap.** - Marginal cost $MC(q) = C(q) - C(q-1)$ and marginal revenue $MR(q) = R(q) - R(q-1)$ measure what the $q$-th unit adds. Average cost $C(q)/q$ describes the whole batch.
- $AC(q) - AC(q-1) = \dfrac{MC(q) - AC(q-1)}{q}$: the average falls when the marginal unit is below it.
- A sunk cost is the same under every option and cancels from any comparison. Fixed costs are not always sunk.
- Profit is $\pi(0)$ plus the sum of $MR(k) - MC(k)$. If that difference switches sign once, from positive to negative, profit is largest at the last unit before the switch.
- A price-taker has $MR = p$ and produces the units with $MC \le p$. That schedule is its supply curve.
- With a sunk fixed cost, produce only if $p \ge AVC(q)$ at the chosen quantity; otherwise shut down. If the fixed cost is avoidable, the test is $p \ge AC(q)$.

## Problems

The first three repeat the lesson's calculations, the next three ask you to apply the ideas, and the last two extend them.

**Problem 1.** A lemonade stand's revenue for $q = 0, \dots, 5$ jugs is 0, 50, 90, 120, 140, 150 dollars and its cost is 30, 50, 65, 85, 115, 155 dollars. Compute $MR$ and $MC$ for each jug, find the best quantity with the marginal rule, and confirm it with the profits.

**Solution.** $MR$: 50, 40, 30, 20, 10. $MC$: 20, 15, 20, 30, 40. $MR - MC$: $30, 25, 10, -10, -30$. The sign switches once, after the third jug, so $q^* = 3$. Profits: $-30, 0, 25, 35, 25, -5$. The largest is 35, at three jugs, and each profit is the previous one plus $MR - MC$.

**Problem 2.** A train run costs \$12,000 plus \$5 per passenger. With 160 tickets sold, find the average cost per passenger and the marginal cost of one more. A last-minute traveler offers \$40. Should the operator accept, and what happens to the average cost?

**Solution.** $AC(160) = 12000/160 + 5 = 80$ dollars, and $MC(161) = 5$ dollars. Accepting adds \$40 of revenue and \$5 of cost, a gain of \$35, so accept. Since $MC(161) = 5 < AC(160) = 80$, the average falls: by the theorem, by $(80 - 5)/161 \approx 0.47$ dollars, to about \$79.53.

**Problem 3.** The lemonade stand of the first problem becomes a price-taker at \$25 a jug, with the same costs. The \$30 fixed cost is sunk. How many jugs should it make, and what is its profit? Should it shut down?

**Solution.** Marginal costs are 20, 15, 20, 30, 40. The jugs with $MC \le 25$ are the first three, and the difference $25 - MC$ switches sign once, so make three. Revenue is 75 and cost is 85, a loss of \$10. Variable cost is $85 - 30 = 55$, which revenue covers, so operating (losing 10) beats shutting down (losing 30). In terms of averages: $AVC(3) = 55/3 \approx 18.3 < 25$.

**Problem 4.** You paid \$60 for a concert ticket that cannot be refunded. On the night you are tired: you would now value attending at \$30, and a friend offers a dinner you value at \$45. (a) What should you do? (b) What if you learn that you can resell the ticket for \$50?

**Solution.** (a) The \$60 is sunk and appears in both options. Attending is worth 30 and the dinner is worth 45, so go to dinner. Counting the \$60 as a reason to attend is the sunk cost fallacy. (b) Now \$50 of the ticket's cost is recoverable, so it is no longer sunk. The options are: attend, worth 30; or sell and dine, worth $50 + 45 = 95$. Sell. Attending now has an opportunity cost of \$50 that it did not have in (a).

**Problem 5.** Mara's landlord replaces the \$60 daily fee with a charge of \$20 per cake sold. Use the original table, where she sets her own price. How many cakes does she now make, and does she prefer the old arrangement?

**Solution.** The fixed cost is now 0 and every marginal cost rises by 20, to 40, 35, 40, 45, 65, 85. Marginal revenue is 90, 70, 50, 30, 10, $-10$, so $MR - MC$ is $50, 35, 10, -15, \dots$ and the best quantity is three. Variable costs before the charge are 20, 35, 55 for one to three cakes, so profit at three is $210 - 55 - 60 = 95$. Under the old fee she made four cakes and \$100. She slightly prefers the old arrangement, and the landlord collects \$60 either way. A per-unit charge changes the quantity; a fixed fee does not.

**Problem 6.** A student has an average of 80 on four tests and scores 70 on the fifth. Find the new average using the average-marginal formula. Then prove: if $AC(q) \le AC(q-1)$ and $AC(q) \le AC(q+1)$, so that average cost is lowest at $q$, then $MC(q) \le AC(q) \le MC(q+1)$.

**Solution.** The fifth score plays the role of the marginal value: the new average is $80 + (70 - 80)/5 = 78$. For the proof, apply the theorem twice. From $AC(q) - AC(q-1) = \frac{MC(q) - AC(q-1)}{q} \le 0$ we get $MC(q) \le AC(q-1)$. Rewrite the same identity as $q\,AC(q) = (q-1)\,AC(q-1) + MC(q)$; since $AC(q-1) \ge AC(q)$, this gives $q\,AC(q) \ge (q-1)\,AC(q) + MC(q)$, so $MC(q) \le AC(q)$. From $AC(q+1) - AC(q) = \frac{MC(q+1) - AC(q)}{q+1} \ge 0$ we get $MC(q+1) \ge AC(q)$. So marginal cost passes from below average cost to above it at the quantity where average cost is lowest, as in the figure, where $25 \le 35 \le 45$.

**Problem 7.** (Uses calculus.) A firm has revenue $R(q) = 60q - 2q^2$ and cost $C(q) = 100 + 12q + q^2$ for $q \ge 0$. Find the profit-maximizing quantity, the price, and the profit, and verify that it is a maximum.

**Solution.** $R'(q) = 60 - 4q$ and $C'(q) = 12 + 2q$. Setting them equal, $48 = 6q$, so $q = 8$. Profit is $\pi(q) = 48q - 3q^2 - 100$, with $\pi''(q) = -6 < 0$, so $q = 8$ is the maximum of this downward parabola. Revenue is $R = Pq$, so the price is $P = 60 - 2q = 44$. Profit is $\pi(8) = 384 - 192 - 100 = 92$. Check: $R(8) = 480 - 128 = 352$ and $C(8) = 100 + 96 + 64 = 260$, difference 92.

**Problem 8.** For some product, $MR(k) - MC(k)$ for units 1 to 5 is $-20, -5, +10, +20, -10$. A student says: "Marginal revenue is below marginal cost on the very first unit, so the firm should make nothing." Find the best quantity and explain which hypothesis the student overlooked.

**Solution.** By part 1 of the marginal rule, profit relative to making nothing is the running total: $-20, -25, -15, +5, -5$. The largest value is $+5$, at four units, which beats the 0 from making nothing. The student applied part 2, which requires the differences to be positive up to $q^*$ and negative after it. Here the sign goes negative, positive, negative, so part 2 does not apply, and "stop at the first unit that does not pay" is not valid. The early units lose money that the later ones more than recover, as happens when a product has high start-up costs per batch. When the sign pattern is irregular, compare totals.

---

# Consumer surplus, and what a tax destroys

> Measure what a market is worth to its buyers and sellers, then tax it. Some of the loss reaches nobody, and who bears the rest depends on slopes, not the law.

Series: Economics (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/surplus-and-taxes/
Keywords: consumer surplus, producer surplus, deadweight loss, tax incidence, per-unit tax, market efficiency, who pays a tax, total surplus

[Figure 1, animation: A tax per helmet is raised from $2 to $30 and then set at $15. The tax is the vertical gap between what buyers pay and what sellers keep. Buyers' surplus (blue) and sellers' surplus (orange) shrink, the government's revenue (gold) appears, and the red triangle is surplus that goes to nobody.]

A city puts a tax of \$15 on every bicycle helmet sold. It collects \$7,500 a month. Add up what the tax costs the people in the market and, in the example worked out below, the answer is \$8,250 a month: \$5,500 from buyers and \$2,750 from sellers. So \$750 a month left the buyers and sellers and did not arrive at the treasury. Where did it go?

There is a second puzzle in the same numbers. The law makes sellers hand over the tax, yet buyers bear two thirds of it. Both puzzles need a way to measure what a market is worth to the people who trade in it. That measure is built person by person first, in a market small enough to list.

## What a trade is worth to each person

Take the used-textbook market from [the lesson on supply and demand](@economics/supply-and-demand). Eight students each want one copy of a calculus book, and the most they would pay is \$95, \$85, \$75, \$65, \$55, \$45, \$35 and \$25. Call them, in that order, Ben, Fay, Dev, Hoa, Ana, Gus, Cho and Eli. Eight owners each have a copy, and the least they would accept is \$10, \$20, \$30, \$40, \$50, \$60, \$70 and \$80. Everyone takes the going price as given. At any price from \$50 to \$55 the five buyers with the highest willingness to pay want to buy and the five owners with the lowest costs want to sell, so five copies trade. Say the price is \$52.

Ben would have paid \$95 and pays \$52. He ends up as well off as if he had paid his limit and then been handed \$43. The owner with a cost of \$10 would have sold for \$10 and receives \$52: she is \$42 ahead.

**Definition.** A buyer with willingness to pay $v$ who buys one unit at price $p$ gets a **consumer surplus** of $v - p$. A seller with cost $c$ who sells one unit at price $p$ gets a **producer surplus** of $p - c$. The consumer surplus and producer surplus of a market are the sums over everyone who trades, and their sum is the **total surplus**. People who do not trade get zero.

| Buyer would pay | 95 | 85 | 75 | 65 | 55 | Sum |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Consumer surplus at \$52 | 43 | 33 | 23 | 13 | 3 | 115 |
| **Seller's cost** | **10** | **20** | **30** | **40** | **50** | |
