**Problem 5.** Maya builds a better oven and now bakes a loaf in 10 minutes. Nothing else changes. (a) What are the new opportunity costs and the new range of mutually beneficial prices? (b) Leo has not improved at anything. Can he be better off than before? Illustrate with a price of 2.5 loaves per fish and 5 fish traded.

**Solution.** (a) Maya can now make 60 loaves or 15 fish, so a fish costs her $40/10 = 4$ loaves. Leo's cost is still 1. The range widens from $(1, 2)$ to $(1, 4)$ loaves per fish. (b) Yes. At 2.5, Leo sells 5 fish for 12.5 loaves and has 5 fish and 12.5 loaves, against 5 fish and 7 loaves at the old price of 1.4. Maya has 5 fish and $60 - 12.5 = 47.5$ loaves, and her own frontier at 5 fish allows $60 - 20 = 40$, so she also gains. Prices above 2 were impossible before, because Maya would have refused them. Her improvement at bread made fish scarcer in her terms and raised what she will pay for Leo's fish. The model does not guarantee that the price rises, only that it now can.

**Problem 6.** A critic says: "Leo needs 60 minutes per fish and Maya 40. A plan that has the slower fisher catch all the fish must waste time." Starting from the specialized plan (Maya 30 loaves, Leo 10 fish), move one fish from Leo's day to Maya's and compute what happens to total output. Then say exactly what is wrong with the critic's argument.

**Solution.** If Maya catches one fish she spends 40 minutes and bakes 2 fewer loaves. Leo catches one fish fewer, which frees 60 minutes, and he bakes 1 loaf. Total fish are unchanged at 10 and total loaves fall from 30 to 29. Each fish moved to the "faster" fisher costs the island a loaf. The critic compares Maya's minutes with Leo's minutes as if a minute saved by one could be spent by the other. It cannot: Maya's 40 minutes come out of Maya's baking, where a minute yields three times what Leo's minute yields. The right measure of cost is the bread given up, and by that measure Leo is the cheaper fisher.

**Problem 7.** Let A and B have equal opportunity costs, $c_A = c_B = c$. Use the gains formulas from the proof of the theorem to show that no price lets both gain. Then explain in a sentence why two producers with the same opportunity cost have nothing to offer each other, even if one is far more productive.

**Solution.** With A buying X, the gains are $(c - p)q$ for A and $(p - c)q$ for B. These add to zero, so if one is positive the other is negative, and both are zero only at $p = c$. If the roles are reversed, with A selling X, the same formulas hold with the signs exchanged, and again they add to zero. So no trade makes both better off. The reason: trade lets you turn one good into the other at the price $p$ instead of at your own cost, and when both producers convert at the same rate $c$, the only price both accept is $c$, the rate each already had at home.

**Problem 8.** Suppose Leo works only 120 minutes a day, so he can make at most 2 fish or 2 loaves, and Maya wants 4 fish. Leo catches 2 fish and sells both to Maya at $p$ loaves each, with $1 < p < 2$. Maya is not fully specialized: she catches the other 2 fish herself. Find each one's consumption and show that both are outside their own frontiers. What does this tell you about the theorem's assumption that A makes only Y?

**Solution.** Maya spends 80 minutes on 2 fish and 520 minutes on 26 loaves, then pays $2p$ loaves for Leo's 2 fish. She has 4 fish and $26 - 2p$ loaves. Her frontier at 4 fish allows 22 loaves, and $26 - 2p > 22$ exactly when $p < 2$. Leo has no fish and $2p$ loaves. His frontier at no fish allows 2 loaves, and $2p > 2$ exactly when $p > 1$. With $p = 1.4$ Maya gains 1.2 loaves and Leo gains 0.8, a total of $2 = (2 - 1) \times 2$. So full specialization by both is not needed. What matters is that each unit traded is made by the producer with the lower opportunity cost. A small trading partner specializes completely, while the large one keeps making some of both goods.

---

# The prisoner's dilemma and Nash equilibrium

> How to read a payoff table, find best responses and Nash equilibria, mix strategies when no cell is stable, and see why repeated play can sustain cooperation.

Series: Economics (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/economics/game-theory/
Keywords: prisoner's dilemma, Nash equilibrium, game theory, dominant strategy, best response, mixed strategy, matching pennies, repeated game grim trigger

[Figure 1, animation: Two gas stations, Ava's and Raj's, each choose a High or a Low price. In each cell the blue number is Ava's daily profit and the orange number is Raj's, in hundreds of dollars. Each arrow is a switch that pays the player making it, and every arrow leads to the cell where both price Low.]

Ava and Raj own the only two gas stations in a small town. Each morning, before seeing the other's sign, each posts a High price or a Low price. If both post High, each makes \$300 that day. If both post Low, each makes \$100. If one posts Low while the other posts High, the cheap station takes nearly all the customers and makes \$500, and the other makes nothing.

This is not the market of [supply and demand](@economics/supply-and-demand), where each seller is too small to move the price. Here each owner's profit depends on what the one rival does. Both owners can see that \$300 each is better than \$100 each, and both want only to make money. Yet I claim that each of them, reasoning correctly, will post Low, and both will end with a third of what was available. We will see exactly why, and then what can get the two owners out of it.

## A game is a table

Start by writing the situation down completely. There are two decision makers. Each has a list of options. For every combination of options, each ends up with some result that they care about, which we record as a number.

**Definition.** A **game in normal form** (for two players) consists of: two **players**; for each player a set of **strategies**; and for each pair of strategies, one chosen by each player, a **payoff** to each player, a number of which that player wants as much as possible. The players choose at the same time, each without knowing the other's choice, and both know the whole table.

For the stations, the strategies are High and Low, and the payoffs are profits in hundreds of dollars. The table at the top of the page lists them: rows are Ava's choice, columns are Raj's, and each cell holds Ava's payoff (blue) and Raj's (orange).

The definition hides two assumptions. A payoff is supposed to measure everything the player cares about. If Ava would feel guilty undercutting Raj, the number 5 overstates what Low is worth to her, and we are analyzing the wrong table. And the game is played once. We will lift that second assumption later, and it will matter a great deal.

## Best responses

Ava does not know what Raj will post. So she can ask a conditional question: *if* Raj posts High, what is best for me? And if he posts Low?

[Figure 2, steps: Finding best responses in the gas station game. For each choice by the other player, circle the payoff of the best reply. Ava's circles are both in the Low row and Raj's are both in the Low column, so the only cell with two circles is Low, Low.]

  - step: Suppose Raj posts High: the left column. Ava compares her two payoffs there, 3 from High and 5 from Low. Low is better, so circle the 5.
  - step: Suppose Raj posts Low: the right column. Ava compares 0 with 1. Low is better again.
  - step: Now Raj, row by row. If Ava posts High he compares 3 with 5. If she posts Low he compares 0 with 1. He circles Low both times.
  - step: One cell has both payoffs circled: Low, Low. There each is doing as well as possible given what the other is doing.
**Definition.** Write $u_1(s_1, s_2)$ and $u_2(s_1, s_2)$ for the payoffs to players 1 and 2 when they choose strategies $s_1$ and $s_2$. A strategy $s_1$ is a **best response** to $s_2$ if $u_1(s_1, s_2) \ge u_1(s_1', s_2)$ for every strategy $s_1'$ of player 1. A strategy is **strictly dominant** if it gives a strictly higher payoff than each of the player's other strategies against *every* strategy of the opponent. (Best responses and dominance for player 2 are defined the same way.)

For Ava, Low is the best response to High (5 beats 3) and to Low (1 beats 0), so Low is strictly dominant. She does not need to guess what Raj will do, because Low is better either way. The table is symmetric, so the same holds for Raj. Both post Low and each earns 1.

Here is the uncomfortable part. Each owner's reasoning was airtight, yet the result, 1 each, is worse for both than the 3 each they would get from High. You might object that they should just see this and both choose High. But look at what that proposal asks of Ava: to post High when, whatever Raj does, Low would pay her more. If she expects Raj to post High, that is a reason to post Low and collect 5.

## Nash equilibrium

Dominant strategies are rare, and we need a notion of a "solved" game that does not depend on them. The last step of the figure suggests one: a cell where both payoffs are circled.

**Definition.** A pair of strategies $(s_1^*, s_2^*)$ is a **Nash equilibrium** if $s_1^*$ is a best response to $s_2^*$ and $s_2^*$ is a best response to $s_1^*$. Equivalently, neither player can get a strictly higher payoff by changing their own strategy while the other's stays fixed.

An equilibrium is a cell that nobody wants to leave alone. It is a statement about stability and says nothing about whether the cell is good.

**Theorem.** If each player has a strictly dominant strategy, then the pair of dominant strategies is a Nash equilibrium, and it is the only one.

**Proof.** Let $s_1^*$ and $s_2^*$ be the dominant strategies. A strictly dominant strategy is a best response to every strategy of the opponent, in particular to the opponent's dominant strategy, so $(s_1^*, s_2^*)$ is a Nash equilibrium. Now let $(s_1, s_2)$ be any Nash equilibrium. If $s_1 \ne s_1^*$, dominance gives $u_1(s_1^*, s_2) > u_1(s_1, s_2)$, so $s_1$ is not a best response to $s_2$, a contradiction. Hence $s_1 = s_1^*$, and in the same way $s_2 = s_2^*$.

So (Low, Low) is the unique Nash equilibrium of the station game. Games with its shape have a name. Call the two strategies Cooperate and Defect, and let $R$ be the reward when both cooperate, $P$ the payoff when both defect, $T$ the temptation payoff to a lone defector and $S$ the payoff to a lone cooperator. A **prisoner's dilemma** is a symmetric game with $T > R > P > S$. Since $T > R$ and $P > S$, Defect is strictly dominant, and since $R > P$, the equilibrium is worse for both than mutual cooperation. The stations have $T = 5$, $R = 3$, $P = 1$, $S = 0$. The name is usually credited to Albert Tucker, who in 1950 told the game as a story of two suspects questioned separately, each offered a lighter sentence for testifying against the other.

The same table describes an arms race: each of two rival countries is safer armed whatever the other does, and both would be better off with neither arming. Whether a real situation satisfies $T > R > P > S$ is an empirical question about the real payoffs. When people play one-shot prisoner's dilemmas for money in laboratories, a sizable fraction cooperate. The theorem is untouched by this, because for those people money is not the whole payoff, and so the game they are playing is not the one in the table.

**Pause and try.** Change one number: suppose a station that posts Low against High earns 2 instead of 5 (the price cut wins customers but the margin is thin). Redo the circles. Is Low still dominant? What are the Nash equilibria?

**Answer.** Now if Raj posts High, Ava compares 3 (High) with 2 (Low) and prefers High. If Raj posts Low she compares 0 with 1 and prefers Low. Neither strategy is dominant: her best response is to match Raj. By symmetry the same holds for Raj. Both payoffs are circled in (High, High) and in (Low, Low), so two cells are Nash equilibria.

## Two equilibria: a coordination game

That exercise produced a new kind of game. Here is its cleanest form. Two phone makers must each pick a charging plug, X or Y. If they pick the same plug, customers can share chargers and both sell more; plug X is a little better, so matching on X pays 2 each and matching on Y pays 1 each. If they differ, each gets 0.

[Figure 3, image: A coordination game with best responses circled. Each firm's best reply is to match the other, so both payoffs are circled in two cells. Both cells are Nash equilibria, including the one where the firms are stuck on the worse plug.]

Nobody has a dominant strategy, and two cells are Nash equilibria. (Y, Y) is worse for both than (X, X), and it is still an equilibrium: if the other firm is using Y, switching alone to X drops you from 1 to 0. Nash equilibrium tells us which outcomes are stable. When there are several it does not tell us which will happen. History, convention or a public announcement has to do that.

## No stable cell: matching pennies

Can a game have no Nash equilibrium at all? Try this one. Two players each put a penny on the table, Heads or Tails up, hidden under a hand. If the pennies match, the Matcher wins a dollar from the Mismatcher. If they differ, the Mismatcher wins a dollar from the Matcher.

**Pause and try.** Write the four cells of the table, with the Matcher's payoff first. Circle best responses. Which cells are Nash equilibria?

**Answer.** (Heads, Heads): $1, -1$. (Heads, Tails): $-1, 1$. (Tails, Heads): $-1, 1$. (Tails, Tails): $1, -1$. The Matcher's best response is always to copy, and the Mismatcher's is always to differ. In every cell one player has payoff $-1$ and would get $+1$ by switching. No cell has two circles, so no pair of strategies is a Nash equilibrium.

[Figure 4, animation: Matching pennies. Starting from any cell, the player who is losing switches, which makes the other player the loser, who switches in turn. The switches chase each other around the table and never stop: no cell is stable.]

The definition is reporting something true about the game. Anyone who has played knows that the one thing you must not be is predictable. If the Matcher could count on Heads from you, you would lose every time. So let the players do what real players do, and randomize.

**Definition.** A **mixed strategy** assigns a probability to each of a player's strategies, and the player lets chance choose according to those probabilities. (The original strategies are called **pure**.) A player's payoff from mixed strategies is the expected value of the payoff, and best responses and Nash equilibrium are defined as before, with expected payoffs.

Recall that the [expected value](@probability/expected-value) of a random payoff is the sum of each possible payoff times its probability. Suppose the Matcher shows Heads with probability $p$. If the Mismatcher shows Heads, she loses a dollar when the Matcher also shows Heads (probability $p$) and wins one otherwise:

$$
\text{Heads: } (-1)p + (1)(1 - p) = 1 - 2p, \qquad \text{Tails: } (1)p + (-1)(1 - p) = 2p - 1.
$$

If $p > \frac12$, Tails pays more, so her best response is always Tails. If $p < \frac12$, always Heads. Only at $p = \frac12$ are the two equal, both zero, and then every mix is a best response for her. The same computation for the Matcher, with $q$ the probability that the Mismatcher shows Heads, gives $2q - 1$ for Heads and $1 - 2q$ for Tails.

[Figure 5, steps: Best responses in matching pennies, plotted in the square of mixed strategies: p is the probability that the Matcher shows Heads and q the probability that the Mismatcher does. The two best-response curves cross at exactly one point, p = q = \frac12.]

  - step: The Mismatcher's best reply to each p. If the Matcher favors Tails (p below 0.5) she shows Heads for sure, if he favors Heads she shows Tails for sure, and at exactly 0.5 any q is as good as any other.
  - step: The Matcher's best reply to each q. If the Mismatcher favors Heads (q above 0.5) he shows Heads for sure, and if she favors Tails he shows Tails.
  - step: A Nash equilibrium is a point on both curves. There is exactly one: both players mix half and half.
**Theorem.** Matching pennies has exactly one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies: each player shows Heads with probability $\frac12$. Each player's expected payoff is 0.

**Proof.** Let $(p, q)$ be a Nash equilibrium. If $p > \frac12$, the Mismatcher's only best response is Tails, so $q = 0$. Against $q = 0$ the Matcher gets $2q - 1 = -1$ from Heads and $+1$ from Tails, so his only best response is $p = 0$, contradicting $p > \frac12$. If $p < \frac12$, her only best response is $q = 1$, against which his only best response is $p = 1$, again a contradiction. So $p = \frac12$, and the same argument with the roles exchanged gives $q = \frac12$. Conversely, at $q = \frac12$ the Matcher gets $0$ from Heads and from Tails, so every $p$, including $\frac12$, is a best response; likewise for the Mismatcher at $p = \frac12$. So $(\frac12, \frac12)$ is a Nash equilibrium, with expected payoff 0 to each.

Notice what fixes each player's probabilities. The Matcher mixes half and half to leave the Mismatcher with nothing to exploit, and the mix that does this is the one that makes *her* indifferent. His own payoff is the same whatever he does. This is typical of mixed equilibria.

The square in the figure also makes the general fact plausible. One curve runs from the left edge to the right, the other from bottom to top, and they have to cross.

**Theorem.** **(Nash, 1950; cited without proof.)** Every game with finitely many players, each having finitely many pure strategies, has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.

The proof needs a fixed-point theorem from topology and is beyond our tools. What it tells us is that the hunt for an equilibrium never fails for a table of finite size, as long as mixing is allowed.

**Key idea.** A Nash equilibrium is a choice of strategy for each player from which nobody gains by changing alone. To find one, mark best responses. A game may have one equilibrium that is bad for everyone, several, or none until the players randomize, and then it always has one.

## Playing again and again

Back to Ava and Raj. Their real situation differs from the table in one respect: they post prices every morning, with no end in sight. That changes the game, because today's choice can now depend on what the other did yesterday, and a price cut can be answered.

Payoffs now arrive at different dates, so we need to compare them. Suppose each owner values a dollar received one day later at $\delta$ dollars today, with $0 < \delta < 1$. This is the **discount factor** from the lesson on [present value](@economics/compound-interest-present-value), where it was $\frac{1}{1+r}$ for an interest rate $r$ per period; it can also absorb the chance that the game ends. A stream of payoffs $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ is worth $a_0 + a_1\delta + a_2\delta^2 + \cdots$, and for a constant stream the [geometric series](@precalculus/geometric-series) gives

$$
a + a\delta + a\delta^2 + \cdots = \frac{a}{1 - \delta}.
$$

Consider this plan, called the **grim trigger**: post High as long as nobody has ever posted Low, and after anyone posts Low, post Low forever. Suppose Raj follows it. Is it a best response for Ava to follow it too?

**Pause and try.** Take $\delta = 0.8$. If Ava follows the plan she gets 3 every day. If she posts Low today she gets 5 today and, since Raj then posts Low forever, at most 1 every day after. Find the discounted total of each stream. Which is larger?

**Answer.** Following: $\frac{3}{1 - 0.8} = 15$. Cutting: $5 + (0.8 + 0.8^2 + \cdots) = 5 + \frac{0.8}{0.2} = 9$. Following the plan is worth much more. The cut gains 2 today and loses 2 on every later day.

[Figure 6, animation: Running discounted totals for Ava when Raj plays the grim trigger and \delta = 0.8, in hundreds of dollars. If she keeps posting High the total climbs toward 15. If she cuts her price on day 1 she is ahead for two days and then falls behind for good, with a total that approaches 9.]

How patient must the owners be for this to work? Do the same computation with letters.

**Theorem.** **(Grim trigger.)** Consider a prisoner's dilemma with payoffs $T > R > P > S$, repeated forever, with discount factor $0 < \delta < 1$. Both players following the grim trigger is a Nash equilibrium of the repeated game if and only if

$$
\delta \ge \frac{T - R}{T - P}.
$$

**Proof.** Suppose player 2 follows the grim trigger. If player 1 does too, both cooperate forever and player 1's total is $R + R\delta + R\delta^2 + \cdots = \frac{R}{1 - \delta}$. Now suppose player 1 uses some other plan that leads her to defect at some point, and let day 0 be the first day she does (if that day comes later, both streams below are the same up to then, and the comparison is multiplied by a power of $\delta$). On day 0 she gets $T$. From day 1 on, player 2 defects forever, so on each later day she gets $P$ or $S$, at most $P$. Her total is at most $T + P\delta + P\delta^2 + \cdots = T + \frac{\delta P}{1 - \delta}$, and she gets exactly this by defecting forever. So no deviation is profitable if and only if

$$
\frac{R}{1 - \delta} \ge T + \frac{\delta P}{1 - \delta}.
$$

Multiply by $1 - \delta > 0$: $R \ge T(1 - \delta) + \delta P$, that is $\delta(T - P) \ge T - R$. Since $T > P$ we may divide, which gives the condition. The same holds for player 2.

For the stations, $\frac{T - R}{T - P} = \frac{5 - 3}{5 - 1} = \frac12$. Cooperation survives if each owner values tomorrow's dollar at 50 cents or more today.

[Figure 7, image: The two totals from the proof, each multiplied by 1 - \delta so that they fit on one scale: always High is worth 3 per day, and cutting once is worth 5(1-\delta) + \delta = 5 - 4\delta. The lines cross at \delta = \frac12. To the right of the crossing, in the shaded region, cutting does not pay.]

The threshold has a reading. $T - R$ is what a defector gains today, and $T - P$ is the whole distance between the best and the punished payoff. A larger temptation raises the threshold, and a harsher punishment lowers it. The table has not changed, and High is still not a best response in the one-day game. What changed is that the future became a hostage.

The theorem proves a Nash equilibrium of the repeated game, which tests each plan only against the other's whole plan. A stricter test, **subgame perfection**, asks that the plans also be mutual best responses after every possible history, so that no threat is one a player would decline to carry out. The grim trigger passes it under the same condition: once anyone has posted Low, both plans say Low forever, and Low is a best response to Low every day.

Three limits on this result. First, it shows that cooperation *can* be an equilibrium, not that it must be: both owners posting Low every day, whatever has happened, is also a Nash equilibrium of the repeated game. Second, it needs an open-ended future. If both know the game ends on day 100, then on day 100 nothing can be punished, so both post Low; knowing that, day 99 cannot be rewarded or punished either, and the argument runs all the way back to day 1. Third, each must be able to see what the other did.

## Worked examples

**Worked example.** **Find all pure Nash equilibria. Player 1 chooses Up or Down, player 2 chooses Left or Right, and the payoffs (player 1 first) are: (Up, Left) $2, 3$; (Up, Right) $1, 1$; (Down, Left) $4, 0$; (Down, Right) $2, 2$.**

Player 1 compares within each column. Against Left: 2 from Up, 4 from Down, so Down. Against Right: 1 from Up, 2 from Down, so Down. Down is strictly dominant for player 1. Player 2 compares within each row. Against Up: 3 from Left, 1 from Right, so Left. Against Down: 0 from Left, 2 from Right, so Right. Player 2 has no dominant strategy.

The only cell where both are best responses is (Down, Right), with payoffs $2, 2$. *Check:* from there, player 1 switching to Up gets 1, and player 2 switching to Left gets 0. Neither gains.

**Worked example.** **A penalty kick. The kicker aims Left or Right and the goalkeeper dives Left or Right at the same instant. The probability of a goal is 0.5 if both go Left, 0.9 if the kick goes Left and the dive Right, 0.8 if the kick goes Right and the dive Left, and 0.2 if both go Right. The kicker wants that probability high and the keeper wants it low. Find the mixed equilibrium.**

There is no pure equilibrium, since the keeper wants to match and the kicker does not. Let the keeper dive Left with probability $q$. The kicker's chance of scoring is $0.5q + 0.9(1 - q) = 0.9 - 0.4q$ from Left and $0.8q + 0.2(1 - q) = 0.2 + 0.6q$ from Right. The keeper must leave him indifferent, or he would always pick the better side: $0.9 - 0.4q = 0.2 + 0.6q$ gives $q = 0.7$.

Let the kicker aim Left with probability $p$. The scoring chance is $0.5p + 0.8(1 - p) = 0.8 - 0.3p$ if the keeper dives Left and $0.9p + 0.2(1 - p) = 0.2 + 0.7p$ if Right. Indifference for the keeper: $0.8 - 0.3p = 0.2 + 0.7p$, so $p = 0.6$.

*Check.* At $q = 0.7$ both of the kicker's options score with probability $0.9 - 0.28 = 0.62$, and at $p = 0.6$ both of the keeper's options concede with probability $0.8 - 0.18 = 0.62$. Studies of professional penalty kicks have found that players' actual frequencies are close to what such calculations predict.

**Common mistake.** **"The Nash equilibrium is the outcome that is best for the players."** Equilibrium means that no *single* player gains by changing alone. It makes no comparison between cells for the group. In the prisoner's dilemma the equilibrium is the one cell that both players rank below another, and in the plug game (Y, Y) is an equilibrium although (X, X) is better for both.

**Common mistake.** **Choosing your mix to make yourself indifferent.** In the penalty example, students often set the kicker's two payoffs equal and solve for the kicker's own $p$. But the kicker's payoffs depend on the keeper's $q$, and that equation determines $q$. In a mixed equilibrium each player's probabilities are pinned down by the *other* player's indifference.

Stepping back: the hard step was to give up asking what is best and ask instead what is stable, cell by cell, one player at a time. The reusable tool is the best-response check, which works on any table: fix what the others do, and see whether anyone wants to move. The prisoner's dilemma shows that stable and good can come apart, and the repeated game shows one way to bring them back together.

**Check yourself.** In a game with payoffs (player 1 first) (A, A) $4, 4$; (A, B) $0, 5$; (B, A) $5, 0$; (B, B) $2, 2$, what are the pure Nash equilibria?
Answer: (B, B) only B is strictly dominant for each player (5 beats 4, and 2 beats 0), so (B, B) is the unique equilibrium. This is a prisoner's dilemma with $T = 5$, $R = 4$, $P = 2$, $S = 0$.

**Recap.** - A normal-form game lists players, strategies and a payoff to each player for every combination of strategies.
- A best response is a strategy that does as well as possible against a given strategy of the opponent. A strictly dominant strategy is the best response to everything.
- A Nash equilibrium is a pair of mutual best responses. If both players have strictly dominant strategies, it is unique.
- Prisoner's dilemma: $T > R > P > S$. Defect is dominant and the equilibrium is worse for both than cooperation.
- Some games have several equilibria (coordination) and some have none in pure strategies (matching pennies). With mixed strategies an equilibrium always exists (Nash), and each player's mix makes the other indifferent.
- Repeated forever with discount factor $\delta$, the grim trigger sustains cooperation exactly when $\delta \ge \frac{T - R}{T - P}$.

## Problems

Work these on paper before opening the solutions. The first two repeat the lesson's moves, the next four combine them, and the last goes further.

**Problem 1.** Two countries each choose to Arm or Disarm. If both disarm each gets 4. If both arm each gets 2. If one arms and the other disarms, the armed one gets 5 and the other gets 1. Is this a prisoner's dilemma? Find the Nash equilibrium.

**Solution.** With Disarm as "cooperate": $R = 4$, $P = 2$, $T = 5$, $S = 1$, and $5 > 4 > 2 > 1$, so it is a prisoner's dilemma. Arm is strictly dominant: against Disarm it gives 5 instead of 4, and against Arm it gives 2 instead of 1. The unique Nash equilibrium is (Arm, Arm) with payoffs 2 each, worse for both than the 4 each from mutual disarmament.

**Problem 2.** Two hunters each choose Stag or Hare. A stag needs both hunters and is worth 4 to each. A hare can be caught alone and is worth 3. A hunter who goes for the stag alone gets 0. (a) Find the pure Nash equilibria. (b) How sure must a hunter be that the other will choose Stag before Stag is his best response?

**Solution.** (a) Payoffs: (Stag, Stag) $4, 4$; (Stag, Hare) $0, 3$; (Hare, Stag) $3, 0$; (Hare, Hare) $3, 3$. Against Stag the best response is Stag ($4 > 3$). Against Hare it is Hare ($3 > 0$). So (Stag, Stag) and (Hare, Hare) are both Nash equilibria, and there is no dominant strategy. (b) If the other hunts Stag with probability $q$, Stag has expected payoff $4q$ and Hare has $3$. Stag is a best response when $4q \ge 3$, that is $q \ge \frac34$. The better equilibrium is the riskier one, since it takes 75% confidence in the partner.

**Problem 3.** The plug game has a third Nash equilibrium, in mixed strategies. Find it, and each firm's expected payoff there.

**Solution.** Let firm 2 choose X with probability $q$. Firm 1 expects $2q$ from X and $1 \cdot (1 - q)$ from Y. Firm 1 is willing to mix only if these are equal, so $2q = 1 - q$ and $q = \frac13$. The game is symmetric, so firm 1 also chooses X with probability $\frac13$. Each is then indifferent, so each mix is a best response to the other. The expected payoff is $2q = \frac23$ for each firm, lower than in either pure equilibrium, because the firms mismatch with probability $\frac13 \cdot \frac23 + \frac23 \cdot \frac13 = \frac49$.

**Problem 4.** Ann hides a coin in one hand: a \$1 coin if she uses her left, a \$2 coin if she uses her right. Bob guesses a hand. If he is right he keeps the coin, and Ann loses it; if he is wrong nothing changes hands. Find the mixed Nash equilibrium and Bob's expected winnings.

**Solution.** Let Ann hide in the left hand with probability $p$. Bob's expected winnings are $1 \cdot p$ from guessing left and $2(1 - p)$ from guessing right. Ann must make these equal, or Bob would always pick the better guess: $p = 2 - 2p$ gives $p = \frac23$. Let Bob guess left with probability $q$. Ann's expected loss is $1 \cdot q$ if she hides left and $2(1 - q)$ if she hides right; equal when $q = \frac23$. In equilibrium Ann hides the cheaper coin two thirds of the time, and Bob guesses the cheaper hand two thirds of the time. Bob's expected winnings are $p = \frac23$ of a dollar per play. There is no pure equilibrium: if Ann's hand were predictable Bob would guess it, and then she would switch.

**Problem 5.** A repeated prisoner's dilemma has $T = 7$, $R = 4$, $P = 2$, $S = 0$. (a) For which discount factors does the grim trigger sustain cooperation? (b) Does it work if the interest rate is 50% per period? 100%? (c) Verify (b) by computing both totals at 100%.

**Solution.** (a) $\delta \ge \frac{7 - 4}{7 - 2} = 0.6$. (b) At $r = 50\%$, $\delta = \frac{1}{1.5} = 0.667 \ge 0.6$: yes. At $r = 100\%$, $\delta = 0.5 < 0.6$: no. (c) At $\delta = 0.5$, cooperating forever is worth $\frac{4}{0.5} = 8$, and defecting is worth $7 + \frac{0.5 \times 2}{0.5} = 9$. Defecting pays more, so the grim trigger is not an equilibrium.

**Problem 6.** Ava and Raj will post prices on exactly two mornings, and both know it. Payoffs are those of the station game, added over the two days without discounting. Show that in a Nash equilibrium in which each owner's day-2 choice is a best response whatever happened on day 1, both post Low on both days.

**Solution.** Work from the end. On day 2 nothing follows, so each owner's day-2 payoff is just the one-day table, in which Low is strictly dominant. So both post Low on day 2 whatever happened on day 1, and each gets 1 on day 2 regardless. On day 1, then, an owner's total is her day-1 payoff plus 1, and her day-1 choice cannot change the second part. So day 1 is again the one-day game with 1 added to every payoff, which does not change any comparison: Low is strictly dominant. Both post Low on both days. A promise to post High on day 2 as a reward for High on day 1 would not be kept, so it cannot support High on day 1.

**Problem 7.** **(A forgiving punishment.)** In the repeated station game, replace the grim trigger by this plan: post High; if anyone posts Low, both post Low for the next $k$ days and then return to High. Compare following the plan with cutting once and then following it. Show that the cut is unprofitable exactly when $\delta + \delta^2 + \cdots + \delta^k \ge 1$. What does this say for $k = 1$, for $k = 2$, and as $k \to \infty$?

**Solution.** Following gives 3 every day. Cutting on day 0 gives 5 on day 0, then 1 on each of days 1 to $k$, then 3 again. The two streams differ only on days 0 to $k$: the cut gains $5 - 3 = 2$ on day 0 and loses $3 - 1 = 2$ on each of days 1 to $k$. In discounted terms the cut is unprofitable when $2(\delta + \delta^2 + \cdots + \delta^k) \ge 2$, which is the stated condition. For $k = 1$ it reads $\delta \ge 1$, impossible for $\delta < 1$: one day of punishment never deters. For $k = 2$ it reads $\delta^2 + \delta - 1 \ge 0$, that is $\delta \ge \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2} \approx 0.618$. As $k \to \infty$ the sum approaches $\frac{\delta}{1 - \delta}$, and $\frac{\delta}{1 - \delta} \ge 1$ means $\delta \ge \frac12$, the grim trigger threshold. Shorter punishments are more forgiving of mistakes and demand more patience. (A full check would also confirm that each owner is willing to carry out the punishment; she is, since during those $k$ days the other posts Low and Low is her best response to that on each day.)

---

# What "learning" means: fitting a line to data

> A model is a formula with adjustable numbers, a loss scores its misses, and training lowers the loss. All three, worked by hand on four house prices.

Series: Machine Learning (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/machine-learning/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/machine-learning/fitting-a-line/
Keywords: what is machine learning, linear regression, mean squared error, loss function, model parameters, loss surface, convex function, training a model

[Figure 1, animation: Four house sales and a line that predicts price from size. Each miss is drawn as a square. As the slope and intercept change, the average area of the squares, which is the mean squared error, falls from 1.25 to its smallest possible value, 0.2.]

A house of 2500 square feet comes up for sale in a neighborhood where four houses have sold recently. What will it sell for?

| House | Size (thousands of sq ft) | Price (hundreds of thousands of \$) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1.5 |
| 2 | 2 | 3.5 |
| 3 | 3 | 3.5 |
| 4 | 4 | 5.5 |

No house of that size is in the table, so you cannot look the answer up. You would probably reason that bigger houses cost more and that 2500 square feet sits between houses 2 and 3, which both sold for \$350,000, so something near that. That reasoning is a prediction rule, and it stops working once the table has forty houses and no two neighbors agree. Machine learning makes such rules explicit enough that a computer can find a good one. The phrase "learning from data" sounds mysterious, but for this problem every part of it can be written down and checked with a pencil.

## A rule with two dials

The simplest rule that says "bigger costs more" is a straight line. Write $x$ for the size of a house in thousands of square feet and $\hat y$ (read "y hat") for the predicted price in hundreds of thousands of dollars, and let

$$
\hat y = wx + b.
$$

The two numbers $w$ and $b$ are not fixed yet. Think of them as dials. The dial $w$ is the [slope](@algebra/slope-and-lines): how much each extra thousand square feet adds to the price. The dial $b$ is the intercept, a baseline that shifts the whole line up or down. Every setting of the two dials is a different rule.

A common rule of thumb is "a hundred dollars per square foot". A thousand square feet then costs \$100,000, which in our units is $w = 1$ and $b = 0$: the rule $\hat y = x$. It predicts prices of $1, 2, 3, 4$ for the four houses. They actually sold for $1.5, 3.5, 3.5, 5.5$. The rule is too low every time, by $0.5, 1.5, 0.5$ and $1.5$.

Is that good or bad? Compared with what? We cannot improve a rule until we can say, in one number, how wrong it is.

## Scoring the misses

For each house, call the prediction minus the actual price the **error** of the rule on that house:

$$
e_i = \hat y_i - y_i = wx_i + b - y_i.
$$

For the rule of thumb the four errors are $-0.5, -1.5, -0.5, -1.5$. A natural first idea is to add them up, and it fails: a rule that is \$100,000 too high on one house and \$100,000 too low on another would score zero, the same as a rule that is exactly right on both. Misses in opposite directions must not cancel. The repair used throughout statistics, as in [the lesson on the line of best fit](@statistics/correlation-and-regression), is to square each error first. Squares are never negative, so nothing cancels, and a miss twice as large counts four times as much. Then average, so that the score does not grow just because the table got longer.

For the rule of thumb the squared errors are $0.25, 2.25, 0.25, 2.25$, and their average is $5/4 = 1.25$.

[Figure 2, image: The rule of thumb \hat y = x (slope 1, intercept 0) against the four sales. Each error is the vertical gap between a dot and the line, and the square drawn on it has the squared error as its area. The mean of the four squared errors is 1.25.]

**Pause and try.** Since the rule of thumb is too low on every house, raise the whole line by 1: keep $w = 1$ and set $b = 1$. Compute the four errors and the mean of their squares.

**Answer.** The predictions are $2, 3, 4, 5$, and the errors are $2 - 1.5 = 0.5$, $3 - 3.5 = -0.5$, $4 - 3.5 = 0.5$, $5 - 5.5 = -0.5$. Every squared error is $0.25$, so the mean is $0.25$. One turn of one dial cut the score from $1.25$ to a fifth of that.

We now have the three objects that every problem of this kind is made of, and they have standard names.

**Definition.** Let the data be pairs $(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)$ of real numbers.

A **model** is a function that turns an input $x$ into a prediction $\hat y$ and that depends on some adjustable numbers, its **parameters**. The **linear model** with parameters $w$ and $b$ is $\hat y = wx + b$.

A **loss function** assigns to each setting of the parameters a single number that measures how badly the model's predictions miss the data. The **mean squared error** of the linear model is

$$
L(w, b) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(wx_i + b - y_i\bigr)^2.
$$

**Training** the model on the data means searching for parameters that make the loss small.

Read this against what we did. The model is the rule with its dials, and the parameters are the dials. The loss is the score, and note what its inputs are: the data are fixed, so $L$ is a function of $w$ and $b$ alone. We found $L(1, 0) = 1.25$ and $L(1, 1) = 0.25$. Training is the dial-turning, and the definition says nothing yet about how to do it. The word "learning" in machine learning refers to this search.

## Turning one dial

The most cautious way to search is to leave $b = 0$ and turn only the slope. With $b = 0$ the four errors are $w - 1.5$, $2w - 3.5$, $3w - 3.5$ and $4w - 5.5$. Their squares add up to $(1 + 4 + 9 + 16)\,w^2 - (3 + 14 + 21 + 44)\,w + (2.25 + 12.25 + 12.25 + 30.25) = 30w^2 - 82w + 57$, and dividing by 4,

$$
L(w, 0) = 7.5w^2 - 20.5w + 14.25.
$$

This is a quadratic in $w$ with a positive leading coefficient, so its graph is a parabola opening upward, and [completing the square](@algebra/completing-the-square) locates its lowest point: $L(w, 0) = 7.5\,(w - \tfrac{41}{30})^2 + \tfrac{29}{120}$. With the intercept held at zero, the best slope is $41/30 \approx 1.37$, where the loss is $29/120 \approx 0.242$.

**Pause and try.** Two lines now score about the same: $w = 1, b = 1$ scores $0.25$ and $w \approx 1.37, b = 0$ scores $0.242$. Try the line halfway between in both dials, roughly $w = 1.2$, $b = 0.5$. Does it beat both?

**Answer.** Its predictions are $1.7, 2.9, 4.1, 5.3$, with errors $0.2, -0.6, 0.6, -0.2$ and a loss of $(0.04 + 0.36 + 0.36 + 0.04)/4 = 0.2$. It beats both. One line got close by lifting, the other by tilting, and doing some of each is better than either.

That exercise shows what is wrong with turning one dial. Repeat the calculation with the intercept held at $0.5$ instead of $0$ and you get a different parabola, $L(w, 0.5) = 7.5\,(w - 1.2)^2 + 0.2$, whose lowest point is at a different slope.

[Figure 3, image: The loss as a function of the slope alone, for two fixed intercepts. With b = 0 the best slope is about 1.37, and with b = 0.5 it is 1.2. The best setting of one dial depends on where the other is.]

So the loss cannot be understood one dial at a time. It is a function of two variables, and to see it whole we need a picture with both dials in it.

## The loss surface

Expand the mean squared error without fixing either dial. Each squared error $(wx_i + b - y_i)^2$ multiplies out to $x_i^2w^2 + 2x_iwb + b^2 - 2x_iy_iw - 2y_ib + y_i^2$, and averaging over the four houses replaces each coefficient by an average over the data: the mean of $x_i^2$ is $7.5$, of $x_i$ is $2.5$, of $x_iy_i$ is $10.25$, of $y_i$ is $3.5$ and of $y_i^2$ is $14.25$. Therefore

$$
L(w, b) = 7.5w^2 + 5wb + b^2 - 20.5w - 7b + 14.25.
$$

Check it against what we know: $L(1, 0) = 7.5 - 20.5 + 14.25 = 1.25$, and $L(1, 1) = 7.5 + 5 + 1 - 20.5 - 7 + 14.25 = 0.25$.

A [function of two variables](@multivariable-calculus/functions-of-two-variables) can be drawn as a map. Put $w$ on the horizontal axis and $b$ on the vertical one, so that each point of the plane is one setting of the dials, which is to say one line. Shade each point by the loss there, and draw curves through points of equal loss, the way a hiking map draws curves through points of equal height.

[Figure 4, image: The mean squared error of every line at once. Each point of this plane is one line \hat y = wx + b, shaded darker where the loss is larger, with curves of equal loss at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8. The rule of thumb is point A, the raised line is B, and the lowest point is the green dot at (1.2, 0.5). Points C and D are two very different lines that both have loss 1.]

The curves of equal loss are ellipses, one inside the next, all centered on the same point. They are long and thin, and they lie along a diagonal. That shape says something concrete about the data. Moving along the diagonal means raising the slope while lowering the intercept, which pivots the line about the middle of the data and changes its predictions there very little. Moving across the diagonal lifts the whole line off the data. The loss is forgiving in the first direction and strict in the second.

**Pause and try.** The figure claims that points C and D have the same loss. Check it. C is the line $\hat y = 2x - 1.5$ and D is the line $\hat y = 0.4x + 2.5$.

**Answer.** For C the predictions are $0.5, 2.5, 4.5, 6.5$ and the errors are $-1, -1, 1, 1$, so the loss is $1$. For D the predictions are $2.9, 3.3, 3.7, 4.1$ and the errors are $1.4, -0.2, 0.2, -1.4$, so the loss is $(1.96 + 0.04 + 0.04 + 1.96)/4 = 1$. One line is five times as steep as the other, and its intercept compensates.

In the next figure a point wanders over the map on the right while the line it stands for moves on the left.

[Figure 5, animation: Left: the line with its squared errors. Right: the same line as a point on the loss map. Sliding the point along the valley pivots the line and the loss changes slowly; stepping across the valley lifts the line off the data and the loss climbs quickly.]

Take the loss as height. Closed curves nested around a single low point are then the contour lines of a basin. The loss surface of the four houses is a long bowl, and the green dot is its bottom.

Training now has a geometric meaning: find the bottom of the bowl. But a picture is not a proof. Is there always exactly one lowest point, or could some data set produce two pits, or a pit hidden outside the window we plotted? And where is the bottom?

## Why the surface is a bowl

For our four houses, completing the square answers both questions at once. Group the terms of $L$ that contain $b$: $b^2 + 5wb - 7b = b^2 + 2b\,(2.5w - 3.5)$, which is $(b + 2.5w - 3.5)^2$ minus $(2.5w - 3.5)^2$. Subtracting $(2.5w - 3.5)^2 = 6.25w^2 - 17.5w + 12.25$ from the remaining terms $7.5w^2 - 20.5w + 14.25$ leaves $1.25w^2 - 3w + 2 = 1.25\,(w - 1.2)^2 + 0.2$. So

$$
L(w, b) = (b + 2.5w - 3.5)^2 + 1.25\,(w - 1.2)^2 + 0.2.
$$

This is two squares plus a constant, and neither square can be negative, so $L \ge 0.2$ everywhere on the plane, with no window to worry about. Both squares vanish only when $w = 1.2$ and $b = 3.5 - 2.5 \times 1.2 = 0.5$. That is the single lowest point, and no other setting of the dials ties it.

The same computation works for any data. For data $(x_i, y_i)$ write $\bar x$ and $\bar y$ for the means, and

$$
S_{xx} = \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2, \qquad S_{xy} = \sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y), \qquad S_{yy} = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2.
$$

We also need the precise word for "bowl-shaped".

**Definition.** A function $L$ of two variables is **convex** if, for any two points $p$ and $q$ of the plane and any $s$ with $0 \le s \le 1$,

$$
L\bigl((1 - s)\,p + s\,q\bigr) \le (1 - s)\,L(p) + s\,L(q).
$$

It is **strictly convex** if the inequality is strict whenever $p \ne q$ and $0 < s < 1$.

The point $(1 - s)p + sq$ runs along the segment from $p$ to $q$ as $s$ goes from 0 to 1, and the right side is the height of the straight chord joining the surface above $p$ to the surface above $q$. So convexity says that between any two points the surface sags below the chord. A surface with two pits fails this, because the chord from one pit to the other passes under the ridge between them.

**Theorem.** Let $(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)$ be data in which the $x_i$ are not all equal, and let $L(w, b) = \frac1n \sum (wx_i + b - y_i)^2$. Then:

- $L(w, b) = (b + w\bar x - \bar y)^2 + \dfrac{S_{xx}}{n}\Bigl(w - \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\Bigr)^2 + \dfrac{1}{n}\Bigl(S_{yy} - \dfrac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}}\Bigr)$.
- $L$ has exactly one minimum point, at $w^* = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $b^* = \bar y - w^*\bar x$.
- $L$ is strictly convex.

**Proof.** (1) Write $u_i = x_i - \bar x$ and $v_i = y_i - \bar y$, so that $\sum u_i = \sum v_i = 0$. Then

$$
wx_i + b - y_i = (wu_i - v_i) + c, \qquad c = b + w\bar x - \bar y,
$$

and $c$ does not depend on $i$. Squaring and summing gives $\sum (wu_i - v_i)^2 + 2c\sum (wu_i - v_i) + nc^2$. The middle sum is $w\sum u_i - \sum v_i = 0$. The first sum is $S_{xx}w^2 - 2S_{xy}w + S_{yy}$, and since $S_{xx} > 0$ (the $x_i$ are not all equal) we can complete the square: it equals $S_{xx}(w - S_{xy}/S_{xx})^2 + S_{yy} - S_{xy}^2/S_{xx}$. Dividing everything by $n$ gives the formula.

(2) In the formula the last term is a constant, and the first two are squares with positive coefficients $1$ and $S_{xx}/n$. Their sum is at least 0, and equals 0 exactly when $w = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $b + w\bar x - \bar y = 0$.

(3) Take two different points $p$ and $q$ and let $(d_w, d_b) = q - p$, which is not $(0, 0)$. At the point $p + t\,(d_w, d_b)$ of the line through them, the error on house $i$ is $e_i + t\,(d_wx_i + d_b)$, where $e_i$ is the error at $p$. So along the line

$$
\varphi(t) = L\bigl(p + t\,(d_w, d_b)\bigr) = At^2 + Bt + C, \qquad A = \frac1n\sum (d_wx_i + d_b)^2.
$$

$A$ is a mean of squares, so $A \ge 0$, and $A = 0$ would force $d_wx_i + d_b = 0$ for every $i$. Because at least two of the $x_i$ differ, subtracting two of these equations gives $d_w = 0$ and then $d_b = 0$, which we excluded. So $A > 0$. Finally, for any quadratic $\varphi$ and any $0 < s < 1$, direct expansion gives

$$
\varphi(s) - \bigl[(1 - s)\,\varphi(0) + s\,\varphi(1)\bigr] = A\,(s^2 - s) = -A\,s\,(1 - s) < 0,
$$

since the terms in $B$ and $C$ cancel. As $\varphi(0) = L(p)$, $\varphi(1) = L(q)$ and $\varphi(s) = L((1 - s)p + sq)$, this is the strict inequality in the definition.

Part 3 has a visual meaning: cut the bowl along any straight line whatever, and the cross-section is a parabola that opens upward. The number $A$ is how sharply it curves.

[Figure 6, animation: Slicing the loss surface along straight lines through point A. Left: the slicing line on the map. Right: the loss along that line, plotted against the distance t along it. Whatever the direction, the slice is an upward parabola; its curvature A changes with direction but never reaches zero.]

**Key idea.** Training the linear model means minimizing $L(w, b) = \frac1n\sum (wx_i + b - y_i)^2$ over the two parameters. As long as the inputs are not all equal, $L$ is a strictly convex quadratic, so its surface is a bowl with exactly one lowest point, and that point is the best line.

## Where the bottom is

Part 2 of the theorem is a formula for the trained model. For the houses, $\bar x = 2.5$ and $\bar y = 3.5$; the deviations are $u = (-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)$ and $v = (-2, 0, 0, 2)$; so $S_{xx} = 5$ and $S_{xy} = 3 + 0 + 0 + 3 = 6$. Hence

$$
w^* = \frac{6}{5} = 1.2, \qquad b^* = 3.5 - 1.2 \times 2.5 = 0.5,
$$

and with $S_{yy} = 8$ the minimum loss is $\frac14(8 - 36/5) = 0.2$, agreeing with the direct calculation. This is the least-squares line of statistics: [the lesson on correlation and regression](@statistics/correlation-and-regression) derives the same slope $S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and intercept $\bar y - w^*\bar x$ by minimizing the sum of squared errors, which is $n$ times our mean and so has its minimum at the same place.

**Pause and try.** Use the trained model to answer the opening question: what does it predict for the house of 2500 square feet? And what price does it predict for 5000 square feet?

**Answer.** In our units the size is $x = 2.5$, so $\hat y = 1.2 \times 2.5 + 0.5 = 3.5$, or \$350,000. This is the mean price because $2.5$ is the mean size, and the best line always passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$, since $b^* = \bar y - w^*\bar x$. For $x = 5$ the model says $6.5$, or \$650,000. That prediction is an extrapolation beyond every house in the table, and nothing in the training guarantees that the straight-line pattern continues out there.

You might object that if a formula gives the answer, there is nothing left to train. But the formula belongs to this model and this loss. It exists because $L$ is quadratic in the parameters, and $L$ is quadratic because the model is linear in them and the loss squares the errors. Change either one, as we will when the model must [output a probability](@machine-learning/logistic-regression) or [contains several layers](@machine-learning/neural-networks), and no formula for the bottom is available. The picture survives: there is still a loss surface over the parameters, and training still means going downhill on it. [Gradient descent](@machine-learning/gradient-descent), the subject of the next lesson, finds the bottom using only the local slope, and it will be tested first on this bowl, where we know the right answer.

## Worked examples

**Worked example.** **A loss surface from scratch.** Three points: $(0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 4)$. Find $L(w, b)$, write it as a sum of squares, and find the best line.

The averages we need are: mean of $x^2$, $(0 + 1 + 4)/3 = 5/3$; mean of $x$, $1$; mean of $xy$, $(0 + 1 + 8)/3 = 3$; mean of $y$, $2$; mean of $y^2$, $(1 + 1 + 16)/3 = 6$. So

$$
L(w, b) = \tfrac53w^2 + 2wb + b^2 - 6w - 4b + 6.
$$

For the sum of squares, use the theorem. $\bar x = 1$, $\bar y = 2$, $u = (-1, 0, 1)$, $v = (-1, -1, 2)$, so $S_{xx} = 2$, $S_{xy} = 1 + 0 + 2 = 3$, $S_{yy} = 6$. Then $w^* = 1.5$, $b^* = 2 - 1.5 = 0.5$, and the minimum loss is $\frac13(6 - 9/2) = 0.5$:

$$
L(w, b) = (b + w - 2)^2 + \tfrac23\,(w - 1.5)^2 + 0.5.
$$

*Check.* The line $\hat y = 1.5x + 0.5$ predicts $0.5, 2, 3.5$, with errors $-0.5, 1, -0.5$, whose squares average $(0.25 + 1 + 0.25)/3 = 0.5$.

**Worked example.** **A model with one parameter.** Suppose we insist that a house of size zero costs nothing, and use the model $\hat y = wx$ on the four houses. What is the best $w$, and how much do we lose by giving up the intercept?

This is the slice $b = 0$ of the surface: $L(w) = 7.5w^2 - 20.5w + 14.25$. A quadratic $\alpha w^2 - \beta w + \gamma$ with $\alpha > 0$ is smallest at $w = \beta/(2\alpha)$, here $20.5/15 = 41/30 \approx 1.367$, where its value is $\gamma - \beta^2/(4\alpha) = 14.25 - 420.25/30 \approx 0.242$. The two-parameter model reaches $0.2$. On the data it was fitted to, the smaller model can never do better than the larger, because every line through the origin is also a line; here it does about 20% worse. Whether the larger model also predicts *new* houses better is a separate question, taken up in [the lesson on overfitting](@machine-learning/overfitting).

## When the bowl has no single bottom

The theorem assumed that the inputs are not all equal. Here is what happens without that. Suppose three houses of the same size, 2000 square feet, sold for $3$, $4$ and $5$. Every error is $2w + b - y_i$, which depends on the dials only through the combination $2w + b$, and

$$
L(w, b) = (2w + b - 4)^2 + \tfrac23.
$$

The loss is as small as possible, $2/3$, at every point of the line $2w + b = 4$. The surface is a trough with a flat floor, and infinitely many lines tie for best: every line through the point $(2, 4)$. The data say what a 2000 square foot house costs on average and nothing about how price changes with size. The surface is still convex, but not strictly: along the floor of the trough, the chord lies in the surface.

[Figure 7, image: Three houses of the same size. Left: three different lines through the mean price at that size, all with the same loss, 0.67. Right: the loss map is a trough with straight, parallel level curves at losses 2, 4 and 8, and the whole green line 2w + b = 4 is its floor. The three dots on it are the three lines on the left.]

The long thin valley on the map of the four real houses is a mild form of the same thing. Their sizes, 1 to 4, are all on one side of zero, so raising the intercept and lowering the slope nearly compensate. The valley will matter in the next lesson, because a method that feels its way downhill moves slowly along a nearly flat floor.

**Common mistake.** **Reading the loss as a typical miss.** A mean squared error of $0.2$ does not mean the predictions are off by $0.2$, that is, by \$20,000. The loss is an average of *squared* errors, in squared units. The errors of the best line are $0.2, -0.6, 0.6, -0.2$, and a fair summary of their size is $\sqrt{0.2} \approx 0.45$, about \$45,000.

## Stepping back

The hard step was a change in what we looked at. We started in the data plane, where the houses are points and the model is a line. The work happened in the plane of the parameters, where each *line* is a point and the data have been absorbed into a single function $L$. There, "which line is best?" becomes "where is this surface lowest?", and for the linear model with squared error the surface is a convex bowl whose bottom has a formula.

Later lessons keep that structure and change its parts: a different model, a different loss, more parameters. The surface stops being a bowl and the formula disappears, but model, loss and training keep their meanings.

**Check yourself.** For the four houses, $L(1, 1) = 0.25$ and the minimum of the loss is $L(1.2, 0.5) = 0.2$. Which statement is correct?
Answer: No straight line has loss below 0.2 on these data; a loss of 0 would need all four points on one line. $L$ is 0.2 plus two squares, and the squares are both zero only at $(1.2, 0.5)$.

**Recap.** - A model is a function with adjustable parameters. The linear model is $\hat y = wx + b$, with parameters $w$ (slope) and $b$ (intercept).
- A loss function turns a setting of the parameters into one number. The mean squared error is $L(w, b) = \frac1n\sum (wx_i + b - y_i)^2$.
- Training means searching for parameters with small loss. The search happens in the plane of parameters, where each point is a line and $L$ is a surface.
- If the $x_i$ are not all equal, $L$ equals two squares plus a constant, is strictly convex, and has exactly one minimum: $w^* = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$, $b^* = \bar y - w^*\bar x$.
- For the four houses, $L = (b + 2.5w - 3.5)^2 + 1.25(w - 1.2)^2 + 0.2$, and the best line is $\hat y = 1.2x + 0.5$. If all the $x_i$ were equal, the surface would be a trough and infinitely many lines would tie.

## Problems

The first three repeat the lesson's computations. The next two ask you to explain or combine. The last one extends the lesson.

**Problem 1.** For the four houses, compute the mean squared error of the line $\hat y = 1.5x$ directly from the errors, and then again from the formula $L(w, b) = 7.5w^2 + 5wb + b^2 - 20.5w - 7b + 14.25$.

**Solution.** The predictions are $1.5, 3, 4.5, 6$ and the errors are $0, -0.5, 1, 0.5$. The squares are $0, 0.25, 1, 0.25$ with mean $1.5/4 = 0.375$. From the formula with $w = 1.5$, $b = 0$: $7.5 \times 2.25 - 20.5 \times 1.5 + 14.25 = 16.875 - 30.75 + 14.25 = 0.375$.

**Problem 2.** For the data $(1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2)$, write $L(w, b)$ in expanded form, find the best line, and find the minimum loss.

**Solution.** The averages are: $x^2$: $14/3$; $x$: $2$; $xy$: $(1 + 6 + 6)/3 = 13/3$; $y$: $2$; $y^2$: $14/3$. So $L = \frac{14}{3}w^2 + 4wb + b^2 - \frac{26}{3}w - 4b + \frac{14}{3}$. For the minimum, $u = (-1, 0, 1)$ and $v = (-1, 1, 0)$, so $S_{xx} = 2$, $S_{xy} = 1$, $S_{yy} = 2$. Then $w^* = 0.5$, $b^* = 2 - 0.5 \times 2 = 1$, and the minimum loss is $\frac13(2 - \frac12) = 0.5$. Check: $\hat y = 0.5x + 1$ predicts $1.5, 2, 2.5$, with errors $0.5, -1, 0.5$ and mean square $(0.25 + 1 + 0.25)/3 = 0.5$.

**Problem 3.** Using $L(w, b) = (b + 2.5w - 3.5)^2 + 1.25(w - 1.2)^2 + 0.2$ for the houses: (a) recompute $L(1, 1)$. (b) Find every point on the valley floor $b = 3.5 - 2.5w$ whose loss is at most $0.25$. (c) What do those lines have in common on the data plot?

**Solution.** (a) $(1 + 2.5 - 3.5)^2 + 1.25 \times 0.04 + 0.2 = 0 + 0.05 + 0.2 = 0.25$. (b) On the valley floor the first square is zero, so the loss is $1.25(w - 1.2)^2 + 0.2 \le 0.25$, which gives $(w - 1.2)^2 \le 0.04$, that is $1 \le w \le 1.4$, with $b = 3.5 - 2.5w$ running from $1$ down to $0$. (c) The condition $b = 3.5 - 2.5w$ says $w \times 2.5 + b = 3.5$: each of these lines passes through the point of means $(2.5, 3.5)$. They are the lines through that point with slopes between 1 and 1.4. Point B of the lesson, $(1, 1)$, is one end of this range.

**Problem 4.** Let $e_i = w^*x_i + b^* - y_i$ be the errors of the best line. Show that $\sum e_i = 0$ and $\sum e_ix_i = 0$ for any data with the $x_i$ not all equal, and verify both for the houses.

**Solution.** In the notation of the proof, $e_i = (w^*u_i - v_i) + c$ with $c = b^* + w^*\bar x - \bar y = 0$. So $\sum e_i = w^*\sum u_i - \sum v_i = 0$. Next, $\sum e_ix_i = \sum e_i(u_i + \bar x) = \sum e_iu_i + \bar x\sum e_i = \sum (w^*u_i - v_i)u_i + 0 = w^*S_{xx} - S_{xy} = 0$, because $w^* = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$. For the houses the errors are $0.2, -0.6, 0.6, -0.2$: their sum is $0$, and $\sum e_ix_i = 0.2 - 1.2 + 1.8 - 0.8 = 0$. (With calculus: these two sums are, up to the factor $2/n$, the [partial derivatives](@multivariable-calculus/partial-derivatives-and-gradient) of $L$ with respect to $b$ and $w$, which vanish at the bottom of the bowl.)

**Problem 5.** A typing error records the price of house 4 as $9.5$ instead of $5.5$. Find the best line for the corrupted data and its prediction for the 2500 square foot house. Why does one bad entry move the line so much?

**Solution.** Now $\bar y = (1.5 + 3.5 + 3.5 + 9.5)/4 = 4.5$ and $v = (-3, -1, -1, 5)$, with $u = (-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)$ as before. $S_{xy} = 4.5 + 0.5 - 0.5 + 7.5 = 12$ and $S_{xx} = 5$, so $w^* = 2.4$ and $b^* = 4.5 - 2.4 \times 2.5 = -1.5$. The slope has doubled. The prediction at $x = 2.5$ is $2.4 \times 2.5 - 1.5 = 4.5$, a full \$100,000 above the earlier \$350,000. Two things make the entry so influential. The loss squares errors, so the old line's error of $-4.2$ on the bad point would contribute $17.64$ to the sum, far more than all other errors together, and the minimizer gives up accuracy on three houses to shrink that one term. And house 4 is at the end of the range of sizes, where pulling on the line tilts it most.

**Problem 6.** (Turning one dial at a time.) Start at the rule of thumb $(w, b) = (1, 0)$ and alternate two moves: (i) with $b$ fixed, set $w$ to the value that minimizes $L$; (ii) with $w$ fixed, set $b$ to the value that minimizes $L$. For the houses, find formulas for both moves, carry out two rounds, and prove that the slope converges to $1.2$.

**Solution.** Collect $L$ as a quadratic in $w$: $7.5w^2 + (5b - 20.5)w + \dots$, minimized at $w = (20.5 - 5b)/15$. As a quadratic in $b$: $b^2 + (5w - 7)b + \dots$, minimized at $b = (7 - 5w)/2 = 3.5 - 2.5w$. Round 1: $w = 20.5/15 \approx 1.3667$, then $b = 3.5 - 2.5 \times 1.3667 \approx 0.0833$; the loss is now about $0.2347$. Round 2: $w = (20.5 - 0.4167)/15 \approx 1.3389$, then $b \approx 0.1528$; the loss is about $0.2241$. For the proof, note that after move (ii) the point satisfies $b = 3.5 - 2.5w$. Substituting this into move (i) shows that each later round sends the slope $w$ to

$$
w' = \frac{20.5 - 5\,(3.5 - 2.5w)}{15} = \frac{3 + 12.5w}{15} = 0.2 + \tfrac56w.
$$

So $w' - 1.2 = \frac56(w - 1.2)$: each round after the first multiplies the distance of the slope from $1.2$ by $5/6$. After round 1 that distance is $41/30 - 1.2 = \frac16$, so after $k$ rounds it is $\frac16(5/6)^{k-1}$, which tends to 0, and then $b = 3.5 - 2.5w$ tends to $0.5$. The method works, but slowly: it needs about 13 rounds to cut the distance by a factor of ten, since $(5/6)^{13} \approx 0.093$. Solving exactly for one block of unknowns at a time is also how [k-means](@machine-learning/k-means-clustering) finds clusters.

# Gradient descent: learning by walking downhill

> Derive the gradient descent update from the tangent line, prove exactly which learning rates converge on a parabola, and watch it train a line on real data.

Series: Machine Learning (https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/machine-learning/)
Canonical: https://www.monocurl.com/monocurl-essays/machine-learning/gradient-descent/
Keywords: gradient descent, learning rate, how gradient descent works, step size too large, stochastic gradient descent, local minimum, saddle point, training a model

[Figure 1, animation: Gradient descent training a line on four house prices: 200 steps at learning rate 0.1, starting from the flat line \hat y = 3. On the right, the same run as a path over the loss map: a few zigzags across the valley, then a long slide along its floor to the lowest point.]

You are standing on a hillside in fog so thick that you cannot see your own feet. You want to reach the valley floor. What do you do?

Almost everyone gives the same answer: feel which way the ground slopes under your boots, take a step downhill, and repeat. It uses no map and no plan, only the slope at the one point where you stand. Yet it is how nearly every machine learning model is trained, including ones with billions of adjustable numbers. It also has a trap that the hillside story hides: take your steps a little too long, and each one carries you *higher* than the last, however carefully you measured the slope.

## The problem: a surface with no formula for its bottom

In [the previous lesson](@machine-learning/fitting-a-line) we fitted a line $\hat y = wx + b$ to four house sales. The model has two **parameters**, the slope $w$ and the intercept $b$. Its **loss**, the mean of the squared errors, is a function of those two numbers,

$$
L(w, b) = 7.5w^2 + 5wb + b^2 - 20.5w - 7b + 14.25,
$$

and **training** meant finding the $(w, b)$ where $L$ is smallest. Algebra found it: the loss surface is a bowl whose lowest point is at $w = 1.2$, $b = 0.5$, where $L = 0.2$.

The algebra worked because $L$ is quadratic. For the models of the coming lessons it is not, and no formula gives the lowest point. What we can still do, for any loss built from differentiable pieces, is evaluate two things at whatever parameters we currently hold: the loss, and its slope. That is the walker in the fog. We will turn "step downhill" into a precise rule, find out exactly when it works on a case simple enough to solve completely, and then run it on the house data, where we know the answer it should reach.

## One dial: stepping down a parabola

Start with one parameter and the simplest bowl there is, $f(w) = w^2$, whose lowest point is at $w = 0$. Suppose we are at $w = 2$. The [derivative](@calculus/what-is-a-derivative) $f'(w) = 2w$ is the slope of the graph, and $f'(2) = 4$ is positive: the curve rises to the right, so downhill is to the left.

How far should we step? A reasonable first rule: in proportion to the slope. Where the curve is steep we are probably far from the bottom and can afford a long step; where it is nearly flat we should tread carefully. Pick a positive number $\eta$ (the Greek letter eta) to set the proportion, and move from $w$ to $w - \eta f'(w)$.

Try $\eta = 0.1$. From $w = 2$ the slope is 4, so we move to $2 - 0.1 \times 4 = 1.6$. There the slope is $3.2$, so we move to $1.6 - 0.32 = 1.28$, then to $1.28 - 0.256 = 1.024$. The steps shrink as the slope does, and $w$ creeps toward 0.

**Pause and try.** Run the same rule from $w = 2$ with $\eta = 0.4$ for three steps. Then look at your numbers and at $2, 1.6, 1.28, 1.024$: in each run, what is the ratio of each $w$ to the one before?

**Answer.** With $\eta = 0.4$: $2 - 0.4 \times 4 = 0.4$, then $0.4 - 0.4 \times 0.8 = 0.08$, then $0.016$. Each value is $0.2$ times the previous one; in the first run the ratio was $0.8$. The larger $\eta$ gets to the bottom much faster.

So a bigger $\eta$ is better? Push it and see.

**Pause and try.** Run three steps from $w = 2$ with $\eta = 0.9$, and three more with $\eta = 1.1$. What is different about the two?

**Answer.** With $\eta = 0.9$: $2 - 0.9 \times 4 = -1.6$, then $-1.6 + 0.9 \times 3.2 = 1.28$, then $1.28 - 0.9 \times 2.56 = -1.024$. The step jumps clear over the bottom and lands on the opposite wall, but lower than where it started: each value is $-0.8$ times the last. With $\eta = 1.1$: $2 - 4.4 = -2.4$, then $-2.4 + 1.1 \times 4.8 = 2.88$, then $2.88 - 1.1 \times 5.76 = -3.456$. Each landing is *higher* than the take-off: the ratio is $-1.2$.

[Figure 2, steps: Gradient descent on f(w) = w^2 from w = 2 at four learning rates. Each hop goes from one value of w to the next, and the column on the right lists the values.]

  - step: Learning rate 0.1: the walker creeps down one side.
  - step: Learning rate 0.4: three steps and it is nearly at the bottom.
  - step: Learning rate 0.9: it jumps over the bottom every time, but lands lower.
  - step: Learning rate 1.1: every hop lands higher, and the walker leaves the plot.
Three questions come out of this experiment. Why step in proportion to the slope at all? Why does a downhill rule sometimes go uphill? And where exactly is the boundary?

## Where the rule comes from

The first two questions have one answer. The derivative $f'(w)$ is the slope of the tangent line at $w$, and near the point of tangency the curve and the line are close. So for a small change $\Delta$ in the parameter,

$$
f(w + \Delta) \approx f(w) + f'(w)\,\Delta.
$$

This is the **first-order approximation** of $f$ at $w$. It reduces our problem to a question about a straight line, and the answer is immediate: $f(w) + f'(w)\Delta$ is smaller than $f(w)$ for any $\Delta$ whose sign is opposite to that of $f'(w)$. The choice $\Delta = -\eta f'(w)$ with $\eta > 0$ always has that property, and it predicts

$$
f\bigl(w - \eta f'(w)\bigr) \approx f(w) - \eta\, f'(w)^2.
$$

The predicted change, $-\eta f'(w)^2$, is negative whenever the slope is not zero.

**Definition.** Let $f$ be a differentiable function of one real variable, $w_0$ a starting value and $\eta > 0$ a number called the **learning rate** (or step size). **Gradient descent** is the sequence

$$
w_{k+1} = w_k - \eta\, f'(w_k), \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots
$$

This is the rule we ran by hand. Notice what its justification does *not* say. The approximation is trustworthy only for small $\Delta$, and $\Delta = -\eta f'(w)$ is small only if $\eta$ is. The tangent line promises a drop of $\eta f'(w)^2$, and the more you ask of it the less the curve agrees.

[Figure 3, image: What the tangent line promises and what the curve delivers, for one step from w = 2 on f(w) = w^2. For \eta = 0.1 the two nearly agree. For \eta = 0.4 the line promises a height of -2.4, which the function never reaches. For \eta = 0.9 the promise is far below the plot.]

## Exactly which learning rates work

The third question can be answered completely for a parabola. On $f(w) = w^2$ every run multiplied $w$ by the same number at each step: $0.8$, $0.2$, $-0.8$, $-1.2$ for $\eta = 0.1, 0.4, 0.9, 1.1$. Those multipliers are all $1 - 2\eta$, because $w - \eta \cdot 2w = (1 - 2\eta)\,w$. The same happens for a parabola of any steepness.

**Theorem.** Let $f(w) = aw^2$ with $a > 0$, let $w_0 \ne 0$, and run gradient descent with learning rate $\eta > 0$. Then $w_k = (1 - 2a\eta)^k\,w_0$ for every $k$, and:

- if $0 < \eta < \dfrac{1}{2a}$, the $w_k$ keep the sign of $w_0$ and shrink to 0;
- if $\eta = \dfrac{1}{2a}$, then $w_1 = 0$: the minimum is reached in one step;
- if $\dfrac{1}{2a} < \eta < \dfrac1a$, the $w_k$ alternate in sign and shrink to 0;
- if $\eta = \dfrac1a$, then $w_k = (-1)^k w_0$: the walker bounces between two points forever;
- if $\eta > \dfrac1a$, the $w_k$ alternate in sign and $|w_k| \to \infty$.

In particular, gradient descent converges to the minimum if and only if $0 < \eta < \dfrac1a$.

**Proof.** Since $f'(w) = 2aw$, the update is $w_{k+1} = w_k - 2a\eta\,w_k = m\,w_k$ with $m = 1 - 2a\eta$. Applying this $k$ times gives $w_k = m^k w_0$, so $|w_k| = |m|^k\,|w_0|$. A power $|m|^k$ tends to 0 if $|m| < 1$, stays at 1 if $|m| = 1$, and grows without bound if $|m| > 1$. The sign of $w_k$ is constant if $m > 0$ and alternates if $m < 0$. It remains to read off $m$ from $\eta$. Because $a > 0$ and $\eta > 0$, we have $m < 1$ always. Then $m > 0$ exactly when $\eta < \frac{1}{2a}$ (case 1), $m = 0$ when $\eta = \frac{1}{2a}$ (case 2), $-1 < m < 0$ when $\frac{1}{2a} < \eta < \frac1a$ (case 3), $m = -1$ when $\eta = \frac1a$ (case 4), and $m < -1$ when $\eta > \frac1a$ (case 5). Convergence to 0 happens in cases 1 to 3 and in no other, which is the final claim.

For $f(w) = w^2$ we have $a = 1$, so the boundary is $\eta = 1$: the rate $0.9$ converged and $1.1$ did not. Shifting the parabola changes nothing: for $f(w) = a(w - w^*)^2 + c$ the update gives $w_{k+1} - w^* = (1 - 2a\eta)(w_k - w^*)$, so the same five cases describe the distance from $w^*$.

[Figure 4, image: The multiplier m = 1 - 2\eta for f(w) = w^2, as a function of the learning rate. Each step multiplies the distance from the minimum by m. Gradient descent converges exactly where m lies strictly between -1 and 1, that is, for 0 < \eta < 1.]

The boundary depends on $a$, which measures how sharply the parabola curves: its second derivative is $f'' = 2a$, so the condition reads $\eta < 2/f''$. A sharply curved bowl demands small steps. The reason is the error of the first-order approximation. For $f(w) = aw^2$ direct expansion gives

$$
f\bigl(w - \eta f'(w)\bigr) = f(w) - \eta\,(1 - a\eta)\,f'(w)^2,
$$

which is the tangent line's promise multiplied by $(1 - a\eta)$: nearly kept when $a\eta$ is small, reversed when $a\eta > 1$.

**Key idea.** Gradient descent repeats $w \leftarrow w - \eta f'(w)$: a step against the slope, in proportion to it. The step is justified by the tangent line, so it can only be trusted while the curve stays near that line. On $f(w) = aw^2$ it converges exactly when $0 < \eta < 1/a$.

## Two dials: the gradient

Now return to the houses and their two parameters. A function of two variables has two slopes at each point, one for each variable, called [partial derivatives](@multivariable-calculus/partial-derivatives-and-gradient): $\partial L/\partial w$ is the derivative of $L$ with respect to $w$ with $b$ held fixed, and $\partial L/\partial b$ the reverse. Together they form a vector, the **gradient**:

$$
\nabla L = \Bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\Bigr) = \bigl(15w + 5b - 20.5,\; 5w + 2b - 7\bigr).
$$

The first-order approximation now reads $L(w + \Delta_w, b + \Delta_b) \approx L(w, b) + \frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\Delta_w + \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\Delta_b$, and the last two terms are the [dot product](@linear-algebra/dot-product) of the gradient with the step $\Delta = (\Delta_w, \Delta_b)$. We want the step that makes it most negative. Since $\nabla L \cdot \Delta = |\nabla L|\,|\Delta| \cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors, a step of given length does best when $\cos\theta = -1$: when $\Delta$ points directly opposite to the gradient. Taking $\Delta = -\eta\,\nabla L$ predicts a change of $-\eta\,|\nabla L|^2$, as in one variable.

**Definition.** For a differentiable function $L$ of several parameters, **gradient descent** with learning rate $\eta > 0$ updates all the parameters at once by

$$
(w, b) \;\leftarrow\; (w, b) - \eta\,\nabla L(w, b), \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad w \leftarrow w - \eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}, \quad b \leftarrow b - \eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}.
$$

For a loss that is a mean over data, the gradient is computed from the errors. With $e_i = wx_i + b - y_i$ and $L = \frac1n\sum e_i^2$, the [chain rule](@calculus/product-and-chain-rule) gives

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac2n\sum e_i x_i, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \frac2n\sum e_i.
$$

Let us run it by hand. Start from the flat line $\hat y = 3$, which guesses \$300,000 for every house: $w = 0$, $b = 3$. The prices are $1.5, 3.5, 3.5, 5.5$ at sizes $1, 2, 3, 4$, so the errors are $1.5, -0.5, -0.5, -2.5$ and the loss is $(2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 6.25)/4 = 2.25$. Then $\sum e_i = -2$ and $\sum e_ix_i = 1.5 - 1 - 1.5 - 10 = -11$, so

$$
\nabla L(0, 3) = \bigl(\tfrac24(-11),\; \tfrac24(-2)\bigr) = (-5.5, -1).
$$

**Pause and try.** Take one step from $(0, 3)$ with learning rate $\eta = 0.05$. Where do you land, and what is the loss there? (Use $L = 7.5w^2 + 5wb + b^2 - 20.5w - 7b + 14.25$.)

**Answer.** $w = 0 - 0.05 \times (-5.5) = 0.275$ and $b = 3 - 0.05 \times (-1) = 3.05$. The loss is $7.5(0.0756) + 5(0.8388) + 9.3025 - 5.6375 - 21.35 + 14.25 \approx 1.326$. One step took the loss from $2.25$ to $1.33$. The tangent approximation promised a drop of $\eta\,|\nabla L|^2 = 0.05 \times 31.25 \approx 1.56$, and the surface delivered $0.92$.

The second step starts from $(0.275, 3.05)$, where the gradient is $(-1.125, 0.475)$, and lands at $(0.331, 3.026)$ with loss $1.269$. The first step lowered the loss by $0.92$ and the second by only $0.06$.

[Figure 5, steps: Gradient descent on the loss map of the four houses, starting from the flat line at (w, b) = (0, 3), for three learning rates. Both axes use the same scale, so each step leaves at a right angle to the level curve it starts on. The green dot is the minimum at (1.2, 0.5).]

  - step: At the start the gradient is (-5.5, -1). The arrow points the opposite way: downhill, straight across the level curves.
  - step: Learning rate 0.05, two steps. The first is a long hop to the valley floor and the second is already short.
  - step: Forty steps at 0.05. The path creeps along the valley floor.
  - step: Forty steps at 0.11. Every step overshoots the floor and lands on the opposite wall, a little lower each time.
  - step: Forty steps at 0.125. Now every overshoot lands higher than the last, and the path leaves the map.
## Why the valley is slow

The figure shows the cases of the one-dial theorem in two directions at once. Across the valley the surface is a steep parabola, and the walker behaves as in cases 1, 3 and 5. Along the valley it is a very shallow parabola, with a multiplier close to 1. Here is why the two directions can be treated separately.

The minimum is $p^* = (1.2, 0.5)$. Writing $\Delta_w = w - 1.2$ and $\Delta_b = b - 0.5$, the gradient formula becomes $\nabla L = (15\Delta_w + 5\Delta_b,\; 5\Delta_w + 2\Delta_b)$, as you can check by expanding. So the gradient is a [linear function](@linear-algebra/matrices-as-transformations) of the displacement from the minimum. Test two displacements. For $(\Delta_w, \Delta_b) = (0.322, -0.947)$, which points along the valley, the gradient is $(15 \times 0.322 - 5 \times 0.947,\; 5 \times 0.322 - 2 \times 0.947) = (0.095, -0.284)$, which is $0.299$ times the displacement, up to rounding. For $(0.947, 0.322)$, across the valley, the gradient is $(15.82, 5.38)$, which is $16.7$ times the displacement. In these two directions the gradient points along the displacement, so a step of gradient descent just rescales it:

$$
\text{along the valley: } \Delta \leftarrow (1 - 0.299\,\eta)\,\Delta, \qquad \text{across it: } \Delta \leftarrow (1 - 16.7\,\eta)\,\Delta.
$$

Every displacement is a sum of a piece along the valley and a piece across it, and because the gradient is linear the two pieces evolve independently, each obeying the one-dial theorem with $2a$ equal to $0.299$ or $16.7$. (The two directions are the [eigenvectors](@linear-algebra/eigenvectors) of the matrix of second derivatives of $L$. Such a perpendicular pair exists for every quadratic bowl, by the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices; here we verified it by multiplication.)

Convergence across the valley needs $|1 - 16.7\eta| < 1$, that is $\eta < 2/16.7 \approx 0.120$, which is why $0.11$ zigzagged home and $0.125$ blew up. But with $\eta$ capped near $0.12$, the multiplier along the valley is at best $1 - 0.299 \times 0.12 \approx 0.964$. With $\eta = 0.05$ it is $0.985$, and shrinking the valley error by a factor of 100 takes $\ln 0.01 / \ln 0.985 \approx 305$ steps. The steep direction sets the speed limit, and the shallow direction has to live with it.

There is a cure for this valley, and it is used everywhere. The valley exists because the sizes $1, 2, 3, 4$ all lie on one side of zero, so tilting the line and shifting it have overlapping effects. Subtract the mean size, $2.5$, from every size and fit $\hat y = w(x - 2.5) + c$ instead. This is the same family of lines, with $c = b + 2.5w$. Its loss is $1.25(w - 1.2)^2 + (c - 3.5)^2 + 0.2$, by the formula of the previous lesson, and the two directions now have $2a = 2.5$ and $2a = 2$: a nearly round bowl.

[Figure 6, image: The same data and the same starting line, before and after centering the sizes. Left: with raw sizes, 40 steps at learning rate 0.05 leave the walker far from the minimum. Right: with the mean size subtracted, the bowl is nearly round, a learning rate of 0.4 is safe, and 5 steps are enough.]

## Cheaper gradients: stochastic and mini-batch descent
